metadata.disclaimer: OSA's own analysis of BSI's Grundschutz++ (GS++), the Anwenderkatalog of 29 October 2026, against SP 800-53 Rev 5. Each clause is one of the catalogue's 652 base requirements, read with its enhancements, which are folded into it. The coverage figure estimates how much of the requirement and its enhancements the listed controls meet when put in place as written. GS++ sets out its own method for running an ISMS as well as security requirements, so coverage is lower for the steps of that method, such as the requirement package and the security levels, and for topics SP 800-53 leaves to the organisation, such as building plans. The requirement ids, uuids, security levels, modal verbs and German titles are BSI's. The English titles, rationale and gaps are OSA's. Check each requirement against BSI's own text before you use this mapping for compliance or audit.
metadata.applicability_note: Mandatory for the federal administration. Section 44(1) of the BSI Act (BSIG) requires the bodies of the federal administration to meet the minimum requirements in BSI's standards and IT-Grundschutz, in the versions BSI publishes as current, and gave BSI the task of modernising IT-Grundschutz. BSI's catalogue names that section as the norm it implements. For other organisations GS++ is a method they choose, and ISO 27001 certification on the basis of GS++ opens on 1 January 2027.

analysis.controls: SP 800-53 Rev 5.2.0 base controls, current ones only. An enhancement that addresses a requirement counts for its base control, and the rationale names it. OSA's rule for customer authentication changes no pair. KONF.11.1 and KONF.11.2 carry IA-08 for external participants from all three raters. BES.4.6 asks the organisation to agree how a supplier authenticates it, as the supplier's customer, and the raters each named a different control for that part (IA-08, IA-02 and SA-09), so none is listed for it. BER.5.8 asks for multi-factor authentication on interfaces reachable from outside, such as VPN access, and lists IA-02.
analysis.method: Each of the 652 base requirements was rated three times, independently, by AI models working from BSI's German text, with BSI's guidance where the wording left the scope open, and from the control statements. Each rater read a requirement together with its enhancements and rated them as one. No rater saw another's rating. The requirements were rated in five groups of practices, by three raters to a group. A control is listed for a requirement where at least two of the three ratings named it, or where OSA's house rule for policy clauses adds it. The coverage figure is the median of the three estimates of how much of the requirement and its enhancements an organisation would meet by putting the listed controls in place. The rationale and gaps were written after the controls were settled, from the raters' reasons and from the gaps at least two of them named.
analysis.agreement_measure: The Jaccard index of each two ratings: the pairs both named, divided by the pairs either named.
analysis.agreement_by_group_note: Each group had its own three ratings, A, B and C. The overall figures pool the ratings with the same letter across the five groups. By group, the index runs from 0.71 to 0.86.
analysis.coverage_agreement: The three coverage estimates for a requirement lie within 10 points of each other for 576 of the 652 requirements. They are 30 points or more apart for 5: BES.2.5, DLS.3.4, GEB.8.3, GEB.10.5 and DET.4.18.
analysis.pairs_note: The file lists 1,406 pairs over 243 controls: the 1,159 named by all three ratings, the 229 named by two and the 18 that OSA's rule for policy clauses adds to GC.5.1. Most requirements list one to three controls (593 of 652). GC.5.1 lists the most, 21, followed by KONF.12.1 with 7. Four requirements list none, because no control was named by two raters: BES.7.3, GEB.1.5, DET.4.7 and DET.4.18. Their coverage is 0. For BES.7.3 the median of the three estimates is 20 (0, 20, 20), from two raters who each named a different control, and with no control listed the file gives 0.

policy_rule.rule: OSA's house rule for policy clauses, set on 1 November 2026: a clause that asks for security policies in general lists PM-01 with every other family's -01 control, the set NIST's crosswalk gives ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.5.1, and PT-01 as well where it covers personal data.

clauses.note: The rule applies through GC.5.1.3 and GC.5.1.4, which ask for a security policy for the whole institution and for top management to authorise it. All three raters named PM-01, PM-06 and PM-09, so the 18 pairs come from the rule. The policy covers security as a whole, so PT-01 stays out.

analysis.not_mapped: Every base requirement is mapped. The 348 enhancements are folded into their base requirements, and each clause lists its enhancements' ids. BSI-Standard 300-1 describes the method and holds no requirements of its own beyond the catalogue's.

check_against_bsi_mapping.purpose: A check, not a source. No pair in this file comes from it.
check_against_bsi_mapping.how: BSI's mapping of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A to GS++ was joined with OSA's ISO/IEC 27001:2022 file, whose pairs rest on NIST's crosswalk, to give GS++ to SP 800-53 pairs. Enhancements count for their base requirement.

check_against_bsi_mapping.bsi_mapping_note: 96 entries map 93 Annex A controls to 365 GS++ references. 22 of those references name 19 ids that the catalogue of 29 October 2026 does not hold. The catalogue version of 29 July 2026, two days after the mapping's last change, did not hold them either, so the check leaves them out: BER.5.1.2, BER.6.8, DET.3.1.13, GC.10.2, GC.6.1.2, GC.6.1.3, GC.6.1.4, GC.7.1.3, GC.8.1.1, GC.8.1.1.1, GC.8.1.3, GC.8.1.4, GC.9.1.2, GC.9.1.3, GEB.5.4, PERF.1.1.1, PERF.5.1.4, PERF.6.1.3, PERF.7.1.
check_against_bsi_mapping.result: The chain reaches 244 of the 652 base requirements and names 1,711 pairs for them, about 7 a requirement. The ratings list 563 pairs for the same requirements, about 2.3 a requirement. 307 pairs are in both: 18% of the chain's and 55% of the ratings'. For 199 of the 244 requirements the two share at least one control. Where BSI calls the match equivalent, 31% of the chain's pairs are in the ratings. Using only the pairs NIST's crosswalk gives, the chain names 1,097 pairs for 239 requirements, and 216 of them are in the ratings.
check_against_bsi_mapping.reading: An Annex A control is broader than a GS++ requirement, and chaining gives every requirement BSI links to it all the controls mapped to that Annex A control. So the chain names about three times as many controls as the ratings, and holds just over half of the ratings' pairs for the same requirements.

clauses.title: Establishing and maintaining an ISMS
clauses.rationale: PM-01 sets up an organisation-wide security programme plan, reviewed and updated, which is the nearest equivalent of a documented ISMS. PM-31 keeps the programme maintained through a continuous monitoring strategy with response actions.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for an ISMS that follows the GS++ method through its plan-do-check-act cycle. Apply the method in full, using the programme plan and monitoring strategy as a base.

clauses.title: Approval of the ISMS
clauses.rationale: Under PM-01, a senior official accountable for the risk approves the security programme plan and its management controls. That matches authorisation by top management at the level of the whole programme.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks top management to authorise each defined ISMS procedure. SP 800-53 has the programme plan approved as a whole, so have top management sign off each procedure too.

clauses.title: Defining the organisation's external context
clauses.title_de: Festlegung des externen Kontextes der Institution
clauses.rationale: PM-16 runs a threat awareness programme that brings in the outside threat landscape through shared threat intelligence. PM-28 identifies and documents the assumptions and constraints that shape risk management, legal and regulatory ones included.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a systematic analysis of every external factor that bears on the ISMS, such as societal, economic, technological and environmental ones. Carry out that analysis and document it.

clauses.title: Defining the organisation's internal context
clauses.title_de: Festlegung des internen Kontextes der Institution
clauses.rationale: PM-07 documents the existing IT infrastructure and information systems in an enterprise architecture built with security in mind. PM-11 defines the mission and business processes and the protection needs that follow from them. PM-28 records internal assumptions, constraints, priorities and risk tolerance.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for an analysis of internal factors such as the organisation's strategy, values, structure and culture. Analyse these alongside the architecture and the business processes.

clauses.title: Compliance management: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: PM-01 gives an overview of the requirements the security programme must meet, compliance included. PM-28 documents the constraints on risk decisions, such as laws and contracts. PT-02 determines and documents the legal authority for processing personal data (GC.3.1.1). AT-03 trains the people responsible for their roles, which helps prevent breaches of obligations (GC.3.1.4).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a register of legal and contractual obligations, each with its priority, including an analysis of contracts (GC.3.1.3). Consult your legal and data protection functions as you build it (GC.3.1.2).

clauses.title: Analysis of external interested parties
clauses.rationale: PM-28 frames risk by documenting the constraints and priorities behind risk decisions. Those include what outside parties, such as regulators and customers, expect of the organisation.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to identify each external interested party, such as regulators, customers, service providers and the public, and their expectations. Then decide which of those expectations become binding obligations for the ISMS.

clauses.title: Analysis of internal interested parties
clauses.rationale: PM-11 derives protection needs from mission and business needs that the organisation's own stakeholders define. PM-28 frames risk in consultation with stakeholders across the organisation and records their priorities and risk tolerance.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to identify each internal interested party and their expectations of the ISMS. Examples are management, the security officer, staff and the works council. Document that analysis.

clauses.title: Setting information security objectives
clauses.title_de: Festlegung von Zielen für die Informationssicherheit
clauses.rationale: PM-06 develops outcome-based measures of performance, which make security goals measurable. PM-09 sets the organisation's overall risk management strategy (GC.5.1.1). PM-01 states management commitment and roles in a programme plan that a senior official approves. That plan serves as the security policy and its approval (GC.5.1.2 to GC.5.1.4). The policy controls of the other families, such as AC-01 and IR-01, supply the policy for each topic, under OSA's rule for policy clauses, which follows NIST's crosswalks.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for concrete, measurable security objectives drawn from the organisation's context. It also asks for a single security policy that top management authorises. Write both, with the programme plan and measures as a base.

clauses.title: Defining the scope of the ISMS
clauses.rationale: PL-02 has a security plan define each system's components and operating environment, which sets the system's boundary. The authorising official approves the plan before the system goes into use.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for one scope for the whole ISMS, naming the units and sites it covers and the areas it leaves out. Define it at organisation level, with the system boundaries inside it.

clauses.title: Procedure for information security classification
clauses.rationale: PM-11 defines the mission and business processes and the information protection needs that arise from them (GC.7.1.1). RA-02 categorises systems and the information they handle by impact, and the authorising official approves the result (GC.7.1.2).
clauses.gaps: GS++ classifies protection needs on two levels, normal and high, for each business process. SP 800-53 categorises systems and information types by impact, so apply the two levels to your processes as well.

clauses.title: Business processes with high protection needs
clauses.rationale: RA-03 assesses the likelihood and impact of threats to a system and the information it handles. That gives the dedicated risk analysis the requirement asks for on processes and information with high protection needs.
clauses.gaps: GS++ makes a high protection need the trigger for a dedicated risk analysis. SP 800-53 asks for a risk assessment of every system, so flag the processes with high needs and give each its own analysis.

clauses.title: Procedure for ISMS resource planning
clauses.rationale: PM-03 includes the resources the security programme needs in capital planning and makes them available. SA-02 determines and allocates the resources needed to protect each system.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for continuous, cost-effective planning of ISMS resources. Include staff and technical resources in that planning, alongside the budget.

clauses.title: Setting up a security organisation
clauses.rationale: PM-01 identifies and assigns roles and responsibilities in the programme plan (GC.9.1.1). PM-02 appoints a senior information security officer with the mission and resources to run the programme (GC.9.1.1.1). PM-29 appoints a senior accountable official for risk and sets up a risk executive function as a governing body. PM-13 defines the skills each security role needs (GC.9.1.1.4). AC-05 separates duties to avoid conflicts of interest (GC.9.1.1.3).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for an independent security officer who reports directly to top management and has a right of direct access to them (GC.9.1.1.1, GC.9.1.1.1.2). It also asks for a deputy for every relevant ISMS role (GC.9.1.1.2).

clauses.title: Defining a procedure for communication management
clauses.rationale: PM-01 reflects in the programme plan the coordination among the internal entities responsible for security. PM-15 sets up standing contact with security groups and associations for external exchange (GC.10.1.1). SA-03 builds security roles and risk management into the system life cycle, so security staff take part in projects at defined stages (GC.10.1.2).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for one procedure that sets who communicates what, when, with whom and how, inside the organisation and outside it. Include the supervisory authorities and your contacts there.

clauses.title: Document control
clauses.rationale: PM-01 has the programme plan reviewed and updated, and protects it from unauthorised disclosure and change. SI-12 manages and retains information, policies and plans included, in line with laws and operational requirements.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for control of each ISMS document across its whole life, with metadata, versioning, release and withdrawal. Set up one document control process for all ISMS documents.

clauses.title: Governance: risk management method
clauses.rationale: PM-09 sets an organisation-wide risk management strategy, with accepted assessment methods, and applies it consistently. PM-28 frames risk with assumptions, constraints, priorities and risk tolerance drawn from the organisation's context. RA-01 puts the method in writing as risk assessment policy and procedures.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the method to take in the business process analysis and the interested parties as well as the context. Name both as inputs to your method.

clauses.title: Defining and bounding the information domain
clauses.rationale: PL-02 has a security plan define each system's components, business context, environment and connections, which together set its boundary. PM-05 keeps an inventory of the organisation's systems, which supports a traceable decision on which systems are in scope.
clauses.gaps: GS++ draws the information domain around people, sites, buildings and outsourced parts as well as systems. SP 800-53 draws a boundary around each system, so add the other elements yourself.

clauses.title: Documenting external interfaces
clauses.rationale: CA-03 documents the interface characteristics and security requirements of each information exchange. PL-02 describes the system's dependencies on and connections to other systems. SA-09 assigns oversight and responsibilities for external system services, the organisational interface to outsourced processes.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for every interface to external processes, organisational and infrastructural ones included. SP 800-53 covers the interfaces between systems and services, so document the other kinds alongside them.

clauses.title: Creating a requirement package
clauses.rationale: PL-10 selects a control baseline for the system, the counterpart of building a requirement package. PL-11 tailors that baseline, scoping controls in or out with a reason and adding new ones (STM.2.1.5 to STM.2.1.7). PL-02 records the selected controls and the reason for each tailoring decision. CM-08 captures the assets the requirements apply to (STM.2.1.2).
clauses.gaps: GS++ assigns each asset to target object categories and models their requirements onto it (STM.2.1.3, STM.2.1.4). Categories pass down the asset hierarchy, and a consolidation check ends the step. Follow the GS++ method for these steps.

clauses.title: Reviewing the assigned security level
clauses.rationale: PL-10 selects a control baseline by impact level, which sets the initial level of protection. PL-11 tailors the baseline to the organisation's own conditions, the counterpart of revisiting the security level when the context changes.
clauses.gaps: GS++ sets a security level for each requirement, either normal (state of the art) or elevated. SP 800-53 sets protection through baselines and enhancements, so review each requirement's level when the context changes.

clauses.title: Carrying out the risk analysis
clauses.rationale: RA-03 has the organisation conduct and document a risk assessment and update it when conditions change. That delivers the risk analysis the GS++ method calls for, such as for high protection needs or requirements left unimplemented.
clauses.gaps: GS++ sets the triggers for a risk analysis. They are a high protection need, a lowered security level, an unimplemented requirement and an asset GS++ leaves uncovered. SP 800-53 asks for a risk assessment of every system, so watch for these triggers yourself.

clauses.title: Setting requirement parameters
clauses.rationale: PL-11 includes assigning values to organisation-defined control parameters as part of tailoring, which is what setting GS++ parameters does. PL-02 records in the security plan how each control is implemented, including the values chosen.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Determining the implementation status
clauses.rationale: CA-02 assesses controls at a set frequency to find whether they are implemented correctly. CA-07 adds ongoing control assessments as part of continuous monitoring. PL-02 records which controls are in place and which are planned.
clauses.gaps: GS++ gives each requirement a yes or no status. A requirement counts as implemented once every requirement it depends on is implemented too, so apply that rule when you record status.

clauses.title: Assessing the residual risk
clauses.rationale: RA-03 determines the likelihood and impact of harm, including harm from controls still missing, which gives the residual risk. RA-07 decides how to treat findings in line with risk tolerance, including whether to accept the risk. CA-06 has the authorising official accept the residual risk before operation.
clauses.gaps: GS++ suggests consolidating the residual risk from requirements left unimplemented, so top management can follow it. Prepare that summary for top management.

clauses.title: Implementation planning
clauses.rationale: CA-05 documents the planned remediation of weaknesses and missing controls in a plan of action and milestones. PM-04 runs an organisation-wide process that keeps those plans developed and maintained.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to look for measures that meet several requirements at once. Build that search into your implementation planning.

clauses.title: Implementation planning: prioritising measures
clauses.rationale: PM-04 reviews plans of action against the risk management strategy and organisation-wide priorities for risk response. RA-07 responds to findings in line with the organisation's risk tolerance, which gives a risk-based order.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to rank measures by their dependencies and the resources available as well as by risk. Add both criteria to your prioritisation.

clauses.title: Naming those responsible for implementation
clauses.rationale: CA-05 documents each planned remediation action in a plan of action and milestones. That plan is the usual place to name the owner of each action.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to name a person or team responsible for each requirement still open. Add an owner to every action in your plan of action and milestones.

clauses.title: Setting implementation deadlines
clauses.rationale: CA-05 sets milestones in the plan of action, which give target dates for each remediation action. PM-04 keeps those plans and their milestones maintained and reported across the organisation.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a realistic target date for each measure. Track those dates and act when one is missed.

clauses.title: Authorising exceptions
clauses.rationale: Under CA-06, a senior official accepts risk when authorising a system, which covers approving deviations. RA-07 allows risk to be accepted, with a justification, in line with the organisation's risk tolerance.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a general exception process for any obligation, with a named person or role who approves each exception. Set that process up alongside system authorisation.

clauses.title: Documenting exceptions
clauses.rationale: PL-02 has the security plan record the reason for each tailoring decision. That documents why a control is scoped out or adjusted, which covers exceptions to the control baseline.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to document every approved exception with its reason, for any obligation. A ticket system or configuration database can hold that record.

clauses.title: Tracking implementation progress
clauses.rationale: CA-05 updates the plan of action and milestones from assessment and monitoring findings as remediation proceeds. PM-04 runs a process that keeps those plans maintained and reported, which tracks progress across the organisation.
clauses.gaps: GS++ recommends tracking progress with key performance indicators. Define indicators for the implementation plan and report against them.

clauses.title: Updating the implementation plan
clauses.rationale: CA-05 updates the plan of action and milestones at a set frequency, using findings from assessments, audits and monitoring. PM-04 keeps those plans maintained as an ongoing, organisation-wide process.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Maintaining compliance during implementation
clauses.title_de: Wahrung von Compliance in der Umsetzung
clauses.rationale: CA-02 checks that controls meet the established security and privacy requirements, which include legal ones. CA-07 keeps assessing controls while measures go in, and CA-07(04) adds compliance monitoring.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a procedure that checks compliance with legal and contractual obligations while measures are put in place. Add those obligations to your checks, for example with checklists or audits.

clauses.title: Procedure for continuous improvement
clauses.rationale: PM-01 reviews and updates the programme plan at a set frequency and after defined events. PM-31 sets response actions to the results of monitoring and assessment. PM-04 turns the resulting findings into actions that plans of action track to completion.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a procedure to improve the ISMS as a whole, on a continuing basis. Build that procedure on top of the plan reviews and monitoring.

clauses.title: Handling nonconformities
clauses.rationale: CA-05 records each weakness found in assessments and audits, with its planned correction. CA-07 correlates and analyses monitoring results, and its trend analyses (CA-07(03)) can show recurring problems. IR-04 feeds lessons learned from incidents back into procedures to prevent recurrence.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a method that finds the root cause of each nonconformity and checks whether it could recur. Apply it to every nonconformity, whatever its source.

clauses.title: Adapting the ISMS after nonconformities
clauses.rationale: PM-01 reviews and updates the security programme plan after defined events, such as audit findings or recurring nonconformities. Each of those updates is a point at which to adapt the programme.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to review regularly whether nonconformities point to systemic weaknesses that call for changes to the ISMS. Add that question to each review of the programme plan.

clauses.title: Identifying opportunities for improvement
clauses.rationale: PM-31 correlates and analyses assessment and monitoring information as part of the continuous monitoring strategy. That analysis, with its response actions, can bring opportunities for improvement to light.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a method that looks for improvement opportunities proactively, ahead of any problem, and weighs the pros and cons of each. Set up that method alongside the monitoring.

clauses.title: Corrective measures
clauses.rationale: CA-05 sets out the remediation that corrects weaknesses and deficiencies in a plan of action and milestones. RA-07 responds to the findings in line with the organisation's risk tolerance.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for corrective measures that remove the root cause of each fault as well as its symptoms. Trace each finding to its root cause before you plan the fix.

clauses.title: Improvement measures
clauses.rationale: PM-04 documents and prioritises actions in plans of action and milestones, where improvement measures can be tracked. PM-31 sets response actions that follow from the analysis of monitoring and assessment results.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for proactive measures that take up improvement opportunities, chosen by weighing their pros and cons. Plan these alongside the remediation of weaknesses.

clauses.title: Improvement plan: prioritising measures
clauses.rationale: CA-05 schedules corrective actions in a plan of action with milestones. PM-04 reviews those plans against the organisation-wide priorities for risk response actions, which sets their order.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Reviewing the improvement achieved
clauses.rationale: CA-02 assesses whether controls operate as intended and produce the desired outcome. CA-07 keeps checking their effectiveness over time through ongoing assessments at set frequencies.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Evaluating the improvement achieved
clauses.rationale: PM-06 develops measures of performance that compare effectiveness before and after a change. CA-07 monitors over time, and its trend analyses (CA-07(03)) show whether the security level is improving. PM-31 analyses organisation-wide metrics to show the trend.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to weigh the pros and cons of the improvement achieved. Add that weighing to each evaluation.

clauses.title: Handling compliance violations
clauses.rationale: IR-06 has staff report suspected incidents, policy violations included, within a set time. IR-04 investigates and handles them, with documented follow-up. IR-08(01) adds a process to assess harm to affected individuals and decide whether to notify them of a breach. PS-08 sets a formal sanctions process for people who break security policies.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a procedure that defines and categorises compliance violations, legal and contractual ones included, and respects the rights of the people affected. Extend incident handling to cover them.

clauses.title: ISMS performance evaluation: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: CA-01 sets the policy and procedures for assessment, authorisation and monitoring, which are the rules for measuring and evaluating. PM-06 tracks and reports measures of performance. PM-31 sets organisation-wide metrics, monitoring frequencies, analysis and reporting.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Evaluating the implementation plan
clauses.rationale: CA-05 updates the plan of action and milestones at a set frequency from assessment and monitoring results. PM-04 reviews those plans against the risk management strategy and priorities, and reports on them.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the review to check that each measure meets its deadline and is correct in content. Add both checks to your regular review of the plan.

clauses.title: Keeping the requirements up to date
clauses.rationale: PL-02 reviews the security plans, with their requirements and controls, at a set frequency and updates them when the system or its environment changes. RA-03 updates the risk assessment on significant changes, such as new threats.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to recheck the modelling of the requirement package regularly, usually once a year. Follow the GS++ method for that check.

clauses.title: Reviewing compliance with obligations
clauses.rationale: CA-02 assesses controls against the established security requirements at a set frequency. CA-07 adds ongoing monitoring, including checks after changes, and CA-07(04) adds compliance monitoring.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for regular and event-driven checks against your documented legal and contractual obligations. Add those obligations to the scope of your assessments.

clauses.title: Building and maintaining an audit programme
clauses.rationale: CA-01 sets the assessment policy and procedures behind the audit process. CA-02 selects assessors, plans each assessment's scope and procedures and runs it at a set frequency (PERF.3.1.1, PERF.3.1.4). CA-02(01) adds independent assessors (PERF.3.1.3). PM-14 keeps testing and monitoring plans reviewed against the risk strategy, which makes the programme risk-based (PERF.3.1.2).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to build and maintain one or more audit programmes. Manage each programme as a whole, in the way ISO 19011 describes, over and above single assessments.

clauses.title: Documenting audit results
clauses.rationale: CA-02 produces a report for each assessment, which serves as the audit report. It also gives the results to defined individuals or roles, the stakeholders who need them (PERF.3.2.2).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for one rating scheme for all audit findings (PERF.3.2.1). Define the scheme and use it in every assessment report.

clauses.title: Suitability review of the ISMS
clauses.rationale: PM-04 reports on plans of action, which gives the status of follow-up actions and the implementation plan (PERF.4.1.1, PERF.4.1.7). PM-06 reports the results of measures of performance. PM-31 reports security status to defined personnel at a set frequency. PM-26 collects complaints and feedback from individuals about security practices (PERF.4.1.6).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a management report on the suitability, adequacy and effectiveness of the ISMS. Include changed conditions and prioritised proposals with realistic effort estimates (PERF.4.1.2, PERF.4.1.9).

clauses.title: Report to top management
clauses.rationale: PM-06 reports the results of measures of performance. PM-31 reports security and privacy status to defined personnel at a set frequency, which can include top management.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names top management as the recipient. SP 800-53 lets you choose the recipients, so name top management among them.

clauses.title: Monitoring methods and tools
clauses.rationale: PM-31 sets an organisation-wide continuous monitoring strategy. CA-07 carries it out for each system with set metrics and frequencies, and CA-07(06) adds automation. SI-04 deploys monitoring tools that detect attacks and unauthorised use. RA-05 scans for vulnerabilities at a set frequency.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Risk management: methods to a recognised standard
clauses.rationale: PM-09 sets an organisation-wide risk management strategy, with accepted methods, and applies it consistently. PM-28 frames the context the methods use, such as assumptions, constraints, priorities and risk tolerance. RA-01 puts the methods in writing as risk assessment policy and procedures.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for methods that follow a recognised standard, such as ISO 27005, ISO 31000, BSI Standard 200-3 or NIST SP 800-30. Record the standard you chose.

clauses.title: Risk owner
clauses.rationale: CA-06 makes a senior official the authorising official, who is accountable for a system and accepts its risk. PM-10 designates individuals for defined roles in the risk management process. PM-29 appoints a senior accountable official for risk management and sets up a risk executive function.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for an owner for each risk, with the authority to decide how it's treated. SP 800-53 assigns risk acceptance per system, so name an owner for every risk you record.

clauses.title: Approval of risk management
clauses.rationale: Under PM-01, a senior official accountable for risk approves the programme plan, which describes the risk management roles. PM-09 sets the organisation-wide risk management strategy and its methods. PM-28 documents and distributes the risk tolerance and criteria. PM-29 puts a senior accountable official in charge of risk management.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks top management to authorise the risk management procedures, role definitions and criteria themselves. Have top management sign them off and keep a record of the approval.

clauses.title: Approval of implementation planning
clauses.rationale: CA-05 sets out the plan of action and milestones, the implementation plan for remediation, which forms part of the authorisation package. CA-06 has the authorising official accept the residual risk and authorise operation on that basis.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks each risk owner to authorise the implementation plan. Get that sign-off from the risk owners as well as from the authorising official.

clauses.title: Information and assets: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: CM-01 sets configuration management policy and procedures, which govern the component inventory. MA-01 does the same for maintenance, and MP-01 for media protection, covering marking, storage, transport and sanitisation. Each documents its policy, gives it to the roles that need it and names an official to manage it (ASST.1.1.1 to ASST.1.1.3). SI-12 manages and retains information through its life cycle, in line with laws and policies.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for one set of procedures and rules for information and related assets across their whole life cycle. SP 800-53 spreads this over several control families, so draw their policies together under one process.

clauses.title: Information and assets: regular review
clauses.rationale: CM-01, MA-01 and MP-01 review and update the configuration management, maintenance and media protection policies and procedures. Each does so at a set frequency and after events the organisation defines.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Inventory of information
clauses.rationale: CM-08 keeps an inventory of system components, and CM-08(04) names the people responsible for them (ASST.2.1.1). CM-12 documents where the organisation processes and stores defined information, and who has access to it. PM-05 keeps an inventory of organisational systems, and PM-05(01) adds one for systems that process personal data.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for an inventory of the categories of information the organisation holds, such as customer names and bank details. It also asks for a person or role responsible for each category. Add both to your inventory.

clauses.title: Inventory of systems
clauses.rationale: CM-08 keeps an inventory of system components with details such as an identifier, and CM-08(08) tracks their location. CM-08(03) detects unauthorised components (ASST.2.2.1). PM-05 keeps the inventory of organisational systems up to date. SI-04 detects unauthorised local, network and remote connections (ASST.2.2.1).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Inventory of applications
clauses.rationale: CM-08 lists software components with details such as version, and CM-08(02) keeps the list current by automated means (ASST.2.3.2.1). CM-10 tracks licences and licensed use. CM-07(05) lets only authorised software run, and CM-11 governs what users may install (ASST.2.3.1). SR-04 documents the provenance of components and their data, the job a software bill of materials (SBOM) does (ASST.2.3.2).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for an SBOM for each application. SR-04 records provenance, which covers part of that, so produce the SBOM itself and keep it with the inventory.

clauses.title: Data classification
clauses.rationale: RA-02 categorises the system and the information it processes, stores and transmits by impact level. The impact level states how much protection that information needs.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the organisation to put each set of data into a protection class, such as public, internal or confidential. RA-02 works at the level of systems and information types, so set up a classification scheme for the data itself.

clauses.title: Usage agreements for information and assets
clauses.rationale: PL-04 sets rules of behaviour for using information and systems, and users acknowledge them before they get access. PS-06 has users sign access agreements, such as acceptable use and non-disclosure agreements, before access. AC-21 helps users decide whether a sharing partner may receive information, so they share it on a need-to-know basis (ASST.3.1.1).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Removal of unneeded residual data and metadata
clauses.title_de: Entfernung nicht erforderlicher Rest- oder Zusatzdaten
clauses.rationale: AC-04(25) sanitises data as it passes between security domains, to stop sensitive information spilling across. SI-12(01) limits the personal data elements the organisation processes to those it needs.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the organisation to remove unneeded residual data and metadata, such as author names or location, from all its information. Set that up yourself, for example with automated filters and a manual check.

clauses.title: Labelling of information
clauses.rationale: AC-16 attaches security attributes to information in storage, processing and transmission, and AC-16(05) shows them in readable form on output. MP-03 marks system media with distribution limits and handling caveats. PE-22 marks hardware components with the impact level of the information they may process.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Labels on IT systems free of confidential data
clauses.rationale: SC-38 uses operations security to protect information an adversary could exploit, such as user identities. That extends to the details a label on an IT system shows.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for labels on IT systems to leave out confidential details, such as the assigned staff member, site, network structure or department. Check physical labels and device names against that rule.

clauses.title: Tainting of data
clauses.rationale: SI-20 embeds data or capabilities in systems to detect the exfiltration of organisational data. That is the tainting GS++ describes, which makes data recognisable when it turns up elsewhere.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Verification of information against other sources
clauses.rationale: SI-22 identifies alternative sources of information and uses them when the primary source is corrupted. AU-06(03) and (05) correlate audit records across repositories and with other sources, which checks security events against further information.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a check of important information against a second, independent source, which helps spot false alarms. Choose the information that needs it and set up the check.

clauses.title: Pseudonymisation before sharing
clauses.rationale: SI-19 de-identifies datasets by removing or replacing the elements that identify people. SI-19(04) masks, encrypts, hashes or replaces direct identifiers, which is what pseudonymisation does.
clauses.gaps: SI-19 covers personal data. GS++ also asks for pseudonymisation of other information before the organisation shares it, such as internal IP ranges. Apply the same methods to that information.

clauses.title: Anonymisation before sharing
clauses.rationale: SI-19 de-identifies datasets by removing the elements that identify people. SI-19(05) and (06) add statistical disclosure control and differential privacy, which make it hard to trace data back to a person.
clauses.gaps: SI-19 covers personal data. GS++ also asks for anonymisation of other information before the organisation shares it, such as system configurations or account details. Apply the same methods there.

clauses.title: Keeping data up to date
clauses.rationale: SI-18 checks personal data for accuracy and timeliness and corrects or deletes outdated records. SI-21 refreshes defined information at set frequencies or generates it on demand.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the organisation to keep all its data up to date, for example by comparing it with its sources. SI-18 does this for personal data. SI-21 refreshes information to limit exposure, so add an accuracy check for other data.

clauses.title: Authorisation of data locations
clauses.rationale: CM-12 documents where the organisation processes and stores defined information, and records changes of location. SA-09(05) restricts processing and storage by external services to defined locations. PE-17 sets and documents the alternate work sites staff may use, such as mobile working.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a named person or role to authorise the permitted locations for each category of data. Assign that approval yourself, and record it with the locations these controls document.

clauses.title: Authorisation of systems that process data
clauses.rationale: CA-06 has a senior official authorise each system to operate, and so to process its information. AC-19 authorises mobile devices to connect, and AC-20 sets terms for external systems, with AC-20(03) restricting privately owned devices. CM-07(09) allows only authorised hardware, and MP-07 restricts types of media such as USB drives (ASST.3.11.1).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the organisation to set, for each category of data, which systems and peripherals may process it. Draw up a list of permitted systems for each category, for example keeping highly confidential data on desktop devices.

clauses.title: Authorisation of people or organisations to access data
clauses.rationale: AC-02 approves accounts and authorises access on the basis of a valid authorisation and intended use. AC-03 enforces the approved authorisations for logical access. AC-06 grants each user only the access their assigned tasks need.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Storage of physical assets
clauses.rationale: MP-04 physically controls system media and stores them securely within controlled areas. That covers the media among the physical assets administrators keep in store.
clauses.gaps: MP-04 covers media. GS++ asks administrators to keep all unissued physical assets, such as spare devices, in a designated store, for example a locked room or cabinet. Extend the storage rules to those assets.

clauses.title: Reserve of physical assets
clauses.rationale: MA-06 obtains maintenance support or spare parts within a set time of a failure. A reserve of spare devices is one way to meet that time.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a reserve of spare devices that covers expected demand until the next order arrives and goes into service. Size it from past demand, adjusted for changes such as a growing number of users.

clauses.title: Loan pool of physical assets
clauses.rationale: CM-02(07) issues specially configured devices to staff who travel to locations the organisation sees as high risk. Those devices act as a loan pool for that kind of trip.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for enough loan devices to cover other occasions too, such as events or security incidents. Size the pool from a forecast of demand and keep it beyond the travel case.

clauses.title: Authorisation of interfaces for information exchange
clauses.rationale: CA-03 approves and manages the exchange of information with other systems through agreements. CA-09 authorises and documents internal system connections. These cover technical interfaces, such as an API or encrypted cloud storage.
clauses.gaps: GS++ also counts physical channels as interfaces, such as post or regular meetings in a protected place. Have a named person or role authorise those channels too.

clauses.title: Confidentiality and integrity in transport
clauses.rationale: SC-08 protects the confidentiality and integrity of information in transmission, and SC-08(01) uses cryptography to do it. MP-05 protects and controls media during transport outside controlled areas and keeps them accounted for.
clauses.gaps: GS++ also covers the physical transport of whole systems. MP-05 protects the media inside them, so add measures for the device itself, such as tamper-evident packaging or keeping it on your person.

clauses.title: Authorisation of publications
clauses.rationale: AC-22 designates who may post information on publicly accessible systems. It reviews the content for nonpublic information before it goes up.
clauses.gaps: AC-22 covers publicly accessible systems. GS++ asks a named person or role to approve every publication, such as press releases and research papers. Apply the same approval to those channels.

clauses.title: Proof of receipt
clauses.rationale: AU-10 provides evidence that a recipient received a message, for example through digital message receipts. The sender can then show the message arrived if this is ever disputed.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Agreements on information exchange
clauses.rationale: CA-03 approves and manages information exchange through agreements, such as interconnection or non-disclosure agreements. Each agreement documents the security requirements for the information exchanged.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Documenting maintenance needs
clauses.rationale: MA-02 schedules and documents maintenance in line with manufacturer specifications and organisational requirements. MA-06 defines the components that need timely maintenance, and MA-06(01) sets intervals for preventive maintenance.
clauses.gaps: GS++ also asks for documented maintenance needs for the infrastructure that systems depend on, such as power and cooling. Record those needs alongside the system components.

clauses.title: Managed maintenance
clauses.rationale: MA-02 schedules and performs maintenance in line with manufacturer specifications. MA-06(01) adds preventive maintenance at set intervals, and MA-06(02) adds predictive maintenance.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Authorisation of maintenance
clauses.rationale: MA-02 approves and monitors all maintenance, and approves the removal of components for off-site repair. MA-04 does the same for remote (nonlocal) maintenance.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Handling maintenance as changes and tests
clauses.rationale: CM-03 puts changes made during maintenance through configuration change control. CM-04 analyses each change for its security impact before it goes ahead.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Maintenance windows
clauses.rationale: MA-02 schedules maintenance in advance. With a schedule in place, the organisation can tell users ahead of time when systems will be unavailable.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the organisation to tell users in advance how long a maintenance outage will last and what it affects, such as applications or networks. Send that notice before each maintenance window.

clauses.title: Maintenance by external parties
clauses.rationale: MA-05 has authorised staff with the needed skills supervise maintenance personnel who lack the required access authorisations. MA-05(01) adds escorts for them, which covers unvetted external technicians.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Documentation of maintenance
clauses.rationale: MA-02 keeps maintenance records with content the organisation defines, such as the date, the components, the people involved and the work done. MA-04 keeps records of remote (nonlocal) maintenance too.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Loss of assets
clauses.rationale: IR-06 has staff report suspected incidents, such as a lost or stolen device. IR-04 handles the loss as an incident, with containment and recovery. MP-06(08) purges or wipes information remotely from a lost device.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a set procedure for lost or stolen assets that names each step and who is responsible for it. Write that procedure yourself, building on the incident handling these controls describe.

clauses.title: Return of lost assets
clauses.rationale: SR-10 inspects systems or components for tampering, for example when they have been outside the organisation's control. SI-07 verifies the integrity of software, firmware and information, which detects unauthorised changes before the device goes back into use.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a set procedure for assets that come back after going missing, to check them before they return to use. Write that procedure yourself, using these inspections as its checks.

clauses.title: Conformity check on return of assets
clauses.rationale: SR-10 inspects returned systems or components for physical and logical tampering. CM-02(07) applies defined controls to devices when their users return from travel.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for one check on return that the asset still meets its requirements, for example an untampered device that still gets security updates. Combine these controls into that single check.

clauses.title: Reset to initial state on return
clauses.rationale: CM-02 restores the system to its documented baseline configuration, which gives the defined starting state. MP-06 sanitises media before reuse, for example by clearing, purging or cryptographic erase, which deletes data left over from use.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Uninstalling unneeded applications
clauses.rationale: CM-07 configures systems to provide only the capabilities they need. CM-07(01) reviews systems at a set frequency and removes unnecessary software and services.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Retention and deletion periods
clauses.rationale: SI-12 retains information in line with laws, regulations and operational requirements, including long-term archiving (ASST.7.2.1). AU-11 retains audit records for a period that matches the retention policy.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Managed deletion or destruction
clauses.rationale: SI-12(03) disposes of, destroys or erases information when its retention period ends. MP-06 sanitises media before disposal, release or reuse, with a strength that matches the classification (ASST.7.3.1, ASST.7.3.2). SR-12 disposes of components with defined techniques.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for destruction to a recognised standard and security level, such as DIN 66399, and names BSI-approved erasure tools as an option (ASST.7.3.3). Choose techniques that meet those standards.

clauses.title: Recovery test to confirm deletion
clauses.rationale: MP-06(01) verifies sanitisation actions, and MP-06(02) tests sanitisation equipment and procedures. Trying to recover the data with recovery tools is one way to run that verification.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Destruction equipment for paper documents
clauses.rationale: MP-06 sanitises non-digital media too, for example by shredding paper. MP-04 keeps media physically protected until they are destroyed or sanitised with approved equipment.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for destruction equipment, such as shredders or locked bins, at every site that handles paper documents, protected from unauthorised access. Install and secure that equipment at each of those sites.

clauses.title: Authorisation of asset disposals
clauses.rationale: MP-06(01) reviews, approves, tracks and documents sanitisation and disposal actions. PE-16 authorises and controls system components that leave the facility. SR-12 disposes of components with defined techniques.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Removing labels before disposal
clauses.rationale: MP-06 sanitises media, which removes digital identifiers such as hostnames and stored accounts. SR-12 disposes of components with defined techniques, which can include removing identifying labels.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the organisation to remove every label that links an asset to it before disposal, such as asset tags and logo stickers. Add that step to your disposal techniques.

clauses.title: Personnel: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: PS-01 sets personnel security policy and procedures, documents them, gives them to the roles that need them and names an official to manage them. AT-01 does the same for awareness and training, which covers the training and development of staff.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Personnel: regular review
clauses.rationale: PS-01 reviews and updates the personnel security policy and procedures at a set frequency and after defined events. AT-01 sets the same review cycle for the awareness and training policy and procedures.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Tasks with boundaries and interfaces
clauses.rationale: PM-01's information security programme plan assigns roles and responsibilities and sets the coordination between organisational entities. PS-09 writes security roles and responsibilities into position descriptions.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the organisation to define tasks for every activity in scope, such as network monitoring or penetration testing. Each task needs clear boundaries and interfaces to the others. Draw them up from GS++'s practices and requirements.

clauses.title: Roles with objectives and qualifications
clauses.rationale: PM-13 sets up a workforce programme that defines the knowledge, skills and abilities security roles need. PS-09 writes security and privacy roles and responsibilities into position descriptions.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 covers security and privacy roles. GS++ asks for roles for every activity in scope, each with its objectives, tasks, competences and qualifications. Extend your role descriptions to all those activities.

clauses.title: Separation of roles
clauses.rationale: AC-05 has the organisation identify duties that need separating, such as directory and virtualisation administration, and support the separation with access authorisations (PERS.2.3.1, PERS.2.3.2). CA-02(01) uses independent assessors, which separates implementing security requirements from checking them (PERS.2.3.3).
clauses.gaps: GS++ names the pairs of duties to separate, such as implementation and testing (PERS.2.3.4). AC-05 lets you choose the duties, so include every pair GS++ names.

clauses.title: Responsibilities for roles
clauses.rationale: In PL-02, each system's security plan names the people who fill its roles. PM-01's programme plan assigns roles and responsibilities across the security programme.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for enough staff in every role, with deputies where the role needs them. Check staffing for each role and name deputies yourself.

clauses.title: Confidentiality in the employment or service contract
clauses.rationale: PS-06 has staff sign access agreements, such as non-disclosure agreements, before they get access. PS-06(03) covers the duties to protect organisational information that continue after employment ends.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Procedural instructions on joining
clauses.rationale: PL-04 gives new users the rules of behaviour and has them acknowledge the rules before they get access. AT-02 includes security literacy training in the initial training for new users.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Trade and business secrets
clauses.rationale: PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that state each user's responsibilities for handling information. PS-06 has staff sign non-disclosure agreements, and PS-06(03) tells them at the start about duties that continue after they leave.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the organisation to define which information counts as a trade or business secret, such as customer data or patents. Write that definition and give it to new staff when they join.

clauses.title: Job descriptions
clauses.rationale: PS-09 writes security roles and responsibilities into position descriptions. PS-02 assigns each position a risk designation and the screening criteria that go with it.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a full job description before the organisation advertises a post, with its tasks, responsibilities, authority and security criteria. Write it at that point and include the risk designation from PS-02.

clauses.title: Checking application documents
clauses.rationale: PM-13 sets standards for measuring the qualifications of applicants for security positions. PS-03 screens people before they get access, and that screening can confirm the qualifications they claim.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the organisation to check every applicant's qualifications against their application documents before filling a post. PM-13 sets standards for security positions, so apply the check to all posts.

clauses.title: Trustworthiness of applicants
clauses.rationale: PS-03 screens people before they get access, for example with background checks. PS-02 sets screening criteria for each position, with deeper checks for security-relevant posts (PERS.3.6.1).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Onboarding new staff
clauses.rationale: AT-02 gives new users initial security literacy training. AT-03 gives role-based training before staff take up their assigned duties, so they learn the security side of their role from the start.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for structured onboarding that introduces new staff to their tasks and systems as well as to security. Plan that onboarding beyond the training these controls set.

clauses.title: Review of qualification needs
clauses.rationale: PM-13 sets up a workforce development programme that defines the knowledge and skills security staff need and develops them. AT-03 gives role-based training at a set frequency and updates its content regularly.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a regular review of each staff member's qualification needs against their tasks. An annual training plan for each team is one way to do it. Set up that review for all staff.

clauses.title: Role-specific training and awareness
clauses.rationale: AT-02 gives all users literacy and awareness training when they join and at a set frequency after that. AT-03 adds role-based training before staff take up their duties, at a set frequency and when systems change. SA-16 has the developer provide training on the product's security functions, which serves as product-specific training for administrators (PERS.4.2.1).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Disciplinary action
clauses.rationale: PS-08 sets up a formal sanctions process for staff who fail to comply with security and privacy policies and procedures. Breaches of security instructions then lead to defined measures.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Insider threats
clauses.rationale: PM-12 sets up an insider threat programme with a cross-discipline team to handle cases. AT-02(02) trains staff to recognise and report signs of insider threat. SI-04 monitors systems for unauthorised use, and SI-04(19) adds closer monitoring of people identified as higher risk.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Trustworthiness check for security-critical roles
clauses.rationale: PS-02 assigns risk designations that identify the security-critical positions. PS-03 rescreens the people in them at a set frequency and when defined conditions arise.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Procedure for staff leaving
clauses.rationale: PS-04 disables system access when someone leaves, revokes their credentials, holds an exit interview and retrieves organisational property. AC-02 tells account managers about leavers and removes their accounts in step (PERS.6.1.1). PE-02 removes leavers from the facility access list.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for each of the leaver's responsibilities to pass to someone else (PERS.6.1.2). Assign each one to a named person or role as part of the leaving process.

clauses.title: Procurement: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: SA-01 sets acquisition policy and procedures, documents them, gives them to the roles that need them and names an official to manage them. SR-01 does the same for supply chain risk management, which covers the security side of choosing suppliers and contracts.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for each procurement task to go to a named person or role. SP 800-53 sets roles and responsibilities at the level of the policy, so assign the tasks yourself.

clauses.title: Procurement: regular review
clauses.rationale: SA-01 reviews and updates the acquisition policy and procedures at a set frequency and after events the organisation defines. SR-01 does the same for the supply chain risk management policy and procedures.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Register of suppliers and service providers
clauses.rationale: PM-30(01) identifies and prioritises the suppliers of critical products and services. SR-04 records where delivered components come from, and SR-04(01) identifies the elements and people across the whole supply chain (BES.1.3.1).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 asks you to identify critical suppliers. GS++ asks for a register of every direct supplier and service provider, with contact details and what each one delivers. Keep that register yourself.

clauses.title: Outsourcing strategy
clauses.rationale: PM-30 sets an organisation-wide strategy for the supply chain risks of acquiring systems and services, which covers the risk side of an outsourcing strategy. SA-09(01) assesses risk before security services are outsourced and has named roles approve the move (BES.1.4.1).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a strategy that also sets out the goals and opportunities of outsourcing, approved by top management. SA-09(01) asks for approval of outsourced security services, so extend that approval to the whole strategy.

clauses.title: Authorising the cloud deployment model
clauses.rationale: CA-06 has an authorising official approve the cloud service for use and accept the controls it inherits from the provider. That decision covers the chosen deployment model and its shared responsibility. SA-09(01) has named roles approve the outsourcing, and SA-09 sets out oversight roles and responsibilities for the external service.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a decision on the deployment model of each cloud service, such as public, private, community or hybrid cloud. Name the model in each authorisation.

clauses.title: Documenting the cloud deployment model
clauses.rationale: PL-02 has the security plan describe the operating environment, dependencies on external services and the controls in place, inherited ones included. SA-09 defines and documents the oversight and user roles and responsibilities for each external service, which records the split of shared responsibility.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for the chosen deployment model of each cloud service to be on record. Add it to the security plan next to the split of responsibilities.

clauses.title: Agreeing shared responsibility with the cloud provider
clauses.rationale: SA-04 writes the allocation of security responsibility between the parties into the acquisition contract. SA-09 requires the provider to meet the organisation's security requirements and defines each side's roles and responsibilities.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Recording procurement needs
clauses.rationale: SA-02 determines the security requirements of a system or service during business planning. SA-04 puts functional requirements and the intended operating environment into the acquisition, which covers system prerequisites (BES.2.1.3). PM-11 defines business processes and their protection needs, the core of a business process profile (BES.2.1.2). CM-10 keeps software use within licence terms and tracks licences (BES.2.1.5). MA-06 obtains maintenance support and spare parts within set times (BES.2.1.6).
clauses.gaps: GS++ names the purpose of use and compatibility with your interfaces, network connection, administration model and data management model. Its business process profile also shows interfaces and dependencies between processes. Record each of these by name.

clauses.title: Documenting jurisdiction and data location for cloud services
clauses.title_de: Dokumentation des Rechtsraums und der Datenlokation
clauses.rationale: CM-12 identifies and documents where information is processed and stored. SA-09(05) sets the locations where the provider may process and store data and run its services.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to record the provider's legal jurisdiction as well as the data location. The two can differ, as with a provider headquartered outside Europe that stores data at European sites.

clauses.title: Agreeing jurisdiction and data location with the cloud provider
clauses.title_de: Vereinbarung des Rechtsraums und der Datenlokation
clauses.rationale: SA-04 writes the location requirements into the contract with the provider as security requirements. SA-09(05) restricts processing, storage and services to the locations the organisation permits.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to agree the legal jurisdiction with the provider as well as the data location. SA-09(08) covers US jurisdiction, so write the jurisdiction you need into the contract.

clauses.title: Consulting users on procurement needs
clauses.rationale: SA-02 determines the security requirements for a system or service during mission and business planning. That is the step where the needs of users feed into a procurement.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to consult users when you capture a procurement need, for example through a survey or a test group. Build that step into your procurement process.

clauses.title: Consulting administrators on procurement needs
clauses.rationale: SA-02 determines the security requirements for a system or service during mission and business planning. That is the step where administrators can raise maintainability and compatibility before a purchase.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to consult administrators when you capture a procurement need, so they can check how the product will be run and updated. Add them to your needs assessment.

clauses.title: Outsourcing based on business process profiles
clauses.rationale: PM-11 defines business processes and their protection needs, which gives the profiles an outsourcing decision rests on. SA-09(01) assesses risk before outsourcing and has named roles approve it.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks management to approve each outsourcing contract on the basis of the process profiles. SA-09(01) asks for this approval for security services, so extend it to every outsourced process.

clauses.title: Classifying supplier relationships
clauses.rationale: AC-21 helps staff decide whether a partner may receive given information, which is what a supplier class is for. PM-30(01) identifies and prioritises suppliers of critical items. SR-06 assesses each supplier's supply chain risks, such as foreign ownership or influence, which gives the inputs for a class.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to place every supplier relationship in a security class, for example by the data shared or the supplier's function. Set up that classification scheme yourself.

clauses.title: Supplier selection criteria
clauses.rationale: SR-05 sets acquisition strategies and methods for choosing trustworthy suppliers, and SR-05(02) assesses candidates before selection. SR-06 assesses each supplier's supply chain risks, including its processes and controls, by the organisation itself or a third party. SR-03(01) uses a diverse set of sources, which limits dependence on single suppliers (BES.3.2.2).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to weigh a supplier's financial stability and its certificates or attestations when you choose it (BES.3.2.1). Add both to your selection criteria.

clauses.title: Excluding unreliable suppliers
clauses.rationale: SR-05 sets acquisition strategies and methods that guard against untrusted sources, for example trusted or controlled distribution. SR-11 sets anti-counterfeit procedures that keep components from unknown sources out of the system.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to ban purchases from unknown or unreliable sources. Write that ban into your procurement rules.

clauses.title: Classifying procurement projects
clauses.rationale: RA-02 categorises the system and the information a procurement affects, which gives the basis BSI suggests for the class. RA-03(01) assesses supply chain risk for the system, component or service being bought.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to give each procurement project a class. Where a supplier has its own classification scheme, map your classes to the supplier's.

clauses.title: Documenting procurement criteria
clauses.rationale: SA-04 records the criteria for each acquisition, such as security requirements, strength of mechanism, assurance and documentation requirements and acceptance criteria. SR-05 sets acquisition strategies and procurement methods that address supply chain risk.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Procurement based on the defined criteria
clauses.rationale: SA-04 puts the defined requirements and criteria into each acquisition contract, so each purchase follows them. SR-05(02) assesses the system, component or service against them before selection and acceptance.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Contract template for outsourcing
clauses.rationale: SA-04 has the organisation state its security requirements in standardised contract language. SA-09 sets the requirements and controls that providers of external services must meet.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a standard policy for outsourcing contracts. It sets basic criteria, such as data locations, test and approval procedures and compliance risks at subcontractors. Use it for every outsourcing contract.

clauses.title: Security by design
clauses.rationale: SA-08 applies security engineering principles in specification, design and development. SA-04 carries the security requirements into the contract, and SA-04(03) asks the developer to show a secure development life cycle (BES.4.5.1). SA-15 asks for a documented development process that addresses security. SA-17 asks the developer for a security architecture and design, which counts as agreed security by design once it is part of the contract. SC-04 prevents information transfer through shared resources, the basis of tenant separation (BES.4.5.2).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a defined tenant separation agreed with the outsourcing provider. SC-04 covers shared resources, which is part of that, so set out the full separation in the contract.

clauses.title: Security by default
clauses.rationale: SA-04(05) asks for delivery with defined security configurations in place as the default, and SA-08(23) applies the principle of secure defaults. SC-08 and SC-28 protect information in transit and at rest, here encryption by the provider (BES.4.6.2). SR-09 sets a tamper protection programme that covers the delivery route (BES.4.6.3).
clauses.gaps: GS++ also asks the organisation to agree how a service provider authenticates anyone acting for it before giving access to its information or services (BES.4.6.1). Agree concrete methods with each provider, such as a customer password, one-time codes or passkeys.

clauses.title: ISMS at the service provider
clauses.rationale: SA-04 writes the organisation's security and assurance requirements into the contract. SA-09 requires the provider to meet those requirements and to employ the controls the organisation defines.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the outsourcing provider to run an information security management system (ISMS), which a certificate can show. Name the ISMS and the certificate you accept in the contract.

clauses.title: Evidence of conformity from the supplier
clauses.rationale: SA-04 puts assurance and documentation requirements into the contract, which set the evidence the supplier must provide. CA-02(03) uses assessments by external organisations, such as certificates and attestations (BES.4.8.1, BES.4.8.2). SR-06(01) has third parties test and analyse the supplier. SR-08 sets agreements with suppliers to share the results of assessments or audits.
clauses.gaps: GS++ also asks for an analysis of the provider's infrastructure by BSI's IT-Grundschutz method (BES.4.8.3). It asks the provider to disclose the risk analysis from its ISMS (BES.4.8.4). Write both into the contract.

clauses.title: Security screening of supplier staff
clauses.rationale: PS-03 screens individuals before they get access. PS-07 sets personnel security requirements for external providers, screening included, and requires them to comply. SA-21 sets screening criteria for the developer's staff where the supplier develops the system.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Security competences of supplier staff
clauses.rationale: PS-07 sets personnel security requirements for external providers, including the security roles and responsibilities their staff must meet. AT-03 gives role-based security training to people in security roles, which defines the knowledge each role needs.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to agree the information security competences that supplier staff must have, such as minimum skills or certificates. Write those competences into the contract.

clauses.title: Service level agreement
clauses.rationale: SA-04 writes availability and other security requirements into the contract. SA-09 sets the requirements and controls providers must meet and monitors their compliance, which is the basis for agreed service levels.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for measurable service levels, such as availability as a percentage, recovery time objectives and support hours. Set those figures in the agreement with the provider.

clauses.title: Compliance obligations in supplier contracts
clauses.rationale: SA-04 writes security and privacy requirements drawn from laws, regulations and contracts into the acquisition contract. SA-09 requires providers to comply with the organisation's security and privacy requirements, legal ones included.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks suppliers to meet all your compliance obligations, such as the intellectual property rights of third parties. Add obligations outside security and privacy to the contract yourself.

clauses.title: Information security controls in supplier contracts
clauses.rationale: SA-04 puts the controls needed to meet the security requirements into the contract. SA-09 requires providers of external services to employ the controls the organisation defines.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Rules on the use of data and assets
clauses.rationale: SA-04(12) writes the organisation's ownership of its data into the contract. SA-09(05) restricts processing and storage to the locations the organisation permits (BES.5.5.1). AC-02 approves and manages accounts for supplier staff against defined criteria (BES.5.5.2).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for rules on when and where the provider may use your data and related assets. It also asks you to name the uses you forbid. Write those rules into the contract.

clauses.title: Rules for subcontracting
clauses.rationale: SA-09 holds external providers to the organisation's requirements for the services they pass on to others. SR-03(03) flows the contract's controls down to subcontractors (BES.5.6.1). SR-04(02) tracks critical components through the supply chain (BES.5.6.3).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to approve each subcontractor your supplier uses (BES.5.6.2). Write that approval step into the contract with the supplier.

clauses.title: Training on delivered security mechanisms
