clauses.rationale: SA-16 requires the developer to train the organisation's staff in the correct use of the security functions it delivers, such as encryption or access controls.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Rights to intellectual property created under the contract
clauses.rationale: SA-04(12) writes the organisation's ownership of its data into the contract. That is the nearest SP 800-53 provision to ownership of work created under a contract.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to agree who owns the intellectual property developed during the contract, such as code, data models, concepts and documentation. Write those ownership rights into the contract.

clauses.title: Handling changes to the service
clauses.rationale: SA-09 requires the provider to follow the organisation's requirements and agreed controls for the service. SA-10 has the developer control changes, implement only the changes the organisation approves and document their security impact (BES.5.9.1).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for agreed rules on changes, such as how much notice the provider gives before it changes the service. Set those notice periods in the contract.

clauses.title: Handling incidents with suppliers
clauses.rationale: SR-08 sets agreements with suppliers to notify the organisation of compromises (BES.5.10.2). IR-04(10) coordinates incident handling with the organisations in the supply chain. IR-06(03) sends incident information to the provider of the affected product or service. SA-10 has the developer track security flaws and their resolution and report them (BES.5.10.3).
clauses.gaps: GS++ also asks the supplier for a vulnerability disclosure process that follows a recognised standard (BES.5.10.3.1). It asks for a way to settle disputes and for remedies when the supplier breaches the contract. Write these into the contract.

clauses.title: Right to audit
clauses.rationale: SA-09 sets methods to monitor the provider's compliance with its controls on an ongoing basis. SR-06 assesses and reviews suppliers, either by the organisation itself or by an independent third party.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for your right to audit the provider's security processes and measures. Write that right into the outsourcing contract.

clauses.title: Duty to report on the effectiveness of security measures
clauses.rationale: SA-04(08) asks the developer for a plan to monitor control effectiveness continuously. SA-09 monitors the provider's compliance with its controls on an ongoing basis. SR-08 sets agreements for suppliers to report the results of assessments or audits.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Provision of backups by the provider
clauses.rationale: CP-09 backs up user and system information at set frequencies and protects the backups. SA-09 requires the provider to employ the controls the organisation sets, which can include regular delivery of backups.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the provider to hand backup copies to you regularly. It also asks for your data in a standard format (BES.5.13.1). Name both in the contract.

clauses.title: Deletion rules for data held by the provider
clauses.rationale: SI-12 manages and retains information in line with laws and other requirements, and SI-12(03) disposes of it at the end of the retention period. SA-09 requires the provider to apply the organisation's retention and deletion rules.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Revoking access rights on termination
clauses.rationale: AC-02 disables and removes accounts when they are no longer needed. PS-07 requires external providers to report the transfer or termination of their staff who hold credentials or badges.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to agree that all access tied to the contract ends when the contract does. That covers accounts, technical interfaces, access cards and VPN access. Make contract end a trigger for revoking them.

clauses.title: Deleting data on termination
clauses.rationale: SA-04(12) requires the contractor to remove all organisational data from its systems and return it. MP-06 sanitises media with techniques that leave the data unrecoverable (BES.6.2.1).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Data portability on termination
clauses.rationale: SA-04(12) puts data ownership into the acquisition contract. It requires the contractor to remove the organisation's data from its systems and return it, here when the contract ends.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for portability of configurations and functionality as well as data, in a complete, machine-readable format. Agree that format in the contract so you can move to a new provider.

clauses.title: Handover of support services on termination
clauses.rationale: SA-22 provides alternative sources of support for system components, in house or from another provider. It applies when the original support ends, as it does when a contract ends.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the outgoing provider to hand over support in an orderly way, with documentation, maintenance logs, access details and contacts. Agree that handover in the contract.

clauses.title: Handling retained records on termination
clauses.rationale: AU-11 keeps audit records for the retention period the organisation sets. SI-12 manages and retains information as laws, regulations and other requirements demand. Together they set which records to retain and for how long.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to agree controls with the provider over records it keeps after the contract ends. Those controls keep the records complete and protected. Write them into the contract.

clauses.title: Return of assets on termination
clauses.rationale: SA-04(12) puts data ownership into the acquisition contract. It requires the contractor to remove the organisation's data from its systems and hand it back, which covers data as one kind of asset.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for the return of every asset the organisation provided, such as IT systems, storage media and paper copies, when the contract ends. Agree their return in the contract.

clauses.title: Incoming inspection against acceptance criteria
clauses.rationale: SA-04 sets acceptance criteria in the contract, and SR-05(02) assesses the product or service against them before acceptance. CM-04(01) tests changes in a separate environment for flaws and incompatibility (BES.7.1.1). CA-02 assesses controls before use, including the criteria for the network connection (BES.7.1.2).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Processes before connecting to the provider's network
clauses.rationale: CA-03 approves the connection to the provider's network under an agreement that documents interfaces, security requirements and responsibilities. SC-07 connects to external networks only through managed interfaces with boundary protection.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Consulting those involved in the outsourced process
clauses.rationale: SP 800-53 leaves consulting the people involved in an outsourced process to the organisation.
clauses.gaps: No SP 800-53 control is mapped to this requirement. GS++ asks the organisation to consult every person or role involved in an outsourced process, such as IT operations staff, security experts or the legal department.

clauses.title: Completeness of delivered documentation
clauses.rationale: SA-17 asks for the developer's security architecture (BES.7.4.1). SA-05 obtains documentation on secure configuration and security functions (BES.7.4.2, BES.7.4.3). SA-04(01), (02) and (09) ask for descriptions of controls and design and the ports, protocols and services in use (BES.7.4.5). CM-08 inventories the delivered hardware and software (BES.7.4.4). SR-04(04) validates the composition and provenance of components, which a software bill of materials records. SA-09 documents the split of responsibilities, and SA-09(02) identifies the ports, protocols and services each external service needs (BES.7.4.6, BES.7.4.8).
clauses.gaps: GS++ also asks for an outsourcing register and a service profile for each cloud service (BES.7.4.9, BES.7.4.10). It asks you to keep a software bill of materials (SBOM) to a recognised standard for delivered software. Add these to your records.

clauses.title: Keeping alternative suppliers available
clauses.rationale: SR-03(01) uses a diverse set of sources for defined components and services. SR-05(01) ensures an adequate supply of critical components, which reduces dependence on a single supplier.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Procedures for transferring outsourced business processes
clauses.rationale: CP-02 plans how essential functions keep running through a disruption, such as the loss of a provider. CP-02(07) coordinates the plan with the providers' own plans. CP-07 sets up an alternate processing site with agreements to transfer and resume operations.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for procedures to transfer outsourced business processes when the contract ends, planned or unplanned. List alternative providers that offer the security level you need.

clauses.title: Internal resources for the end of an outsourcing contract
clauses.rationale: CP-02 assigns contingency roles to named people, and CP-02(02) plans the capacity needed for processing and support during contingency operations. SA-02 determines and allocates the resources needed to protect the system or service.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to keep enough qualified staff and infrastructure in house to take over if the outsourcing contract ends, planned or unplanned. Plan that capacity and budget for it.

clauses.title: Custom implementation of critical components
clauses.rationale: SA-20 has critical components re-implemented or custom developed for the organisation. The organisation chooses which components count as critical, such as cryptographic modules or authentication mechanisms.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Escrow agreements
clauses.rationale: SA-15(11) has the developer archive the released system with its source code and supporting evidence. SA-22 provides alternative support when the vendor's support ends, which an escrow agreement makes possible.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for escrow agreements with a trusted third party. Set release conditions in them for the source code and for the keys or passwords needed to use it.

clauses.title: Service providers: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: SA-01 sets acquisition policy and procedures, external services included, and names an official to manage them. It documents them and gives them to the roles that need them. SR-01 does the same for supply chain risk management, which covers ongoing oversight of providers. SA-09 defines oversight roles for external service providers and monitors their compliance, which is how the organisation controls its service contracts.
clauses.gaps: SA-09 covers oversight while a contract runs. GS++ also asks for a procedure to end service contracts in an orderly way, so add the exit steps to your procedures.

clauses.title: Service providers: regular review
clauses.rationale: SA-01 c reviews and updates the acquisition policy and procedures at a set frequency. It also reviews them after defined events, such as a serious security incident or new legal requirements. SR-01 c does the same for the supply chain risk management policy and procedures.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Multi-factor authentication for online services
clauses.rationale: IA-02(01) and (02) ask for multi-factor authentication on privileged and non-privileged accounts. For online services, such as cloud office applications, that means a second factor like a one-time password.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Transport encryption to the service provider
clauses.rationale: SC-08(01) uses cryptography to protect the confidentiality and integrity of data on its way to the provider. SC-13 sets the type of cryptography for each use, for example to a recognised standard.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Full encryption before transfer to the service provider
clauses.rationale: SA-09(06) has the organisation keep exclusive control of the keys for data stored at or sent through an external provider. SC-12 manages those keys so they stay with the organisation. SC-28(01) encrypts the data at rest, for example per file or in an encrypted container.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Service provider compliance with security requirements
clauses.rationale: SA-09 c monitors the provider's compliance with security requirements on an ongoing basis. SR-06 assesses and reviews suppliers at a set frequency. CA-02(03) uses the results of assessments by external organisations, such as audits or certificates (DLS.3.1.1).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Checkup of the outsourcing decision
clauses.rationale: RA-03 updates the risk assessment at a set frequency and when threats or conditions change. RA-03(01) does the same for supply chain risk. SR-06 reviews suppliers and the services they provide at a set frequency.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to review the outsourcing decision itself against your business process profiles. Use those profiles as input each time you update the supply chain risk assessment.

clauses.title: Outsourcing strategy check
clauses.rationale: PM-30 reviews and updates the supply chain risk management strategy when the organisation changes. PM-11 reviews and revises the business process definitions and their protection needs, which the strategy depends on.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to check the outsourcing strategy for completeness and correctness whenever a business process profile changes. Make each change to a profile a trigger for that check.

clauses.title: Consulting the service provider on security measures
clauses.rationale: SA-09 b defines the oversight roles and responsibilities for an external service. That oversight gives the organisation a channel to hear the provider on planned security measures.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to consult the provider on security measures for the target objects it serves. Tell the provider what you plan and give it time to comment.

clauses.title: Blocking unreliable service providers
clauses.rationale: SR-06 assesses suppliers and identifies the unreliable ones. SR-05 shapes acquisition strategies and methods to exclude untrusted suppliers. AC-20 b prohibits the use of named external systems, such as a service run by an unreliable provider. SR-03(03) carries the contract controls down into the contracts of sub-providers.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Portability of the outsourced process
clauses.rationale: CP-07 sets up an alternate processing site where operations can resume, which here means a site away from the provider. CP-04(02) tests the contingency plan at that alternate site.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for regular tests that the outsourced process works in an environment away from the provider. Add the outsourced process to your contingency plan tests at the alternate site.

clauses.title: Decommissioning a service before the contract ends
clauses.rationale: SA-04(12) has the contract require the provider to return the organisation's data and remove it from its systems at the end. AC-02 disables the accounts used for the contract when the need for them ends (DLS.4.1.2). PE-02 removes the provider's staff from the facility access list (DLS.4.1.2). CP-04 tests can show that processing runs independently of the provider (DLS.4.1.1).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a planned procedure to decommission the whole service relationship before the contract ends. Write that procedure yourself, with the data return and the removal of access rights as steps in it.

clauses.title: Changes and tests: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: CM-01 sets configuration management policy and procedures, documents them, gives them to the roles that need them and names an official to manage them. CM-03 brings changes under change control, including adding and removing components. CM-09 sets out roles and responsibilities for configuration management in a plan, which assigns the tasks (TEST.1.1.2).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Changes and tests: regular review
clauses.rationale: CM-01 has the organisation review and update its configuration management policy and procedures at a set frequency and after defined events. That covers both the regular review and the review after an event, such as a serious security incident.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Restricting changes to administrators
clauses.rationale: CM-05 defines and enforces access restrictions for changes, and CM-05(05) limits who holds change privileges in production. AC-06 applies least privilege, so only the administrators who need change rights get them.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Version history of changes
clauses.rationale: CM-03 documents decisions on changes and keeps records of the changes made. CM-02(03) keeps previous versions of the baseline configuration, which gives a history of how the system has changed.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Impact assessment before changes
clauses.rationale: CM-03 sets the types of change that go through change control, which sorts changes into categories (TEST.2.2.1). CM-03(01) documents each proposed change (TEST.2.2.2). CM-04 analyses the security and privacy impact of a change before it goes ahead, including the effect on dependent systems (TEST.2.2.3).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Security testing of changes
clauses.rationale: CM-03(02) tests each change and documents the results before it goes live (TEST.3.1.1). CM-04(01) tests in a separate environment (TEST.3.1.5), and CM-04(02) checks the controls after the change. SA-03(02) controls the use of live data in test environments (TEST.3.1.4). SA-11 has developers test their work, with penetration testing in SA-11(05) and fuzzing as part of dynamic analysis in SA-11(08). SI-07 checks the integrity of software (TEST.3.1.3). SR-05 keeps out components from untrustworthy sources (TEST.3.1.2).
clauses.gaps: For a higher security level, GS++ suggests load tests and chaos engineering, which simulates disruptions to test resilience. It also suggests composition analysis, which tests what each change is made of. Add the tests you choose to your test plan.

clauses.title: Test coverage
clauses.rationale: SA-11 has developers test their work, and SA-11(07) checks that testing covers the required controls at a set breadth and depth. PM-14 reviews testing plans against the organisation's risk priorities.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a regular review of test coverage, which includes code coverage. Measure how much of the code your tests run, as well as which controls they check.

clauses.title: Authorisation of changes
clauses.rationale: CM-03 approves or rejects each change after weighing its security impact, and records the decision (TEST.4.1.3). AC-05 separates the people who approve a change from those who carry it out (TEST.4.1.1). CM-04(01) tests changes in a separate environment before they reach production (TEST.4.1.2).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a staging environment that matches production as closely as possible (TEST.4.1.2). Build the separate test environment of CM-04(01) to mirror production.

clauses.title: Signature on the approval statement
clauses.rationale: AU-10 gives irrefutable evidence that a named person approved the change, for example through a digital signature. CM-03 documents each decision to approve a change.
clauses.gaps: GS++ accepts a handwritten signature on the approval statement as well as a digital one. AU-10 covers the digital kind, so file signed paper approvals with the change records.

clauses.title: Fallback solution for changes
clauses.rationale: CM-02(03) keeps previous configurations, so a change can be rolled back. CP-09 backs up the system, which lets you restore the state from before a failed change. CP-10 recovers the system to a known state after a failure.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Rules for emergency changes
clauses.rationale: CM-03 brings unscheduled changes under change control, with defined review and approval. CM-09 sets the roles and responsibilities for configuration management in a plan. SI-02 installs security fixes within set times, and a critical fix is a typical emergency change.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a separate procedure for emergency changes, with the resources it needs and the minimum test steps each change must pass. Add that procedure to your change rules.

clauses.title: Informing groups affected by a change
clauses.rationale: CM-03(01) notifies the personnel the organisation chooses about each proposed change, and again once the approved change is complete. This keeps the people in the change process informed.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to inform everyone a change affects, such as users and the monitoring team. Tell them about expected downtime and any settings they need to change themselves.

clauses.title: Encrypted deployment
clauses.rationale: SC-08 protects the confidentiality and integrity of deployment artefacts in transit to the target environment. SC-13 sets the type of cryptography for each use, including the deployment channel.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Gradual rollout of changes
clauses.rationale: CM-03 puts approved changes into effect in a controlled way. A gradual rollout, one group at a time, is one way to do that.
clauses.gaps: GS++ suggests rolling out a change in stages, for example one site or one group of users at a time. Plan the stages as part of each change.

clauses.title: Persistence of changes
clauses.rationale: CM-02 writes each change into the baseline configuration, so it survives a rebuild or a restore. CM-04(02) checks after a change that the affected controls work as intended. SI-06 verifies security functions at transitional states, such as startup and restart.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to test that a change stays in place after a system update or a restore from a configuration backup. Add those cases to the tests after each significant change.

clauses.title: Deployment retrospective
clauses.rationale: CM-03 monitors and reviews the activities linked to each change. CM-04(02) checks after a change that the controls work as intended and meet the security requirements.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a regular review of whether deployments reached their goals. Use the findings to plan later changes and reduce their risks.

clauses.title: Buildings: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: PE-01 sets the physical and environmental protection policy and procedures and names an official to manage them. It documents them and gives them to the roles that need them. The policy covers the physical protection of sites that process or store sensitive information.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Buildings: regular review
clauses.rationale: PE-01 c reviews and updates the physical and environmental protection policy and procedures at a set frequency. It also reviews them after defined events, such as a serious security incident or new legal requirements.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Authorisation of sites for assets
clauses.rationale: PE-23 plans the location of a facility with physical and environmental hazards in mind. CA-02 assesses the controls at a site against set criteria before it goes into use (GEB.1.3.1). PE-17 documents the alternate work sites the organisation allows and assesses their controls.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to authorise each site formally before you place assets there. Base each authorisation on the assessment results and record it.

clauses.title: Placing assets outside exposed areas
clauses.rationale: PE-18 positions system components to minimise damage from hazards and the chance of unauthorised access. That keeps them out of places such as a basement at risk of flooding. PE-23 plans the facility's location with physical and environmental hazards in mind.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Structural plans of buildings and utilities
clauses.rationale: SP 800-53 leaves plans of buildings and sites to the organisation.
clauses.gaps: No SP 800-53 control is mapped to this requirement. GS++ asks for plans of each site: floor plans and the routes of physical perimeters, utility lines, network connections and exits, emergency exits included.

clauses.title: Installing security perimeters
clauses.rationale: PE-03 enforces physical access authorisations at the facility's entry and exit points. PE-03(07) adds physical barriers that limit access to the facility.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Documentation of public areas
clauses.rationale: PE-03 c controls access to the areas the organisation designates as publicly accessible, such as reception or delivery zones.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to document each area open without authentication, with the reason it's open. Record that reason when you designate the area as publicly accessible.

clauses.title: Reconnaissance from public space
clauses.rationale: PE-18 positions system components to keep their information out of sight and earshot of people near entry points. RA-06 uses technical surveillance countermeasures surveys, which examine the facility inside and out for weaknesses an attacker could exploit.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to test the site's protection against being seen or heard from public space. Run those checks from the public side, as an outsider would.

clauses.title: Electromagnetic shielding
clauses.rationale: PE-19 protects against information leakage through electromagnetic emanations, such as screen content picked up from outside the building. CA-02 assesses whether controls such as the shielding work as intended.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a specific test of the electromagnetic shielding. CA-02 assesses controls in general, so add the shielding to your assessment plan as a test of its own.

clauses.title: Monitoring of entry points
clauses.rationale: PE-06 monitors physical access to the facility. PE-06(01) adds intrusion alarms and surveillance equipment, and PE-06(03) adds video surveillance (GEB.3.1.1). PE-03 has guards or access devices control the entry points. PE-03(02) checks at the perimeter for components or information being taken out (GEB.3.1.2).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Registration and reception areas
clauses.rationale: PE-03 controls entry to the facility and access to its publicly accessible areas. It also escorts and controls visitors. PE-08 keeps records of visitor access.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to set up registration and reception areas at each site. Place them where visitors arrive, as the dividing point between public and protected zones.

clauses.title: Authentication before entry
clauses.rationale: PE-02 keeps the list of people allowed into the facility and issues their credentials. PE-03 checks each person's authorisation before entry, with guards or an access control system (GEB.3.3.1), and keeps access logs (GEB.3.3.2). PE-08 records visitor access, which supports the authorisation of visits (GEB.3.3.3).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Visible authorisation badges
clauses.rationale: PE-02 issues authorisation credentials, such as badges, to the people allowed into the facility. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour for users, which can tell them to wear their badges.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to tell users to wear their badges where others can see them, everywhere inside the security perimeter. Put that duty in your rules of behaviour.

clauses.title: Burglary resistance
clauses.rationale: PE-03(07) limits access to the facility with physical barriers, such as the walls and doors around server rooms or media archives.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for burglary-resistant components built to a recognised standard, such as EN 1627. Choose the resistance class from the risk to the assets and the likely attackers.

clauses.title: Intrusion alarm systems
clauses.rationale: PE-06(01) monitors physical access with intrusion alarms and surveillance equipment. PE-06(02) recognises intrusions automatically and starts a response.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for intrusion alarm systems built to a recognised standard. Name that standard in your requirements and choose a system that meets it.

clauses.title: Review of physical access controls
clauses.rationale: CA-02 assesses at a set frequency whether physical access controls work as intended. CA-08(03) tests physical access points with announced or unannounced attempts to get past them. PE-06 reviews physical access logs at a set frequency.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Setting up secure areas
clauses.rationale: PE-03(01) enforces separate physical access authorisations for spaces inside the facility that hold system components, such as server rooms. Each such space then works as a secure area with its own perimeter.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Separate authorisation for secure areas
clauses.rationale: PE-02 approves the list of people allowed into the secure area. PE-02(01) grants that access by position or role, and PE-02(03) restricts unescorted access. PE-03(01) enforces those authorisations at the entrance to the secure area.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Security airlocks at access points
clauses.rationale: PE-03(08) uses access control vestibules at defined entry points. Like an airlock, a vestibule has two doors that open one after the other, so one person or item passes at a time.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Single-person entry systems at access points
clauses.rationale: PE-03 controls each entry point with physical access devices. PE-03(08) adds access control vestibules, which let one person through at a time and stop tailgating.
clauses.gaps: PE-03(08) names vestibules. GS++ also names turnstiles and similar single-person entry systems, so choose the type that suits each access point.

clauses.title: Delivery access point
clauses.rationale: PE-16 authorises and controls the components that enter and leave the facility. Its discussion points to isolating delivery areas from the rest of the facility. PE-03 controls access between the delivery area and the rest of the site.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Protection against tampering
clauses.rationale: PE-03(04) keeps system components in lockable casings, and PE-03(05) uses anti-tamper technologies to prevent or detect tampering. SR-09 runs a tamper protection programme for the system and its components.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Physical microsegmentation
clauses.rationale: SC-32 partitions system components into separate physical domains, such as separate racks or rooms. PE-03(01) enforces access authorisations at each of those spaces, which turns them into access-controlled zones inside a shared facility.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for building measures that keep the zones apart, such as separate entrances, utilities and ventilation for each zone. Build them into the design of the shared facility.

clauses.title: Access to output devices
clauses.rationale: PE-05 controls physical access to output devices, such as printers and monitors. That covers devices that show or print sensitive content, such as the HR department's network printer.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Protected placement of IT systems
clauses.rationale: PE-18 positions system components to minimise the chance of unauthorised access. PE-03(01) enforces access authorisations to the rooms that hold system components, such as the server rooms for host systems (GEB.6.2.1).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Network components in technical infrastructure rooms
clauses.rationale: PE-18 positions network components to minimise damage from hazards and the chance of unauthorised access. PE-03(01) restricts access to the rooms that hold them. PE-04 controls physical access to distribution and transmission lines, for example with locked wiring closets.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Standard-compliant data centres
clauses.rationale: PE-23 plans the location of the facility with physical and environmental hazards in mind. PE-18 positions system components within the facility to minimise damage from those hazards.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to place server rooms only in data centres built and maintained to a recognised standard, such as EN 50600 or ISO/IEC 22237. Make that standard a condition when you choose a data centre.

clauses.title: Key custodians for buildings and rooms
clauses.rationale: PE-03 e secures keys, combinations and other physical access devices. PE-03 f keeps an inventory of them, and PE-03 g changes keys and combinations, for example when a key is lost.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to give the management of keys to named people or roles, such as facility management or the reception desk. Name them in your site procedures.

clauses.title: Safekeeping of keys
clauses.rationale: PE-03 e secures keys and other physical access devices. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that tell users their responsibilities, which can include keeping keys safe.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to tell users how to keep their keys safe, for example by carrying them or locking them in a key cabinet. Add that instruction to your rules of behaviour.

clauses.title: Key audit for buildings and rooms
clauses.rationale: PE-03 f inventories keys and other physical access devices at a set frequency. PE-03 g changes keys when one is lost or compromised.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Separate storage of business-critical media
clauses.rationale: MP-04 physically controls media and stores them securely within controlled areas. Those areas can be locked cabinets or safes, or a dedicated media archive (GEB.8.1.1).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Dust and dirt protection for archived media
clauses.rationale: MP-04 protects stored media until they're destroyed or sanitised. PE-14 maintains environmental conditions at levels the organisation sets, which can include limits on dust.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for measures that protect archived media from dust and dirt, such as dust-tight cabinets and dry cleaning. Add them to your archive procedures.

clauses.title: Protection of storage media from fire damage
clauses.rationale: CP-09(03) keeps backups of critical information in a fire-rated container. MP-04 stores all media securely within controlled areas, such as a media archive.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for fire-resistant containers certified to a recognised standard, such as EN 1047-1 or ISO 11799. Choose data safes or fire-resistant cabinets with that certification.

clauses.title: Monitoring media-friendly temperature and humidity
clauses.rationale: PE-14 keeps temperature and humidity within levels the organisation sets and monitors them. PE-14(02) raises an alarm when a change could harm equipment, such as stored media.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Standard-compliant power supply
clauses.rationale: PE-09 protects power equipment and cabling from damage, and PE-09(01) adds redundant cabling. PE-11 provides an uninterruptible power supply that bridges an outage for a set time (GEB.9.1.3). PE-11(01) and (02) add a long-term alternate power supply (GEB.9.1.4).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for power supply and cabling built to electrical standards, such as DIN VDE 0100. It also asks for a regular forward-looking load analysis (GEB.9.1.1) and a dedicated sub-distribution board fed straight from the main low-voltage distribution (GEB.9.1.2).

clauses.title: Load test of the power supply
clauses.rationale: PE-11 provides the uninterruptible power supply and the alternate power source, such as a generator. These are the systems whose capacity a load test checks.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for regular load tests of the uninterruptible power supply (UPS) and generators. Examples are a monthly UPS self-test and a full-load generator run of at least 30 minutes every six months.

clauses.title: Emergency shutoff for utilities
clauses.rationale: PE-10 lets staff cut the power in an emergency. It places the shutoff switches where authorised staff can reach them and protects them against unauthorised activation.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Surge protection
clauses.rationale: PE-09 protects power equipment and cabling from damage. PE-09(02) adds automatic voltage controls for critical system components. PE-21 protects against electromagnetic pulses with measures such as surge suppressors and earthing.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Structured data cabling
clauses.rationale: PE-04 controls physical access to data cabling inside the facility. It protects the cable routes, for example with conduit or locked wiring closets (GEB.9.5.1).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for structured data cabling built to recognised standards, such as EN 50173 and EN 50174. Use those standards when you plan or extend the cabling.

clauses.title: Access to technical infrastructure rooms
clauses.title_de: Zugang zu Räumen für technische Infrastruktur
clauses.rationale: PE-02(01) authorises physical access by position or role, so only the staff who run the infrastructure get in. PE-03(01) enforces those authorisations at the entrance to each technical infrastructure room.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Other uses of technical infrastructure rooms
clauses.rationale: PE-18 positions system components to minimise damage from hazards and the chance of unauthorised access. Using a technical room as an office or a store room would raise both risks.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to use technical infrastructure rooms for their technical purpose alone. Write the ban on other uses into your building rules.

clauses.title: Climate control
clauses.rationale: PE-14 keeps temperature and humidity within levels the organisation sets and monitors them (GEB.10.1.2). PE-14(01) adds automatic environmental controls, and PE-14(02) raises an alarm on changes that could cause harm.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a regular airflow analysis to check the cooling needs of server rooms (GEB.10.1.1). It also asks for redundant climate control systems (GEB.10.1.3).

clauses.title: Fire protection
clauses.rationale: PE-13 provides fire detection and suppression systems. PE-13(01) and (02) make detection and suppression start automatically (GEB.10.2.5 and GEB.10.2.6). PE-13(04) adds fire protection inspections at a set frequency (GEB.10.2.7).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for structural fire protection and fire compartments to the relevant standards (GEB.10.2.1 and GEB.10.2.2). It also asks for smoke-tight rooms and materials that resist fire for a set time (GEB.10.2.3 and GEB.10.2.4).

clauses.title: Protection against water damage
clauses.rationale: PE-15 protects the system from water leakage, for example with shutoff valves. PE-15(01) detects water near the system (GEB.10.3.2). PE-18 positions components away from water hazards, such as rooms at risk of flooding.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for at least one physical barrier against water, built to the relevant standards, between assets and each weather or water hazard. GEB.10.3.1 raises that to two structural barriers.

clauses.title: Lightning protection systems
clauses.rationale: PE-21 protects against electromagnetic pulses, including natural ones such as lightning, with earthing and surge suppression. PE-09 protects power equipment and cabling from damage.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for lightning protection systems built to a recognised standard. It also asks for regular checks that their resistance stays low (GEB.10.4.1).

clauses.title: Static-dissipative floor covering
clauses.rationale: PE-14 maintains environmental conditions within levels the organisation sets. Those conditions can include static charge, which a dissipative floor drains away to earth.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a static-dissipative floor covering close to the systems in technical infrastructure rooms. Lay it to a standard such as EN 14041 or IEC 61340-4-1.

clauses.title: Awareness: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: AT-01 sets and documents awareness and training policy and procedures. It assigns roles and responsibilities, shares the procedures with the people who need them and names an official to manage them. AT-02 sets the awareness training for all users that the procedures govern. AT-03 adds role-based training, which makes the training role-specific.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Measuring the success of awareness
clauses.rationale: AT-02 tests what users know, and AT-02(01) uses practical exercises, such as simulated phishing, to test how they act. AT-04 documents and monitors training activities, which shows how far the training reaches. AT-06 feeds training results back to defined staff at a set frequency. PM-06 develops, monitors and reports security measures of performance, which can include awareness metrics.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for regular checks of awareness success against objective criteria, covering what users know and what they do in practice. Define those criteria yourself and review the results against them.

clauses.title: Awareness of the protection goals
clauses.rationale: AT-02 gives all users literacy training on the need for security. That need includes the protection goals of availability, confidentiality and integrity, which belong at the core of the content.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names availability, confidentiality and integrity as training topics. SP 800-53 lets you choose the topics, so cover each goal by name.

clauses.title: Reporting channels and information sources
clauses.rationale: AT-02 teaches users how to respond to suspected incidents and where to report them. IR-06 has staff report suspected incidents to the incident response team, which fixes the reporting channel. IR-07 provides a support resource, such as a help desk, that advises users on handling and reporting incidents.
clauses.gaps: GS++ also asks users to know where to find answers to general security questions, such as the intranet or handbooks. Point users to those sources in your awareness training.

clauses.title: Using encryption and signature functions
clauses.rationale: AT-02 lets the organisation set its awareness content, which can cover the encryption and signature functions of applications. SA-05 has the user documentation describe the security functions available to users and how to use them effectively.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for training on encryption and signature functions, such as signing an email or checking a messenger's end-to-end encryption. Add these to your awareness content by name.

clauses.title: Use of unauthorised assets
clauses.rationale: PL-04 bans unauthorised assets in rules of behaviour that users acknowledge, and AT-02 carries the ban to users. AC-20 and AC-20(03) restrict or prohibit external systems, such as private devices and unapproved cloud services. CM-07(09) bans the use or connection of unauthorised hardware (SENS.2.4.1). CM-11 sets and enforces the rules on what software users may install. MP-07 restricts media types and portable storage with an unknown owner.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Areas of responsibility and their protection needs
clauses.rationale: AT-02 bases awareness content on the systems users can access and their work environment. AT-03 gives role-based training on the security requirements of each person's duties and the systems in their area of responsibility.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for each user to learn the protection needs of their own area and of its interfaces with other areas. Add both to the training for each role.

clauses.title: Bypassing security functions
clauses.rationale: AT-02 teaches the user actions that keep systems secure, such as leaving safeguards in place. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that forbid users to disable or bypass security functions.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names bypassing security functions as a training topic, such as switching off antivirus software. Cover it by name in your awareness content.

clauses.title: Changing security configurations
clauses.rationale: AT-02 teaches the user actions that keep systems secure and can explain the risk of changing security settings. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that forbid unauthorised changes to security-relevant configurations.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names unauthorised changes to security settings, such as firewall rules or user rights, as a training topic. Cover them by name in your awareness content.

clauses.title: Reporting security events
clauses.rationale: AT-02 covers how users respond to suspected incidents, and AT-02(04) teaches them to recognise anomalous system behaviour, such as unexpected warnings (SENS.2.8.1). IR-06 requires staff to report suspected incidents within a set time. PL-04 makes reporting an instruction in rules of behaviour that users acknowledge.
clauses.gaps: GS++ also asks users to report routine error and warning messages, beyond suspected incidents. Name those messages in your reporting instructions.

clauses.title: Risks of malware
clauses.rationale: AT-02 gives all users awareness training on security risks. AT-02(04) teaches them to recognise suspicious communications and anomalous system behaviour using indicators of malicious code.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Opening files in a sandbox
clauses.rationale: SC-44 provides a detonation chamber, or sandbox, where users can open suspicious attachments and files in isolation. AT-02 training can tell users to open suspicious files only there.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to tell users to open suspicious files only in the sandbox. Add that instruction to your awareness training.

clauses.title: Converting suspicious files to a non-executable format
clauses.rationale: AT-02 lets the organisation set its awareness content. That content can teach users to convert suspicious files to a non-executable format before they open or use them.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks users to convert suspicious files, such as those from unknown sources, to a non-executable format before use. Teach the method and give users a tool to do it.

clauses.title: Handling personal authenticators
clauses.rationale: AT-02 teaches users how to handle authenticators. IA-05 requires individuals to protect their authenticators. IA-05(01) sets password strength rules (SENS.4.1.3), and IA-05(18) provides password managers (SENS.4.1.4). PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that forbid sharing, reusing or writing down passwords. PL-04(01) bars the use of organisational passwords on external sites (SENS.4.1.2).
clauses.gaps: GS++ also asks for training on entering credentials out of sight of others and on how biometric features can be forged. Add both topics to your awareness content.

clauses.title: Shared use of accounts
clauses.rationale: IA-02 identifies and authenticates each user uniquely, which account sharing defeats. AC-02 sets the allowed account types, and AC-02(09) permits shared or group accounts only under defined conditions. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that forbid sharing accounts. AT-02 explains to users why one account belongs to one person.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Logging off after use
clauses.rationale: AC-11 lets users lock the device before they leave it unattended, which GS++ counts as part of logging off. AC-12 ends sessions on defined triggers, and AC-12(01) gives users a way to log out. AT-02 reminds users to log off or lock their device after use.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Structured data filing
clauses.rationale: AT-02 training can cover the structured filing scheme that users must follow, such as a file register or a content management system. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that can require users to keep to that scheme.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks users to keep to a structured filing scheme. Design the scheme yourself, for example in a content management system, and teach it to users.

clauses.title: Passing on information
clauses.rationale: AC-21 helps users decide whether a sharing partner's access rights match the restrictions on the information before they share it. AT-02 training can cover the conditions for passing on information.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks users to know the legal and contractual conditions for passing on information, and which channel suits each group of recipients. Set those conditions out for users yourself.

clauses.title: Passing on contact details
clauses.rationale: AT-02(03) trains users on social engineering and social mining, which exploit published contact details. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that can forbid disclosing such details, and PL-04(01) restricts posting organisational information on public websites and social media.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks users to keep contact details, such as phone numbers and internal extensions, from unauthorised third parties. That covers passing them on directly as well as publishing them. Name contact details in your rules of behaviour.

clauses.title: Residual and additional data in documents
clauses.rationale: AT-02 training can teach users to remove hidden data before they send a document. That data includes the metadata fields and change history in office or PDF files.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks users to avoid or remove residual data, such as metadata and change history, before they send a document. Teach the steps for each file type you use.

clauses.title: Deletion at the end of retention periods
clauses.rationale: AT-02 teaches users the retention periods and how to delete information when they end. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that instruct users to delete or destroy information at the end of its retention period. SI-12 manages and retains information under the applicable rules, and SI-12(03) sets the techniques to dispose of it afterwards. MP-06 sanitises digital and paper media before disposal or reuse.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Destroying paper documents
clauses.rationale: AT-02 teaches users to destroy confidential documents. MP-06 sanitises or destroys media before disposal, including paper, with a strength matched to the information's classification. SI-12(03) sets the techniques for destroying information after the retention period.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Scanning received removable media
clauses.rationale: SI-03 scans files from external sources in real time at endpoints, including files on removable media, which meets the scan GS++ asks for. AT-02 tells users to scan the removable media they accept. PL-04 makes the scan an instruction in rules of behaviour that users acknowledge.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Encrypting removable media
clauses.rationale: SC-28(01) encrypts information at rest on defined media, including removable media. MP-05 protects media in transport outside controlled areas, for example by encryption. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that require users to encrypt removable media, and AT-02 carries that instruction to them.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Awareness for specific target objects
clauses.rationale: AT-02 bases awareness content on the systems users can access and their work environment. AT-03 tailors role-based training to each group's duties and the specific systems it uses.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for awareness shaped to each target group and the target objects it uses. Work out your target groups first, then tailor the content to each.

clauses.title: Virus scan of files from external sources
clauses.rationale: SI-03 scans files from external sources in real time as they are downloaded or opened. AT-02 tells users to check files from external sources, such as email or messenger attachments, before they open them.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Confidential data in automatic replies
clauses.rationale: AT-02 can warn users against putting confidential details in automatic replies, and AT-02(03) covers social mining, which such replies can feed. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that keep confidential content out of automatic replies.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks users to keep confidential data out of automatic replies, such as out-of-office notices. Set out in your rules what such a reply may contain.

clauses.title: Spam: deleting or reporting
clauses.rationale: AT-02(04) trains users to recognise suspicious messages, such as spam, and to respond to them. IR-06 requires staff to report suspected incidents, and a suspicious email counts as one.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Spam: not replying
clauses.rationale: AT-02 gives users awareness training, and AT-02(04) teaches them to recognise suspicious email and how to respond to it. Leaving spam unanswered is part of that response.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks users to leave spam unanswered, since a reply confirms to the sender that the address is in use. Name this step in your awareness training.

clauses.title: Spam: opening links
clauses.rationale: AT-02(04) teaches users to spot suspicious links, and AT-02(01) exercises, such as simulated spear phishing, let them practise the response. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that forbid opening links in unsolicited messages.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Spam: opening attachments
clauses.rationale: AT-02(04) teaches users the signs of malicious attachments, and AT-02(01) exercises simulate opening one. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that forbid opening attachments in unsolicited messages.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Recognising forged emails
clauses.rationale: AT-02(04) trains users on the signs of suspicious email, such as a known sender's name with an unfamiliar address. AT-02(03) covers phishing and the impersonation of known senders.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Active content in office documents
clauses.rationale: SC-18 defines acceptable mobile code. SC-18(04) blocks its automatic execution and enforces actions, such as prompting the user, before it runs. AT-02 tells users to check active content, such as macros, before they enable it.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Disconnecting unneeded host-guest connections
clauses.rationale: CM-07 keeps only the functions, ports and interfaces a system needs, such as a shared folder or USB pass-through between host and guest. AT-02 training can tell users of virtualisation to disconnect unneeded host-guest connections.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names host-guest connections and asks users of virtualisation to disconnect the unneeded ones themselves. Add that task to your awareness training, alongside the CM-07 configuration.

clauses.title: Covert recording in video conferences
clauses.rationale: AT-02 can warn users against secret audio or video recording in video conferences. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that forbid recording other participants unless they consent.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names covert recording in video conferences as an awareness topic, including recordings analysed with AI. Cover it in your training and in your rules for video conferences.

clauses.title: Risks of public WLANs
clauses.rationale: AC-19 sets connection requirements and guidance for mobile devices outside controlled areas, which tell users which networks to use. AT-02 bases awareness on users' work environment, such as telework, where the risks of public WLANs belong.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names the risks of public WLANs, such as fake hotspots and intercepted traffic, as an awareness topic. Add them by name to your training for mobile users.

clauses.title: Risks of unencrypted WLANs
clauses.rationale: AC-19 sets connection requirements for mobile devices outside controlled areas, which can exclude unencrypted networks or require a VPN. AT-02 training can cover the risks of unencrypted WLANs.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names the risks of unencrypted WLANs as an awareness topic, such as open networks protected only by a login page. Add them by name to your training for mobile users.

clauses.title: Use of unauthorised WLANs
clauses.rationale: AC-19 sets connection requirements that define which networks mobile devices may join outside controlled areas. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that forbid connecting to unauthorised WLANs. AT-02 carries that ban to users.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Social engineering calls
clauses.rationale: AT-02(03) trains users to recognise and report social engineering, including pretexting and impersonation by phone. That covers a caller who poses as IT support or a manager to get a password.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Voicemail PINs and similar credentials
clauses.rationale: IA-05 replaces default authenticators, such as a voicemail PIN, before first use. It also has individuals protect their authenticators. AT-02 tells users to set their own PIN or password for recordings, such as voicemail.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Unencrypted telephone calls
clauses.rationale: AT-02 training can tell users which channels are encrypted and suit confidential calls with which recipients. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that keep sensitive conversations to encrypted channels.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names unencrypted calls as an awareness topic, such as a conference where one participant dials in over the public phone network. Cover such cases by name in your training.

clauses.title: Mobile devices in secure areas
clauses.rationale: SC-42 prohibits devices with sensors, such as cameras and microphones, in defined areas. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that forbid carrying unauthorised devices into secure areas. AT-02 carries the ban to users.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Unencrypted SMS or MMS
clauses.rationale: PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that can forbid SMS and MMS for organisational or sensitive communication. AT-02 carries the ban to users and explains that these messages usually travel unencrypted.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names SMS and MMS as channels to avoid. Name them in your rules of behaviour and point users to encrypted messengers or VoIP instead.

clauses.title: Authenticating the other party in a conversation
clauses.rationale: AT-02(03) trains users to recognise social engineering, such as pretexting and impersonation, which checking the other party's identity defeats. AC-21 has users check that a sharing partner may receive the information, which means knowing who the partner is.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks users to confirm who they are talking to before they pass on information, by phone or in person. Set up that check yourself, for example a call back to a number from your own directory.

clauses.title: Legal uncertainty of faxes
clauses.rationale: AT-02 lets the organisation set its awareness content, so the training can cover the legal limits of documents that users send or receive by fax.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks users to know that a fax lacks the original handwritten signature. A fax therefore fails a legal written-form rule, such as the one in the German Civil Code. Brief users on where this matters.

clauses.title: Unencrypted fax lines
clauses.rationale: AT-02 lets the organisation set its awareness content, so the training can cover the risks of unauthenticated and unencrypted fax. Others can intercept or alter such a fax with ease.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names the risks of fax as an awareness topic. Its guidance suggests announcing a fax in advance and confirming that it was sent and received. Build those steps into your fax procedure.

clauses.title: Geolocation on mobile devices
clauses.rationale: SC-42 restricts remote activation of sensors, such as GPS, and shows users when sensors are in use. AT-02 informs users about the location functions of their mobile devices.
clauses.gaps: GS++ also asks users to know that mobile network operators can locate a device from its signal. Include that in your training, alongside the device's own location settings.

clauses.title: Certificate warnings
clauses.rationale: AT-02 training can cover certificate warnings as a sign of attack. PL-04 sets rules of behaviour that forbid overriding a certificate warning unless the override is authorised.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names certificate warnings in web browsers as an awareness topic. Tell users to ask through the known reporting channels before they go on to the site.

clauses.title: Screen lock
clauses.rationale: AC-11 has users lock the device before they leave it unattended. AT-02 gives users that instruction in awareness training, and PL-04 sets it as a rule of behaviour.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Clean desk
clauses.rationale: AT-02 tells users in awareness training to put confidential papers and media away, and PL-04 makes it a rule of behaviour. MP-04 physically controls digital and paper media and stores them securely.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Risks of using mobile devices
clauses.title_de: Risiken der Nutzung von mobilen Endgeräten
clauses.rationale: AC-19 sets requirements and implementation guidance for mobile devices, including outside controlled areas, where users must protect the devices themselves. AT-02 builds the risks of mobile devices, and of settings such as telework, into awareness content.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Closing doors and windows
clauses.rationale: AT-02 reminds users in awareness training to lock doors and windows, and PL-04 makes locking rooms on leaving a rule of behaviour. PE-03 controls physical access at entry and exit points, which depends on locked doors.
clauses.gaps: GS++ also has users close windows against the weather, such as rain and frost, to protect IT and other assets. Cover weather damage in the instruction as well as intruders.

clauses.title: Bringing in unauthorised IT systems
clauses.rationale: AT-02 conveys the ban in awareness training, and PL-04 sets it as a rule of behaviour. CM-07(09) prohibits using or connecting unauthorised hardware. PE-16 authorises and controls components that enter the facility. SC-42 can bar devices with sensors, such as phones with cameras, from defined areas.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names handing devices in at reception, or leaving them in lockers at the entrance, as one way to apply the ban. Provide such a place if you choose that route.

clauses.title: Escorting external visitors
clauses.rationale: AT-02 tells staff in awareness training to escort external visitors, and PL-04 sets it as a rule of behaviour. PE-03 requires escorts for visitors and controls their activity.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Supervising external visitors in sensitive areas
clauses.rationale: AT-02 tells staff in awareness training to supervise external visitors in sensitive areas, and PL-04 sets it as a rule of behaviour. PE-03 controls visitor activity in defined circumstances. MA-05 has designated staff supervise maintenance personnel who lack access authorisation, such as IT service providers.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Safekeeping of IT systems and media on site
clauses.rationale: AT-02 covers locking away IT systems and data media in awareness training. MP-04 has the organisation physically control media and store them securely in controlled areas.
clauses.gaps: MP-04 covers media. GS++ asks users to lock away IT systems as well, especially in rooms that outsiders use, such as conference rooms. Apply your storage rules to devices too.

clauses.title: Return of assets no longer needed
clauses.rationale: AT-02 reminds users in awareness training to return assets, and PL-04 makes it a rule of behaviour. PS-04 retrieves organisational property when employment ends. PS-05 has people hand back keys, cards and other items when they move to a new role.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks users to hand back an asset whenever they stop needing it, such as at the end of a project. Add that case to the return rules you apply when people leave or change roles.

clauses.title: Avoiding fire loads near technical rooms
clauses.rationale: AT-02 explains the fire risk of combustible material in awareness training and conveys the ban. PL-04 makes it a rule of behaviour to keep such material away from technical rooms.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks users to keep combustible material, such as cardboard boxes and batteries, away from technical rooms and utilities. Set the safe distance yourself, by the size of the fire load and the room's protection needs.

clauses.title: Use of fire protection equipment
clauses.rationale: AT-03(01) trains defined staff to use environmental controls, including handheld fire extinguishers. PE-13 provides the fire detection and suppression equipment that staff learn to use.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Use of water protection equipment
clauses.rationale: AT-03(01) trains defined staff to use environmental controls. PE-15 keeps master shutoff valves accessible and working, and makes sure key personnel know about them.
clauses.gaps: GS++ counts simple aids, such as sandbags and water barriers, as water protection equipment. Train staff on each aid you provide, as well as on the shutoff valves.

clauses.title: Processing confidential information in public
clauses.rationale: AT-02 covers the risk of working on confidential data in public, as part of content on telework and travel. PL-04 forbids processing confidential information where others can see or hear it. AC-19 gives guidance for mobile devices used outside controlled areas.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Caution against eavesdropping in mobile working
clauses.rationale: AT-02 provides awareness training, and its content can warn users about being overheard during mobile working. PE-17 sets controls for alternate work sites, such as home offices, which can include rules for confidential calls.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names the risk of being overheard during mobile working, such as on a journey or in public, as an awareness topic. Add it to your training content and your rules for confidential calls.

clauses.title: Safekeeping of IT systems and media away from the office
clauses.rationale: AT-02 covers keeping devices and media safe during mobile working, and PL-04 sets rules for storing them away from the office. AC-19 notes that users must physically protect mobile devices outside controlled areas. MP-05 protects and controls media outside controlled areas.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Mobile working with paper documents
clauses.rationale: AT-02 covers the handling of paper documents during mobile working in awareness training. MP-05 protects and controls non-digital media, paper included, during transport outside controlled areas.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Taking IT systems and media to mobile working
clauses.rationale: AT-02 awareness content can advise users to take only the devices and media their task needs. PL-04 can limit what users take off site through the rules of behaviour.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks users to take only the IT systems and media they need, judged by the permitted data locations and their tasks. Set that limit yourself in your rules for mobile working.

clauses.title: Taking IT systems and media abroad
clauses.rationale: AT-02 conveys the ban and the risks of foreign travel in awareness training. PL-04 can forbid taking unneeded devices and media abroad as a rule of behaviour. CM-02(07) issues specially configured devices to people travelling to high-risk locations and applies controls on their return.
clauses.gaps: CM-02(07) provides prepared devices for travel. GS++ also asks users to take abroad only the IT systems and media the business needs. Write that limit into your travel rules.

clauses.title: Travel and safety advice for trips outside Europe
clauses.rationale: AT-02 awareness content can point travellers to official travel and safety advice. AT-02(06) brings the current threat environment into training, which can include the risks of the destination country.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks users to check the German Federal Foreign Office's travel and safety advice before trips outside Europe. Point travellers to that source in your awareness content.

clauses.title: Basic principles of system administration
clauses.rationale: AT-03 gives role-based training to people in administrator roles, matched to their duties. For system and network administrators, that training covers the principles of secure administration.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Handling privileged access rights
clauses.rationale: AT-03 trains administrators in the use of privileged rights, and PL-04 sets separate rules of behaviour for privileged users. AC-06(02) has privileged users switch to non-privileged accounts for non-security tasks. IA-05 protects authenticators, and IA-05(07) keeps unencrypted credentials out of scripts and applications.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: System administration: security incidents
clauses.rationale: AT-03 gives administrators role-based training on the incident procedures and their duties in an incident. IR-02 gives incident response training that matches each person's assigned roles and responsibilities.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: System administration: structured cabling
clauses.rationale: AT-03 gives network administrators role-based training, which can cover structured cabling. PE-04 protects distribution and transmission lines, for example with conduits and locked wiring closets, and structured cabling supports that protection.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for awareness of structured cabling, where cable routes and connections follow one documented plan. Base the training on a cabling standard, such as EN 50173, and on your own labelling scheme.

clauses.title: System administration: internet use
clauses.rationale: AC-06(02) has administrators use non-privileged accounts for non-security tasks, such as web browsing. AT-03 trains administrators on the risk of browsing with administrator rights. PL-04 forbids internet access from administrator accounts in the rules for privileged users.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Awareness for top management
clauses.rationale: AT-02 includes managers and senior executives in literacy training and awareness, which covers the need for security. AT-03 gives senior leaders role-based training on their security responsibilities.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for top management to learn why information security matters for protecting business processes. Build that link into the training content for senior leaders.

clauses.title: Leading by example
clauses.rationale: AT-02 includes managers in literacy training and awareness, alongside other staff. AT-03 gives managers role-based training on their responsibilities, and that training can cover leading by example.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for managers to learn that they set the example for information security, so staff apply their training in daily work. Add that role-model duty to managers' training.

clauses.title: Whaling attacks on executives
clauses.rationale: AT-02(03) trains users, executives included, to recognise social engineering such as phishing and impersonation. AT-02(05) covers advanced persistent threats, which can target executives. AT-03(03) runs practical exercises that include whale phishing aimed at senior leaders.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: High risks from the risk analysis
clauses.rationale: AT-02(06) brings current threat information into literacy training and awareness. RA-03 shares the results of the risk assessment, including the high risks it finds, with defined personnel.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Architecture: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: SC-01 sets system and communications protection policy and procedures and names an official to manage them. It documents them and gives them to the roles that need them. PL-08 describes the security architecture, including how the network and connected infrastructure are protected.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for procedures and rules for the network architecture in particular. SC-01 covers system and communications protection as a whole, so give network architecture its own section in those procedures.

clauses.title: Architecture: regular review
clauses.rationale: SC-01 has the organisation review and update its system and communications protection policy and procedures at a set frequency and after defined events. PL-08 reviews and updates the security architecture at a set frequency.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Network segments
clauses.rationale: PL-08 sets the segmentation approach in the security architecture. SC-07 controls traffic at key internal interfaces, and SC-07(21) and (29) isolate components and functions in separate subnetworks. SC-32 partitions the system into separate physical or logical domains according to defined circumstances, such as protection needs.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Restricting connections between segments
clauses.rationale: AC-04 enforces approved information flows between segments. SC-07 controls traffic at internal interfaces and puts public services in a DMZ. SC-07(05) denies traffic by default. SC-07(13) isolates management systems and SC-07(15) routes privileged access through jump servers. SC-07(21) and (29) place components in separate subnetworks. SC-32 partitions groups such as operational technology (OT) and test systems into separate domains. CA-09 authorises internal connections, such as printers and OT systems. PE-04 controls physical access to network lines (ARCH.2.2.11).
clauses.gaps: GS++ names specific separations, including IPv4 from IPv6 and, as an option, VoIP from data systems (ARCH.2.2.9, ARCH.2.2.4). Add them to the flow rules at your segment boundaries.

clauses.title: Microsegmentation
