clauses.rationale: AC-04 enforces the allowed information flows for each system and limits which other systems it may talk to. SC-07(12) puts boundary protection, such as a firewall, on each host, and SC-07(21) isolates components from each other.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Inventory of networks
clauses.rationale: CA-03 documents each external connection and its interface. CA-09 does the same for internal connections and the information they carry. CM-08 inventories system components, including network devices. PL-02 describes the connections to other systems and the operating environment in the security plan.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for one inventory of networks, listing internal segments and external connections with the purpose of each. Bring the details these controls record together in that inventory.

clauses.title: Network diagram
clauses.rationale: CM-02 records the network topology and where components sit in the baseline configuration. PL-02 describes the system components and connections to other systems in the security plan. PL-08 describes how the network is arranged and protected in the security architecture.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a network diagram that shows the logical and physical structure of the network. Draw it from the topology and connections these controls record, and keep it up to date.

clauses.title: Network topology monitoring
clauses.rationale: CA-07 assesses controls on an ongoing basis at a set frequency, which can include the network architecture. CM-08(03) detects unauthorised components on the network. SI-04 detects unauthorised connections to the system, and SI-04(14) finds rogue wireless devices.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: WLAN coverage
clauses.rationale: AC-18(05) has the organisation choose antennas and set transmit power so the wireless signal stays within its controlled boundaries. This limits who can pick up the network from outside.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to test WLAN coverage, so the signal reaches the places where people need it. Test reception at key locations under real conditions.

clauses.title: Restricting WLAN signals in secure areas
clauses.rationale: AC-18(05) chooses antennas and sets transmit power so wireless signals stay within defined areas. PE-19 protects against information leaking out through electromagnetic signals, for example by shielding rooms.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Organisation-specific WLAN names (SSIDs)
clauses.rationale: AC-18 sets configuration requirements for each type of wireless access. CM-06 sets secure configuration settings that replace vendor defaults, such as the factory network name (SSID).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for WLAN names specific to the organisation, so users can recognise its networks and tell them apart. Choose descriptive names, such as one that marks the guest network.

clauses.title: Encrypted WLAN connections
clauses.rationale: AC-18(01) protects wireless access with authentication and encryption. SC-08(01) encrypts information in transit, and SC-08(03) also protects data outside the message content, such as addresses. SC-13 sets the type of cryptography for each use, so you can require a recognised standard.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Network access control
clauses.rationale: IA-03 identifies and authenticates devices before they connect to the network, and IA-03(04) bases this on device attestation. CA-09(01) checks components for compliance before an internal connection, as dynamic network access control does (ARCH.4.1.1). CM-08(03) disables network access for unauthorised components or isolates them. SC-07(20) isolates components dynamically, as a quarantine network does (ARCH.4.1.2).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Authorised routing
clauses.rationale: CM-03 reviews and approves configuration changes, such as new routes, under change control. CM-05 restricts who may change router configurations. AC-04 enforces approved authorisations for information flows between connected systems.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks a responsible person or role to authorise each routing connection. Assign that role and send routing changes to it for approval.

clauses.title: Authentication of routing protocols
clauses.rationale: IA-03(01) authenticates routing peers with cryptography before they connect. SC-08 protects routing updates in transit, and SC-08(01) detects any change to them. SC-23 protects the authenticity of routing protocol sessions.
clauses.gaps: GS++ gives route origin validation with RPKI as an example, which protects BGP against route hijacking. Add origin validation alongside the peer authentication these controls cover.

clauses.title: Restricting and inspecting connections
clauses.rationale: AC-04(08) filters content, such as web and DNS traffic. AC-04(04) controls encrypted traffic and AC-04(03) adapts flow rules to changing conditions. CM-07 blocks vulnerable protocols and services, including dynamic routing at the edge. SC-07 denies traffic by default, prevents split tunnelling, routes traffic through proxies and checks protocol formats. SI-03 stops known malicious content at network entry points. SI-04(04) watches traffic in and out for attacks, and SI-04(10) makes encrypted traffic visible. PL-08(01) layers the filters, as P-A-P does, and PL-08(02) takes them from different suppliers.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for the P-A-P structure, two packet filters with an application gateway between them, each on separate hardware. It also asks you to block known illegal content and layer 2 attacks, for example with DHCP snooping.

clauses.title: Blocking direct connections to public networks
clauses.rationale: SC-07 connects the system to external networks only through managed interfaces, which filter the traffic. SC-07(28) prohibits direct connection of the systems you define to a public network.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Controlled paths for wide area connections
clauses.rationale: AC-04(21) separates information flows physically or logically. SC-07(04) gives each external telecommunication service a managed interface and a traffic flow policy. SC-08(05) protects transmission lines with a protected distribution system, which controls the physical path.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names dedicated routes, such as dark fibre, as one way to control the path physically. Use dedicated lines where a link needs that level of control.

clauses.title: Encryption of wide area connections
clauses.rationale: SC-08(01) encrypts information in transit, such as traffic over wide area links. AC-17(02) encrypts remote access sessions. SC-13 sets the type of cryptography for each use, so you can require a recognised standard.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Dedicated host systems for servers
clauses.rationale: CM-07 configures systems to provide only essential capabilities, and SP 800-53 advises one function per component where feasible. SC-32 partitions components into separate physical or logical domains, which can mean a dedicated virtual or physical host for each application.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Dedicated hardware for host systems
clauses.rationale: SC-32 partitions system components into separate physical domains. Choosing physical separation puts host systems on dedicated hardware of their own.
clauses.gaps: GS++ aims to avoid circular dependencies, such as a virtualisation host whose domain controller runs as a virtual machine on that same host. Run the services a host depends on elsewhere.

clauses.title: Separating development and test environments
clauses.rationale: CM-04(01) analyses changes in a separate test environment before they go into operation. SC-32 partitions development and test systems from production into separate domains.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for development and test environments on hosts of their own, apart from production hosts. A fault in test software then stays away from the production hypervisor.

clauses.title: Redundancy in the core network
clauses.rationale: SI-13 provides standby components and a way to swap them in when an active component fails. SI-13(05) adds failover, so the switch happens in real time or near real time.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for redundant components in the core network, so the network stays up when one of them fails. Give each critical core device a standby.

clauses.title: Redundant telephony connections
clauses.rationale: CP-08 sets up alternate telecommunications services that can take over when the primary service fails. CP-08(02) avoids a single point of failure shared with the primary service, and CP-08(03) gets the alternate service from a separate provider.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Redundant servers
clauses.rationale: SI-13(05) provides failover to standby components in real time or near real time. CP-09(06) keeps a redundant secondary system ready to take over without loss of information. SC-36 distributes processing and storage across several locations or domains.
clauses.gaps: GS++ counts a host as redundant when its power supply and network connection are redundant too. Build both into each host the application needs.

clauses.title: Sizing the network connection
clauses.rationale: CP-02(02) plans the processing and telecommunications capacity needed during contingency operations. SC-05(02) manages capacity and bandwidth so services withstand flooding attacks.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to size network connections to the organisation's normal demand. Record what critical processes need and plan link capacity from that.

clauses.title: Load balancing
clauses.rationale: SC-05(02) manages capacity and redundancy so services stay available under heavy load. SC-36 distributes processing across several components or domains, so many systems share the work.
clauses.gaps: GS++ suggests automatic load balancing, run by the network or by the servers themselves. Choose the method that suits each application, such as a load balancer in front of several servers.

clauses.title: Automatic scaling
clauses.rationale: SC-05(02) manages the capacity of the system to limit the effects of flooding and overload. That keeps the application available when demand rises.
clauses.gaps: GS++ suggests scaling an application's instances up and down automatically, based on thresholds such as CPU load or response time. Set those thresholds for each application.

clauses.title: Content delivery network
clauses.rationale: SC-05 limits the effects of denial-of-service attacks, and SC-05(02) adds capacity and redundancy against flooding. SC-36 distributes processing and storage across physical locations, as a content delivery network does.
clauses.gaps: GS++ suggests a content delivery network for applications that must stay available worldwide, to absorb load peaks and denial-of-service attacks. You can run one yourself or use a service provider.

clauses.title: Protection against volumetric denial-of-service attacks
clauses.rationale: SC-05 protects against denial-of-service attacks or limits their effects, using controls the organisation chooses. SC-05(02) manages capacity and bandwidth to absorb floods, and SC-05(03) detects and monitors attacks.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Access rights: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: AC-01 sets access control policy and procedures, documents them, gives them to the roles that need them and names an official to manage them. The policy covers the management of accounts and access rights. IA-01 does the same for identification and authentication, which covers the identity side.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for each identity and access management task to go to a named person or role. SP 800-53 sets roles and responsibilities at the level of the policy, so assign the tasks yourself.

clauses.title: Access rights: regular review
clauses.rationale: AC-01 has the organisation review and update its access control policy and procedures at a set frequency and after defined events. IA-01 does the same for the identification and authentication policy and procedures.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Inventory of authentication and authorisation systems
clauses.rationale: CM-08 keeps an inventory of system components, which can list each authentication and authorisation system, such as directory services, identity providers and single sign-on platforms. CM-08(04) records who is responsible for each component.
clauses.gaps: CM-08 asks for an inventory of all components. GS++ asks for a separate view of the authentication and authorisation systems, so mark them in the inventory with their protocols and connected applications.

clauses.title: Inventory of access rights
clauses.rationale: AC-02 specifies, for each account, its authorised users, its group and role memberships and its access authorisations. That is the core of an access rights inventory. IA-04 assigns each identifier to the intended person, role, service or device, which links people to their identities.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for one inventory across all systems that links people, identities, accounts and access rights. AC-02 works system by system, so bring the account records together into that inventory yourself.

clauses.title: Identity linked to one person or IT system
clauses.rationale: IA-02 uniquely identifies each of the organisation's users and ties that identity to the processes acting for them. IA-03 uniquely identifies devices, which covers the identities of IT systems. IA-04 assigns each identifier to the one person, service or device it is meant for. IA-12 resolves each user identity to a unique individual through identity proofing.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Restricting who can manage identities
clauses.rationale: AC-06 applies least privilege, and AC-06(01) lets only defined roles use security functions such as identity administration. IA-04 requires authorisation from defined roles before an identifier is assigned. IA-04(09) keeps identity attributes in protected central storage.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 asks for authorisation before an identifier is assigned. GS++ also restricts who may change or delete an identity. Give write access to identity records to named roles alone, such as HR or the administrators.

clauses.title: Checking identity master data
clauses.rationale: AC-02 reviews accounts at a set frequency. It also aligns account management with the personnel processes for leaving and transfers, which ties account data to HR records. SI-18 checks personal data at a set frequency for accuracy and completeness, and corrects it. This covers the master data of people's identities.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to check identity master data regularly against source records, such as HR files, network scans or a configuration management database. SI-18 covers personal data, so set up the same check for IT-system identities.

clauses.title: Logging changes to identity master data
clauses.rationale: AC-02(04) automatically audits when accounts are created, changed, enabled, disabled or removed, which covers identity data held in accounts. AU-02 lets the organisation name changes to identity master data as an event type to log. AU-03 makes each record show what happened, when and which account acted. AU-12 generates the records for those event types.
clauses.gaps: AC-02(04) logs changes to accounts. GS++ also covers identity master data held outside accounts. Add changes to that data to the event types you log under AU-02.

clauses.title: Deactivation of identities on leaving
clauses.rationale: AC-02 tells account managers when users leave and disables their accounts in step with the termination process. AC-02(03) disables accounts that have lost their link to a user or have been inactive for a set period. PS-04 disables system access within a set time when someone leaves and revokes their authenticators and credentials.
clauses.gaps: GS++ counts long absences, such as parental leave or a sabbatical, as leaving. PS-04 covers the end of employment, so add long absences to the conditions under which AC-02 disables accounts.

clauses.title: Deletion of identities after the retention period
clauses.rationale: AC-02 removes unneeded accounts in line with defined policy and criteria. SI-12 keeps information for as long as laws and policy require, and SI-12(03) disposes of it when the retention period ends.
clauses.gaps: AC-02 removes accounts. GS++ also asks you to delete identity records securely when their retention period ends. Choose disposal methods under SI-12(03) that also reach copies in backups.

clauses.title: Central management of accounts
clauses.rationale: AC-02(01) supports account management with automated mechanisms. IA-13 uses identity providers and authorisation servers to manage identities and their access rights centrally. PL-09 lets the organisation manage chosen controls, such as account management, centrally across systems.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Authorisation of new accounts
clauses.rationale: AC-02 requires defined people or roles to approve each request to create an account. IA-04 requires authorisation from defined roles before an account identifier is assigned.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Restricting account management to administrators
clauses.rationale: AC-02 assigns account managers, so only designated staff manage accounts. AC-06(01) lets only defined roles use security functions such as account management, and AC-06(05) restricts privileged accounts to defined personnel.
clauses.gaps: GS++ limits account management to administrators. AC-02 lets you choose the account managers, so give that role to administrators.

clauses.title: Logging changes to accounts
clauses.rationale: AC-02(04) automatically audits when accounts are created, changed, enabled, disabled or removed. AU-02 has the organisation select these account actions as event types to log, and AU-12 generates the records. AU-09 protects the records from unauthorised change and deletion, so the log stands up to audit.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Account linked to one identity
clauses.rationale: AC-02 names the authorised user of each account. IA-02 uniquely identifies each of the organisation's users, so every account traces back to one person. IA-04 assigns each account identifier to the one holder it is meant for.
clauses.gaps: AC-02(09) allows shared and group accounts under defined conditions. GS++ asks for each account to belong to exactly one identity, so make that your rule.

clauses.title: Privileged accounts
clauses.rationale: AC-02(07) sets up and administers privileged accounts under a role-based scheme. AC-06(02) has users with privileged access use non-privileged accounts for other work, such as email and web browsing. So administrators use separate accounts for administration.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Single sign-on
clauses.rationale: IA-02(10) provides single sign-on for defined accounts and services. IA-13 has applications rely on central identity providers and authorisation servers to authenticate users and authorise their access.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Account hints in login error messages
clauses.rationale: IA-06 obscures the feedback from authentication, so the message after a failed login hides details such as whether the account exists. SI-11 keeps error messages free of information an attacker could exploit.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names user enumeration, where an attacker probes which accounts exist. Give the same message for a wrong user name as for a wrong password.

clauses.title: Event-driven deactivation of accounts
clauses.rationale: AC-02(03) disables accounts that have expired, have lost their link to a user, breach policy or have been inactive for a set period. AC-02(13) disables the accounts of high-risk individuals. PS-04 disables system access when employment ends.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Login attempt limit on IT systems
clauses.rationale: AC-07 limits the number of consecutive failed login attempts. Once the limit is reached, it locks the account or device for a set time or delays the next login prompt.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Login attempt limit for applications
clauses.rationale: AC-07 limits the number of consecutive failed login attempts, in applications as well as on systems. Once the limit is reached, it locks the account for a set time or delays the next login prompt.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: System lock after inactivity
clauses.rationale: AC-11 locks the device after a set period of inactivity and keeps it locked until the user signs in again. AC-12 ends the session after defined conditions, such as inactivity, which covers the logout that GS++ accepts in place of a screen lock.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Application lock after inactivity
clauses.rationale: AC-11 locks access after a set period of inactivity until the user authenticates again, and the same rule can apply to an application. AC-12 ends a user's session automatically after defined conditions, such as inactivity. IA-11 asks the user to authenticate again in defined situations, such as returning to an idle application session.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 sets the inactivity lock at device level. In each application, build the lock from AC-12 session termination or an IA-11 prompt to sign in again.

clauses.title: Blocking the reuse of accounts
clauses.rationale: IA-04 blocks the reuse of identifiers for a defined period. That stops a former account from passing to another person, role, service or device within that time.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Deletion of accounts after the retention period
clauses.rationale: AC-02 removes unneeded accounts in line with defined policy and criteria. SI-12 sets how long information is held, and SI-12(03) disposes of it when the retention period ends. Account records follow the same timing.
clauses.gaps: GS++ ties account deletion to the legal retention periods and asks for secure deletion, including copies in backups. Apply the SI-12 retention periods to account records and choose disposal methods that reach backups.

clauses.title: Banning shared accounts
clauses.rationale: AC-02 defines the allowed and the prohibited account types, so shared accounts can go on the prohibited list. AC-02(09) allows shared and group accounts only under defined conditions. IA-02 requires each of the organisation's users to be uniquely identified, which calls for individual accounts.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Shared accounts: multi-factor authentication
clauses.rationale: IA-02(01) and (02) require multi-factor authentication for privileged and non-privileged accounts. Every account falls into one of those two types, so they cover shared accounts too.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 sets multi-factor authentication by account type. GS++ names shared accounts. Turn it on for each shared account, for example with several hardware tokens or one-time password apps registered to it.

clauses.title: Shared accounts: documenting handovers
clauses.rationale: AC-02 specifies the authorised users and group membership of each account, which records who may use a shared account. IA-02(05) has each user authenticate individually before using a shared account, which records who used it and when.
clauses.gaps: AC-02 lists who may use an account. GS++ also asks for a record of who could use a shared account at each handover, such as a shift change. Duty rosters can serve as that record.

clauses.title: Shared accounts: password change on leaving
clauses.rationale: AC-02 changes the authenticators of shared or group accounts when someone leaves the group. IA-05 changes the authenticators of group or role accounts whenever their membership changes.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Caching of login credentials
clauses.rationale: IA-05(13) stops cached authenticators from working after a set period. IA-05 also protects the content of authenticators from disclosure, which makes them harder to steal.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to turn off credential caching on IT systems. IA-05(13) limits how long cached authenticators work, so set that period to zero.

clauses.title: Service accounts
clauses.rationale: IA-05 refreshes authenticators on a schedule or after defined events. IA-05(07) keeps unencrypted static credentials out of code and storage, and IA-05(18) uses password managers to generate and manage passwords. SC-12 manages the keys and certificates that service accounts use to authenticate.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for automatic rotation and distribution of service account credentials, free of manual steps. Automate the IA-05 refresh for these accounts, for example with a secrets vault.

clauses.title: Emergency access accounts
clauses.rationale: AC-02 defines emergency accounts as an account type, and AC-02(02) disables or removes them automatically after a set period. AC-03(10) lets defined roles override access controls under defined conditions, with an audit trail, which is the break-glass case.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 treats emergency accounts as short-lived accounts for a crisis. GS++ describes a standing break-glass account, set up in advance. Give it a long password and store it in a safe or split it between administrators.

clauses.title: Emergency access account for directory services
clauses.rationale: AC-02 defines emergency accounts as an account type, which can include one for the directory service. AC-02(02) disables or removes emergency accounts automatically after a set period. AC-03(10) lets defined roles override access controls under defined conditions, with an audit trail, which covers emergency access to the directory.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 treats emergency accounts as short-lived accounts for a crisis. GS++ asks for a standing break-glass account for each directory service, set up in advance. Give it a long password and store it in a safe or split it between administrators.

clauses.title: Alternative authentication on IT systems
clauses.rationale: AC-07(04) allows an alternate authentication factor, different from the primary one, once the login attempt limit is reached. IA-05 sets procedures for lost or damaged authenticators and requires each authenticator to be strong enough for its use.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for the alternative method to be as trustworthy as the primary one. IA-05 asks for sufficient strength, so give the recovery path the same assurance as the normal login.

clauses.title: Alternative authentication for applications
clauses.rationale: AC-07(04) allows an alternate authentication factor, different from the primary one, once the login attempt limit is reached. IA-05 sets procedures for lost or damaged authenticators in applications and requires each authenticator to be strong enough for its use.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for the alternative login to an application to be as trustworthy as the primary one. IA-05 asks for sufficient strength, so give account recovery the same assurance as the normal login.

clauses.title: Principle of least privilege
clauses.rationale: AC-06 gives users and processes only the access their tasks need. AC-03(07) enforces role-based access control (BER.4.1.1). AC-02(06) manages privileges dynamically for just-in-time access (BER.4.1.2), and AC-02(07) runs privileged accounts on a role-based scheme.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Authorisation of access rights
clauses.rationale: AC-02 authorises access on the basis of a valid access authorisation and the intended use of the system. It requires defined roles to approve requests to create accounts and sets the criteria for group and role membership.
clauses.gaps: AC-02 names approvers for new accounts. GS++ asks for named people or roles to authorise every assignment of access rights, so extend the approval step to later grants too.

clauses.title: Justification of access rights
clauses.rationale: AC-02 records the access authorisations of each account and ties each one to the intended use of the system. AC-02(04) audits changes to accounts, which leaves a record of each modification.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a written reason with every grant of access rights and every change to them. Add a justification field to your access request process, for example in your identity and access management system.

clauses.title: Review of access rights
clauses.rationale: AC-02 reviews accounts at a set frequency against the account management requirements, which compares documented with actual access rights (BER.4.4.1). AC-06(07) reviews assigned privileges at a set frequency and removes unneeded ones.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: System functions without authentication
clauses.rationale: AC-14 identifies the user actions a system allows without identification or authentication. It documents them in the system's security plan, with the reasons for each.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Application functions without authentication
clauses.rationale: AC-14 identifies the user actions an application allows without identification or authentication, such as a password reset or public content. It documents them in the security plan, with the reasons for each.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: IT system linked to one account
clauses.rationale: AC-02 specifies the authorised users of a system, which can be a single account. AC-03 enforces the approved authorisations, so only that account can reach the system.
clauses.gaps: GS++ suggests binding an IT system that needs special protection to exactly one account. Limit the authorisations for that system to the one account yourself.

clauses.title: Revocation of access rights
clauses.rationale: AC-02 disables or removes accounts when the need for access ends and aligns this with personnel processes. AC-03(08) revokes access authorisations when security attributes change. PS-04 disables access and revokes credentials when employment ends. PS-05 reviews and modifies access authorisations when people move to other roles.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Issuing, registering and assigning authenticators
clauses.rationale: IA-05 verifies the recipient's identity before it first hands out an authenticator (BER.5.1.1), and sets procedures for initial content and distribution. IA-05(02) maps each key-based identity to its account. IA-12 checks each user's identity evidence at registration, so authenticators go to the right person.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Resetting and replacing authenticators
clauses.rationale: IA-05 sets procedures for authenticators that are lost, compromised or damaged, which covers resetting and replacing them. It also changes or refreshes authenticators when defined events occur, such as a suspected compromise.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Procedure for revoking authenticators
clauses.rationale: IA-05 sets administrative procedures for revoking authenticators, whatever the reason. PS-04 covers people who leave the organisation and revokes their authenticators and credentials when their employment ends.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Only established cryptography for authenticators
clauses.rationale: IA-05 asks for authenticators with enough strength of mechanism for their intended use. IA-05(01) stores passwords with an approved salted key derivation function. SC-13 implements the type of cryptography each use requires, authentication included.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for algorithms from one or more recognised standards. Name yours, such as BSI TR-02102, where SC-13 has you set the cryptography each use requires.

clauses.title: Disabling biometric-only authentication on IT systems
clauses.rationale: IA-02(01) and (02) ask for multi-factor authentication, so a biometric works only together with another factor. IA-05 asks for authenticators strong enough for their intended use. IA-05(12) sets biometric quality requirements, and IA-05(17) detects presentation attacks, such as forged fingerprints.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for sign-in by biometrics alone to be switched off on IT systems, such as fingerprint unlock on a smartphone. SP 800-53 reaches this through multi-factor authentication where IA-02 asks for it, so switch biometric-only sign-in off everywhere else too.

clauses.title: Disabling preconfigured authenticators on IT systems
clauses.rationale: CM-06 sets secure configuration settings that disable vendor default accounts and credentials on each system. IA-05 changes default authenticators before first use, and IA-05(05) has developers and installers provide unique authenticators before delivery.
clauses.gaps: IA-05 asks you to change default authenticators. GS++ asks you to switch them off, hardware tokens and certificates included, so cover these in your CM-06 settings.

clauses.title: Disabling preconfigured authenticators in applications
clauses.rationale: CM-06 sets secure configuration settings that disable vendor default accounts and credentials in applications. IA-05 changes an application's default authenticators before first use, and IA-05(05) has developers and installers provide unique authenticators before delivery.
clauses.gaps: IA-05 asks you to change an application's default authenticators. GS++ asks you to switch them off, tokens and certificates included, so cover these in your CM-06 settings.

clauses.title: Multi-factor authentication at the perimeter
clauses.rationale: IA-02(01) and (02) ask for multi-factor authentication on every account, IA-02(06) puts one factor on a separate device and IA-02(08) makes sign-in resistant to replay. AC-17 sets the connection requirements for each type of remote access, such as multi-factor authentication at the VPN gateway.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for phishing-resistant methods, such as FIDO2 passkeys, on every interface reachable from outside. SP 800-53 asks for replay resistance, which covers part of that, so choose a method that resists fake login pages.

clauses.title: Multi-factor authentication for far-reaching access rights
clauses.rationale: IA-02(01) asks for multi-factor authentication on privileged accounts, such as administrator accounts for the directory service or DNS. IA-02(02) extends it to other accounts, which covers wide access to sensitive data.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Restricting access to authenticators on each IT system
clauses.rationale: AC-03 enforces approved access rights on the system's stores of passwords, keys and tokens, for reading and for writing. IA-05 protects authenticator content from unauthorised disclosure and modification, and IA-05(02) enforces authorised access to private keys.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Restricting access to authenticators in each application
clauses.rationale: AC-03 enforces approved access rights on the application's stores of passwords, keys and tokens, for reading and for writing. IA-05 protects the authenticator content the application holds from unauthorised disclosure and modification.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Two-person access through split authenticators
clauses.rationale: AC-03(02) enforces dual authorisation for defined privileged commands and actions, so two people must act together. That gives the four-eyes principle GS++ applies to data with high confidentiality or integrity needs.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for one authenticator to be split between people, such as one holding the token and the other the password. Set up this split knowledge yourself for the actions that need dual authorisation.

clauses.title: Identity check before resetting or replacing authenticators
clauses.rationale: IA-05 verifies the recipient's identity when it first distributes an authenticator. It also sets procedures for lost or compromised authenticators, which can include that check. IA-12 validates and verifies identity evidence, which a reset process can use to check the requester.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to check the requester's identity before every reset or replacement. IA-05 states the check for first issue, so write it into your procedure for lost or compromised authenticators.

clauses.title: Blocking compromised authenticators
clauses.rationale: IA-05 sets administrative procedures for compromised authenticators, such as revoking them. IA-05(01) keeps a list of compromised passwords and rejects any new password found on it.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to block compromised biometric characteristics too, such as fingerprints in unauthorised hands. IA-05(01) keeps a blocklist for passwords, so extend your blocking to biometrics and other authenticators.

clauses.title: Password manager for users
clauses.rationale: IA-05(18) employs password managers that generate and manage passwords for users. It also protects the passwords the manager stores, which GS++ describes as an encrypted database behind a master password or multi-factor authentication.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Blocking password reuse
clauses.rationale: IA-05(01)(h) lets the organisation set its own composition rules, which can include a password history. IA-05(08) manages the risk that comes from one person holding accounts on several systems, such as password reuse. IA-05(18) password managers generate a unique password for each account.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the system to block a new password that matches an earlier one. SP 800-53 leaves that to the organisation, so add a history rule to your IA-05(01)(h) composition rules.

clauses.title: Blocking trivial passwords
clauses.rationale: IA-05(01) keeps a list of commonly used, expected and compromised passwords. It rejects any new password found on that list, which blocks trivial passwords such as '123456' and passwords exposed in leaks.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Criteria for password quality
clauses.title_de: Kriterien für die Qualität von Passwörtern
clauses.rationale: IA-05 asks for authenticators with enough strength of mechanism for their intended use. IA-05(01)(f) allows long passwords and passphrases, and IA-05(01)(h) sets composition and complexity rules.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to base the criteria on a password's lifetime and the ways it can be attacked. Work both into the strength you set for each intended use under IA-05.

clauses.title: Event-driven password changes
clauses.rationale: IA-05 changes or refreshes authenticators when defined events occur, such as signs of a compromise. An organisation that sets these events and leaves the time period empty gets the event-driven changes GS++ asks for.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for password changes only when there is cause, such as a leak or a phishing incident. IA-05 also allows changes on a fixed schedule, so tailor it to events alone.

clauses.title: Monitoring credentials for compromise
clauses.rationale: AU-13 monitors open sources for disclosed organisational information, such as leaked credentials, and AU-13(01) uses automated tools to do it. IA-05(01) updates the list of compromised passwords whenever passwords are suspected of exposure.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for an automated mechanism that checks your credentials for compromise, for example against leak databases. Include credentials in the information AU-13 monitors for, and automate the check.

clauses.title: Established algorithms for key generation
clauses.rationale: SC-12 sets the requirements for key generation. SC-12(02) and (03) produce symmetric and asymmetric keys with approved key management technology and processes. SC-13 implements the type of cryptography each use requires.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Key length when generating keys
clauses.rationale: SC-12 sets the organisation's key generation requirements, which include key length. SC-13 implements the type and strength of cryptography each use requires, as set by the standards the organisation chooses.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for key lengths from a recognised standard, such as BSI TR-02102. Name the standard and its key lengths in your SC-12 key generation requirements.

clauses.title: Register of public keys
clauses.rationale: SC-12 manages keys under requirements the organisation defines, which can include a register of public keys and their attributes. SC-17 issues certificates under a certificate policy, and each certificate records the holder's identity, validity, key usage and algorithm.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a register of every public key, with its identity, expiry date, purpose, key type and algorithm. Certificates hold most of these details, so build the register from them and add keys held outside certificates.

clauses.title: Key generation on secure IT systems
clauses.rationale: SC-12 sets the requirements for key generation, which can cover the protection of the generating system. SC-12(02) and (03) produce keys with validated or approved key management technology.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to generate each key on a system with at least the protection level of the system that will use it. Add that rule to your SC-12 key generation requirements.

clauses.title: Criteria for random number quality in key generation
clauses.title_de: Kriterien für die Qualität von Zufallszahlen
clauses.rationale: SC-12 sets key generation requirements, which can include criteria for the quality of random numbers. SC-13 implements the required types of cryptography, which can name approved random number generators.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to set criteria for random number generators, such as independently tested generators with an unpredictable source. Write those criteria into your SC-12 key generation requirements.

clauses.title: Established algorithms for key transport
clauses.rationale: SC-08(01) uses cryptography to protect the confidentiality and integrity of keys in transit. SC-12 sets the requirements for key distribution. SC-13 implements the type of cryptography each use requires, key transport included.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to transport secret keys with established algorithms only, such as those in BSI TR-02102. Name the algorithms for key transport in your SC-12 and SC-13 settings.

clauses.title: Transport of private keys only with approval
clauses.rationale: IA-05(02) enforces authorised access to the private keys used for public key-based authentication. SC-12 sets requirements for key access and distribution, which can require approval before a private key leaves its system.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a named person or role to approve each export of a private key. Add that approval step to your SC-12 requirements and assign the role.

clauses.title: Established algorithms for key use
clauses.rationale: SC-13 determines each cryptographic use and implements the type of cryptography it requires. Keys then work only with the approved algorithms set for their use.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Purpose binding for keys
clauses.rationale: SC-12 sets key management requirements, which can bind each key to its registered purpose. SC-17 issues certificates under a certificate policy, and their key usage fields limit what each key may do.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to forbid any use of a key outside its registered purpose, the private key included. Write that rule into your SC-12 requirements and enforce it through key usage settings.

clauses.title: Stopping encryption and signing with expired keys
clauses.rationale: SC-12 manages keys over their life cycle under requirements the organisation defines. These can set a cryptoperiod for each key and end its use for encryption or signing once that period is over.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to stop encrypting and signing with a key once its usage period ends. You can still decrypt and verify old data with it. Write this rule into your SC-12 requirements.

clauses.title: Integrity of secret keys
clauses.rationale: SC-12 sets requirements for storing secret keys and controlling access to them. SI-07 uses integrity verification tools to detect unauthorised changes to defined information, such as stored keys, and SI-07(01) runs the check at defined events.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to verify a secret key's integrity before every use, for example against a checksum held on another system. Add keys to the information SI-07 checks, and make every use a checking event under SI-07(01).

clauses.title: Authenticity of public keys
clauses.rationale: IA-05(02) validates each certificate by building and verifying a certification path to an accepted trust anchor. SC-17 allows only approved trust anchors in the organisation's trust stores.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to check the authenticity of every public key before use, including keys outside certificates, such as SSH host keys. Set up an authenticity check for those keys yourself.

clauses.title: Validity of keys
clauses.rationale: IA-05(02) checks certificate status information, revocation included, when it validates a certificate, and keeps a local cache of revocation data. SC-12 manages keys under requirements that include their cryptoperiods.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a validity check before every use of any key, covering its usage period and revocation status. Set that check in your SC-12 requirements for keys used outside authentication.

clauses.title: Checking keys before they expire
clauses.rationale: SC-12 manages keys over their life cycle under requirements the organisation defines. These can include tracking when each key expires and replacing it in good time.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to check keys regularly for an upcoming expiry, so interfaces and applications keep working. Add a schedule for these checks to your SC-12 requirements.

clauses.title: Procedure for retiring secret keys after use
clauses.rationale: SC-12 sets the organisation's requirements for key destruction. These cover secret keys once their task is done, so the organisation takes them out of service in a controlled way.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to delete ephemeral keys straight after the session. Before you retire a key, re-encrypt the data it protects under a new key. Add both steps to your SC-12 procedure.

clauses.title: Rules for key certification
clauses.rationale: SC-12(03) produces asymmetric keys with certificates issued under requirements the organisation defines. SC-17 issues public key certificates under an organisation-defined certificate policy, which sets the rules for certification.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to name a role for certification and to test keys at request, renewal and revocation. Record each key's certification and revocation status in the public key register. Set these rules in your certificate policy, for example one based on RFC 3647.

clauses.title: Emergency planning: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: CP-01 sets contingency planning policy and procedures, documents them, gives them to defined roles and names an official to manage them. CP-02 assigns contingency roles and responsibilities with contact details and distributes the plan to key personnel (NOT.1.1.2, NOT.1.1.3).
clauses.gaps: GS++ offers an optional business continuity management system to BSI Standard 200-4 (NOT.1.1.4). It reaches further than contingency planning, so follow that standard if you choose the option.

clauses.title: Emergency planning: regular review
clauses.rationale: CP-01 reviews and updates the contingency planning policy and procedures at a set frequency and after defined events. CP-02 reviews the contingency plan and updates it for changes and for problems found.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Emergency and crisis organisation: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: CP-02 sets contingency roles and responsibilities, names the people who hold them with contact details and coordinates with incident handling (NOT.2.1.1). CP-04 tests the plan with exercises, such as tabletop exercises, which covers crisis staff exercises (NOT.2.1.4).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a special organisation for emergencies and crises, with a crisis staff and emergency teams, and a way to alert it (NOT.2.1.2). Build it yourself, for example to BSI Standard 200-4, with a crisis staff room if you choose (NOT.2.1.3).

clauses.title: Restart plan for time-critical systems and applications
clauses.rationale: CP-02 sets recovery objectives and restoration priorities, CP-02(03) plans to resume mission and business functions within a set time, and CP-02(08) identifies critical assets. CP-10 recovers and reconstitutes the system to a known state within the recovery objectives.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Business continuity plan for time-critical processes
clauses.rationale: CP-02 identifies essential mission and business functions and plans how to keep them running during a disruption. CP-02(05) plans for the continuance of those functions.
clauses.gaps: CP-02 plans for each system. GS++ asks for a continuity plan for each time-critical business process, including manual workarounds, such as running a digital process on paper. Write these process plans alongside your system plans.

clauses.title: Awareness of what to do in an emergency
clauses.rationale: CP-03 gives system users contingency training matched to their roles, at set intervals and when systems change. It covers what the organisation expects of each person in an emergency.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Functional test of emergency plans
clauses.rationale: CP-04 tests the contingency plan at a set frequency to confirm that it works and that staff are ready. It then reviews the results and corrects the plan. CP-04(04) includes full system recovery in the tests.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Fallback telecommunications services
clauses.rationale: CP-08 sets up alternate telecommunications services, with agreements that let operations resume when the primary services fail. SC-47 sets up alternate communications paths for command and control, such as out-of-band coordination in a crisis.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Security mechanisms for emergencies
clauses.rationale: CP-13 has the organisation use alternative or supplemental security mechanisms when the primary means is unavailable or compromised, as can happen in an emergency.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Documentation of backup sources
clauses.rationale: CP-09 backs up user-level and system-level information and system documentation on the system components the organisation defines. Those choices set the data each backup covers.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a written list of the data to back up, including data held by service providers or in the cloud. Record your CP-09 choices in that list.

clauses.title: Backup of IT systems
clauses.rationale: CP-09 backs up system-level information and system documentation at a frequency the organisation sets, in line with its recovery time and recovery point objectives.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Backup of applications
clauses.rationale: CP-09 backs up user-level and system-level information, such as application data and configuration, at a set frequency. It applies to the system components the organisation defines, applications among them.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Automated backup
clauses.rationale: CP-09 runs backups of user-level and system-level information at a frequency set to meet the recovery time and recovery point objectives.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for backups to run through an automated mechanism, such as backup software or scheduled scripts, which avoids human error and omissions. Automate your CP-09 backups to meet the requirement.

clauses.title: Archiving data needed in the long term
clauses.rationale: SI-12 manages and retains information as laws, regulations, policy and operational needs require. That covers long-term archiving of the information the organisation must retain.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for archived data to stay usable over time. Archive with it the assets needed to use the data, such as software and keys (NOT.4.5.1), and the documentation (NOT.4.5.2).

clauses.title: Protected storage of backups
clauses.rationale: CP-09 protects the confidentiality, integrity and availability of backup information, and CP-09(03) stores backup copies in a separate facility or fire-rated container. MP-04 physically controls backup media and stores them securely within controlled areas.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Versioned backups
clauses.rationale: CP-09 runs backups at a frequency set by the recovery point objective. Its frequency and retention settings can provide several generations of backups.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for backup versions from different points in time, so data deleted before the last backup can be restored. Set retention to hold several generations, such as three each for the last hours, days, weeks and months.

clauses.title: Encrypted backups
clauses.rationale: CP-09(08) uses cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorised disclosure and modification of backup information. SC-13 implements the required type of cryptography for each use, in line with recognised standards.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Dedicated storage media for backups
clauses.rationale: CP-09(01) tests backup information to verify the reliability of the storage media and the integrity of the information on them.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for storage media used only for backups and suited to the set retention period, which can run from months to years. Choose media that stay readable for that long.

clauses.title: Separate storage of backups
clauses.rationale: CP-06 sets up an alternate storage site for backups, and CP-06(01) separates it from the primary site. CP-09(03) stores backup copies in a separate facility or fire-rated container away from the operational system.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Media archive
clauses.rationale: MP-04 physically controls media and stores them securely in controlled areas, such as a locked media archive. CP-09(03) stores backup copies in a separate facility or fire-rated container.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a dedicated locked room for long-term media storage, in a different fire compartment from the original data. Choose such a room as your controlled area.

clauses.title: Geo-redundant storage of backups
clauses.rationale: CP-06(01) places the alternate storage site far enough from the primary site that the same threats are unlikely to hit both. CP-09(05) transfers backup information to that alternate storage site.
clauses.gaps: GS++ usually takes geo-redundant to mean 200 km or more in a straight line from the original data. Use that figure when you choose the alternate storage site.

clauses.title: Data sovereignty for data held by service providers
clauses.rationale: CP-09 backs up information on the system components the organisation defines, which can include those at service providers. SA-09 requires external service providers to meet the organisation's requirements, such as regular data exports in portable formats.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for regular backups of provider-held data in an open standard format, such as JSON or CSV, under your own control. Make these part of your exit strategy for each provider.

clauses.title: Offline copy of backups
clauses.rationale: CP-09 runs backups at a set frequency, and CP-09(03) holds copies apart from the operational system. SC-28(02) moves defined information from online storage to secure offline storage.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for an offline copy of the backups on a fixed schedule, separated physically or logically from production systems and the network. Set the interval, such as daily or weekly, by how critical the data is.

clauses.title: Restore procedure
clauses.rationale: CP-02 sets restoration priorities and plans full system restoration while preserving the controls in place. CP-10 provides for recovery and reconstitution of the system to a known state.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a written, step-by-step restore procedure, covering for example the order for restoring critical systems and where each backup is stored. Maintain it as a separate document, ready for an emergency.

clauses.title: Testing backups
clauses.rationale: CP-09(01) tests backup information for media reliability and integrity, and CP-09(02) restores a sample of backups during plan testing (NOT.4.16.1). CP-04 tests the contingency plan, including recovery, at a set frequency.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Testing applications after a restore
clauses.rationale: CP-04(04) includes full recovery and reconstitution of the system to a known state in contingency plan testing. CP-09(02) restores selected system functions from sampled backups.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to check that each restored application works, including its data integrity and configuration. Add those functional checks to your recovery tests.

clauses.title: Detection: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: IR-01 sets incident response policy and procedures that cover detection and analysis. It documents them, sets roles and responsibilities and gives them to the people in those roles. SI-01 does the same for system monitoring, and AU-01 for logging.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for procedures and rules for detecting security incidents. SP 800-53 spreads detection across its incident response, system integrity and logging policies. Check that together they describe how you detect incidents.

clauses.title: Detection: regular review
clauses.rationale: IR-01 reviews and updates the incident response policy and procedures at a set frequency and after events you define, such as a serious incident. AU-01 does the same for logging, and SI-01 for system monitoring.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Reporting procedure for security events
clauses.rationale: IR-06 has staff report suspected incidents to the incident response capability within a set time. IR-07 gives users a support resource that advises them on handling and reporting incidents, including immediate actions they take themselves (DET.2.1.1). IR-08 sets out in the incident response plan which incidents to report and how to share incident information.
clauses.gaps: GS++ also asks for report forms and a procedure for feedback to the people who report. Add both to your reporting procedure.

clauses.title: Security operations center
clauses.rationale: IR-04(14) sets up and maintains a security operations center, whose staff detect, analyse and respond to incidents. IR-08 names in the incident response plan the people or roles responsible for incident response.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Round-the-clock on-call duty
clauses.rationale: IR-04 sets up an incident handling capability. IR-04(14) adds a security operations center that monitors for incidents on an ongoing basis and responds to them.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for someone on call around the clock who starts work on a security alert straight away. Set up that rota yourself, and decide which alerts call them out, based on how critical the affected systems are.

clauses.title: Logging of security-relevant events
clauses.rationale: AU-02 sets the event types to log, such as authentications, commands, device connections and errors, and AU-12 generates records for them. AU-03 records what happened, when, where, the source, the outcome and who was involved (DET.3.1.7). AC-06(09) logs the use of privileged functions (DET.3.1.8). AU-11 keeps the records for a set period.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names specific events to log, such as executed commands and connected peripherals. AU-02 leaves the list of events to you, so add the ones GS++ names.

clauses.title: Integration of cloud services into the audit log
clauses.rationale: AU-12(01) compiles audit records from defined components, which can include cloud services, into one system-wide audit trail. AU-16 coordinates audit information with external organisations, such as cloud providers, and AU-16(02) shares it under agreements.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to record events from your cloud services in your own audit log. Name each cloud service as a source for the audit trail, and agree with the provider how its logs reach you.

clauses.title: Filtering of unneeded log content
clauses.rationale: AU-02 selects the event types worth logging and records why, which keeps unneeded events out of the log. AU-03(03) limits personal data in audit records to the elements you define as needed.
clauses.gaps: GS++ also covers content beyond personal data, such as business secrets. Set your own criteria for removing or masking it, especially before logs go to another organisation or a cloud provider.

clauses.title: Log storage capacity
clauses.rationale: AU-04 allocates enough audit log storage to meet the retention requirements. AU-05(01) warns defined roles when the storage reaches a set percentage of its capacity.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Audit-proof logging
clauses.rationale: AU-09 protects audit information from unauthorised changes and deletion and raises an alert when someone tampers with it. AU-09(02) stores audit records on a separate system, AU-09(03) checks their integrity with cryptography and AU-09(04) limits who can manage logging.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to document every authorised change to the audit log in an audit-proof way. Keep that record yourself, for example with cryptographic hashes or version control stored apart from the log.

clauses.title: Non-repudiation
clauses.rationale: AU-10 provides irrefutable evidence that an individual performed the actions you define, such as a high-value transfer. AU-10(01) binds the identity of whoever produced a piece of information to that information.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Monitoring of logging
clauses.rationale: AU-05 alerts defined roles when audit logging fails, and AU-05(02) does so in real time. SI-06 checks that security functions, such as logging, work correctly and alerts on failure.
clauses.gaps: GS++ also asks you to watch how much log data arrives from each source over time. Set an expected volume per source and raise an alert when it drops.

clauses.title: Automated attack detection
clauses.rationale: SI-04 monitors systems for attacks and signs of attack. SI-04(02) analyses events with automated tools in near real time, and SI-04(23) adds host-based monitoring. SI-03 detects malicious code with signature-based and behaviour-based mechanisms.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Monitoring of attack detection
clauses.rationale: SI-04(09) tests the intrusion monitoring tools at a set frequency. SI-06 checks that security functions, such as attack detection, work correctly and alerts on failure.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a continuous watch on attack detection, with an alert as soon as anyone switches it off or its services stop. Set up that alert alongside the periodic tests.

clauses.title: Changes to automated security policies
clauses.rationale: AC-02(07) monitors privileged role assignments and role changes, such as new members of admin groups. CM-03 monitors configuration-controlled changes, and CM-03(07) reviews them to catch unauthorised ones. CM-06 monitors and controls changes to configuration settings, such as firewall rules and antivirus exclusions.
clauses.gaps: GS++ also asks you to watch for security policies and tools being switched on or off. Add those events to the changes you monitor.

clauses.title: Unwanted data leakage
clauses.rationale: SI-04(04) monitors outbound traffic for unusual or unauthorised activity, and SI-04(18) analyses it for covert exfiltration. SC-07(10) prevents exfiltration at the boundary and tests for it. SI-20 embeds tainted data that shows whether information has left the organisation.
clauses.gaps: GS++ also covers data leaving through endpoints, such as copies to removable media. Add data loss prevention on endpoints to the network monitoring.

clauses.title: Anomalous application use
clauses.rationale: SI-04 identifies unauthorised use, and SI-04(13) builds profiles of normal activity so that anomalies stand out. AU-06 reviews audit records for inappropriate or unusual activity. AC-02(12) monitors accounts for atypical use and reports it (DET.4.6.1).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Expiry of domain names
clauses.rationale: SP 800-53 leaves watching domain registrations to the organisation.
clauses.gaps: No SP 800-53 control is mapped to this requirement. GS++ suggests watching for the expiry of the organisation's domain registrations. Keep an inventory of your domains with their expiry dates, and set reminders well before each one runs out.

clauses.title: Issue of new HTTPS certificates
clauses.rationale: SC-17 issues and manages public key certificates, such as the X.509 certificates behind HTTPS, under a certificate policy. That policy can cover renewing each certificate in good time.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to monitor that each internet-facing server gets a new certificate before the old one expires. Add expiry and renewal monitoring yourself, for example with an alert well before the expiry date.

clauses.title: Check-up for tampering
clauses.rationale: SR-10 inspects systems or components at random, at a set frequency or on indication, to detect tampering. SR-09 runs a tamper protection programme for the system and its components. PE-03(05) uses anti-tamper technologies, such as seals, to detect physical tampering.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Host-based decoys
clauses.rationale: SC-26 places decoy components in systems to attract attacks, so the organisation can detect and analyse them. SI-20 embeds data, such as canary files or honeytokens, to detect misuse or removal of information.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for decoys on the hosts themselves, such as fake files or credentials that raise an alert when touched. Plan which lures go on which hosts, and who gets the alert.

clauses.title: Anomalies in networks and at the perimeter
clauses.title_de: Anomalien in Netzen und am Perimeter
clauses.rationale: SC-07 monitors communications at external and key internal interfaces. SI-04 detects unauthorised network connections, and SI-04(04), (11) and (13) watch traffic for anomalies against profiles of normal activity. AC-17(01) monitors remote access, including authentication attempts at external interfaces (DET.4.11.1). SC-26 deploys decoys, such as network honeypots (DET.4.11.2).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to watch critical traffic flows against criteria you set (DET.4.11.3). Define those flows and criteria yourself, for example connections to unknown domains or large uploads to cloud storage.

clauses.title: Monitoring of network availability
clauses.rationale: CA-07 monitors system metrics you define, such as network availability against thresholds. SC-05(03) monitors for signs of denial of service and checks that resources, such as bandwidth, suffice (DET.4.12.1). SC-05(02) manages capacity and bandwidth.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for routine monitoring of network availability and load, against thresholds. SC-05 looks at denial of service, so add both as CA-07 metrics with your own thresholds.

clauses.title: Availability of the host system
clauses.rationale: CA-07 monitors system metrics you define, such as whether a host can be reached, against thresholds. SC-05(03) monitors for signs of a denial-of-service attack against the host and its resources.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for routine reachability monitoring of each host, against thresholds. SC-05 looks at denial of service, so add reachability as a CA-07 metric, with thresholds such as failed checks in a set time.

clauses.title: Availability of the application
clauses.rationale: CA-07 monitors system metrics you define, such as whether an application can be reached, against thresholds. SC-05(03) monitors for signs of a denial-of-service attack that affects the application.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for routine reachability monitoring of the application's own service, against thresholds. SC-05 looks at denial of service, so add service reachability as a CA-07 metric with your own thresholds.

clauses.title: Resource utilisation of host systems
clauses.rationale: SC-05(03) monitors the system resources you define on a host, such as CPU, memory and storage. It checks that enough capacity remains to withstand a denial-of-service attack.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for routine monitoring of host resources against thresholds. SC-05 looks at denial of service, so set your own thresholds from a baseline of normal use.

clauses.title: Resource utilisation of server services
clauses.rationale: SC-05(03) monitors the resources you define, such as those of the server services an application uses. It checks that enough capacity remains to withstand a denial-of-service attack.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for routine monitoring of the load on an application's server services, such as the number of connected clients. SC-05 looks at denial of service, so set your own thresholds from a baseline of normal use.

clauses.title: Application-based capacity management
clauses.rationale: CA-07 monitors metrics you define over time, such as an application's load across its systems. SC-05(03) monitors defined system resources to check that enough remain.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to manage capacity for the application as a whole, across its systems and over time, with peaks and averages. Build that view yourself from the CA-07 metrics.

clauses.title: Public email blocklists
clauses.rationale: SP 800-53 leaves checking public blocklists to the organisation.
clauses.gaps: No SP 800-53 control is mapped to this requirement. GS++ suggests checking public blocklists regularly for entries that name the organisation's own mail servers.

clauses.title: Unauthorised transmitters
clauses.rationale: RA-06 runs technical surveillance countermeasures surveys at defined locations to find hidden transmitters, such as bugs. SI-04(14) uses a wireless intrusion detection system to find rogue wireless devices.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for automated monitoring of rooms for every kind of transmitter. SI-04(14) covers rogue wireless network devices, and RA-06 surveys run at intervals. Add automated detection for other transmitters, such as hidden bugs, where a room needs it.

clauses.title: Timely vulnerability management
clauses.rationale: RA-05 monitors and scans for vulnerabilities, analyses the results and remediates them within response times set by risk (DET.5.1.1). SI-02 identifies, reports and corrects flaws, and SI-02(03) sets benchmarks for the time to fix them.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Vulnerability register
clauses.rationale: CA-05 records known vulnerabilities and their planned remediation in a plan of action and milestones, and keeps it up to date. RA-05 analyses scan reports and shares the findings with defined roles.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to record each vulnerability when you find it, with the affected components, its criticality and its status. Keep that register yourself, for example in a vulnerability management tool that updates automatically.

clauses.title: Vulnerability scans
clauses.rationale: RA-05 scans for vulnerabilities, analyses the results and remediates them. RA-05(05) authorises privileged access for scanning (DET.5.3.1). RA-05(06) and (10) compare and correlate scan results (DET.5.3.2). RA-05(08) reviews historic audit logs to find out whether a vulnerability was exploited earlier (DET.5.3.3).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Regular penetration tests
clauses.rationale: CA-08 runs penetration tests on defined systems at a set frequency. The testers use the methods of real attackers, which shows how well the systems actually defend themselves.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Red teaming
clauses.rationale: CA-08(02) runs red team exercises, in which testers attempt a realistic attack on the organisation's systems. CA-08(01) has an independent agent or team carry out the tests.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Threat hunting
clauses.rationale: RA-10 sets up and maintains a threat hunting capability. It searches the organisation's systems for indicators of compromise at a set frequency, looking for attacks already under way.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Covert channel analysis
clauses.rationale: SC-31 analyses the system for covert storage and timing channels and estimates their bandwidth. SI-04(18) analyses outbound traffic to detect information leaving through covert channels.
clauses.gaps: GS++ also asks for a check for covert channels whenever an incident involves one. Add that check to your incident handling.

clauses.title: Threat analysis
clauses.rationale: RA-03(03) keeps track of the current cyber threat environment on an ongoing basis. SI-05 receives security alerts and advisories from outside and passes them on. PM-16 runs a threat awareness programme that shares threat intelligence with other organisations. RA-05(04) finds what information about the system is publicly discoverable (DET.5.8.1). AU-13 monitors open sources for unauthorised disclosure of the organisation's information, and AU-13(01) automates it (DET.5.8.1.1).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: External vulnerability reports
clauses.rationale: RA-05(11) sets up a public channel for receiving vulnerability reports from outside the organisation. SI-02 corrects the reported flaws and installs the fixes within a set time.
clauses.gaps: GS++ adds an optional bonus programme for people who report vulnerabilities, such as a bug bounty (DET.5.9.1). Set up the rewards and rules yourself if you take it on.

clauses.title: Timely patch management
clauses.rationale: SI-02 tests security updates and installs them within a set time, and SI-02(02) and (04) automate patch status checks and patching (DET.5.10.2, DET.5.10.3). CM-14 installs components only with a verified signature from an approved certificate, which limits patches to trusted sources (DET.5.10.1). SI-07(15) authenticates software and firmware before installation (DET.5.10.4). CM-03 runs patches through configuration change control (DET.5.10.5).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to approve reliable sources for patches (DET.5.10.1). CM-14 covers that for signed patches, so also approve the sources for patches that come unsigned.

clauses.title: Assessment of security events
clauses.rationale: AU-06 reviews and analyses audit records for unusual activity and reports what it finds, and AU-06(01) automates the process. IR-04 makes detection and analysis part of incident handling. IR-05 tracks and documents incidents, and IR-05(01) collects and analyses incident information automatically (DET.6.1.1, DET.6.1.3). SI-04(05) and (12) alert defined roles automatically on signs of compromise (DET.6.1.2).
