clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Assessment of incoming files
clauses.rationale: SI-03 scans files from external sources at entry points and blocks or quarantines malicious code. SC-44 runs suspicious files in a detonation chamber, an isolated environment, to examine what they do (DET.6.2.1).
clauses.gaps: GS++ also asks for a scanning station for removable media (DET.6.2.2). It has staff release files the scanner is unable to check, such as password-protected ones, before users get them.

clauses.title: Incident handling: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: IR-01 sets incident response policy and procedures, documents them, gives them to the roles that need them and names an official to manage them. IR-08 sets out an incident response plan that assigns responsibilities and goes to the responders. IR-04 puts the procedures into practice through an incident handling capability.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Incident handling: regular review
clauses.rationale: IR-01 has the organisation review and update its incident response policy and procedures at a set frequency and after defined events. IR-08 reviews the incident response plan at a set frequency and updates it after changes or when problems come to light.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Incident handling exercises
clauses.rationale: IR-03 tests the incident response capability at a set frequency, for example through exercises and simulations. IR-02(01) builds simulated events into incident response training, so responders practise realistic situations.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Triage and first response
clauses.rationale: IR-04 handles incidents from detection and analysis onward, and the analysis step includes a first assessment of each report. IR-04(03) defines incident classes, each with a set first response.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to give every incident report a priority, so critical incidents get attention first. Add a priority scale to the first assessment.

clauses.title: Automatic first response
clauses.rationale: IR-04(01) automates incident handling and IR-04(02) reconfigures systems dynamically. IR-04(05) disables a system automatically when it detects defined security violations. SI-04(07) alerts responders and takes the least disruptive action automatically to stop suspicious events, as intrusion prevention systems do.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Documenting incidents
clauses.rationale: IR-05 tracks and documents each security incident. The records support later analysis of incident details and of trends across incidents.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Diagnostic data for incidents
clauses.rationale: AU-12(03) lets authorised staff change what is logged, within set time limits, when an incident needs more detail. IR-04(12) analyses malicious code and other artefacts left behind, and IR-04(13) analyses unusual behaviour. SI-04 deploys monitoring at ad hoc locations and raises the level of monitoring when the risk changes.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: IT forensics
clauses.rationale: IR-04(12) analyses malicious code and other artefacts left after an incident. AU-09 protects audit information from unauthorised access and change, and AU-09(03) adds cryptographic integrity, which keeps evidence sound. IR-05 keeps incident records with the information forensics needs. IR-07 gives access to forensic services, and IR-07(02) sets up relations with external providers.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for legally sound documentation of evidence. It also suggests a two-person rule for forensic work and a forensic service provider on call within an agreed time. Agree that response time in the contract with the provider.

clauses.title: Root cause analysis and remediation
clauses.rationale: SI-02(07) analyses the root cause of a flaw and acts on it. IR-04 handles each incident from containment to recovery and coordinates the response inside and outside the organisation (REA.2.6.3). IR-04(15) handles public relations. IR-05 documents each incident and the handling steps (REA.2.6.1). IR-06 reports incident information to the relevant authorities (REA.2.6.2.1). IR-08 assigns responsibilities and plans how incident information is shared, and IR-08(01) covers notifying those affected by a breach.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for an escalation ladder and suggests service levels for how fast incidents are handled (REA.2.6.5, REA.2.6.4). Set both out in the incident response plan.

clauses.title: Improvement through lessons learned
clauses.rationale: IR-04 builds lessons learned from incidents into incident response procedures and training, and puts the changes in place. AT-02 adds lessons from incidents to awareness training. IR-05 keeps incident records, and IR-05(01) collects and analyses them, including the type and extent of each incident (REA.3.1.1).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a regular review of all existing security measures in the light of incident findings. It also asks you to record the damage each incident caused, along with its type and extent.

clauses.title: Configuration: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: CM-01 sets the configuration management policy and procedures, documents them and gives them to the roles that need them (KONF.1.1.1, KONF.1.1.3). CM-09 adds a configuration management plan that sets roles, responsibilities and processes, which assigns the tasks to people or roles (KONF.1.1.2).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Configuration: regular review
clauses.rationale: CM-01 has the organisation review and update its configuration management policy and procedures at a set frequency. It also calls for a review after events the organisation defines, which can include the triggers GS++ gives, such as a serious security incident.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Management of configuration tools
clauses.rationale: CM-08 keeps an inventory of system components, which can list each configuration tool with details the organisation chooses, such as its purpose and supplier. SR-04 documents and maintains the provenance of each tool, which records where it comes from.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a record of the configuration tools in use, with each tool's purpose and origin. Add the tools to the inventory with purpose and source as fields, and cover them in your provenance records.

clauses.title: Restricting access to configuration documentation
clauses.rationale: AC-03 enforces approved authorisations for access to stored configuration documents and the repositories that hold them. AC-06 limits that access to the people and processes that need it. AC-06(01) does the same for security-relevant information, such as configuration parameters. MP-02 restricts access to digital and paper media that hold configuration documents.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Encryption of configuration secrets
clauses.rationale: IA-05 protects authenticator content, and IA-05(07) keeps unencrypted static credentials out of applications and storage. SC-28(01) encrypts sensitive information at rest, such as secrets in configuration files and vaults. SC-12 manages the keys that protect the secrets, including the key that unlocks a secret store.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Baseline configuration for systems
clauses.rationale: CM-02 develops, documents and maintains a baseline configuration under configuration control. CM-02(03) keeps previous versions for rollback (KONF.2.1.1). CM-06 establishes and documents the security configuration settings that make up the baseline, based on common secure configurations such as benchmarks.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Cryptographic methods in IT systems
clauses.rationale: SC-13 determines the cryptographic uses on each system and implements the type of cryptography each use needs. SC-12 establishes and manages the keys that the activated cryptographic functions depend on.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for cryptography to recognised standards, such as BSI TR-02102. It also asks for the settings to follow its access rights practice (BER). Name those standards when you set SC-13's parameters.

clauses.title: Default credentials in IT systems
clauses.rationale: IA-05 has the organisation change default authenticators before first use. That covers factory-set credentials, such as the user names 'root' or 'administrator' with published passwords, which an attacker can find with little effort.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Disabling unneeded system functions
clauses.rationale: CM-07 limits each system to essential capabilities and disables unneeded functions, ports, protocols and services, including cloud connections (KONF.2.4.2). CM-06 applies the most restrictive settings that operations allow, such as turning off weak protocols and telemetry. SC-17 keeps only approved trust anchors in certificate stores, which removes unneeded certificates (KONF.2.4.1).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Review of the system configuration
clauses.rationale: CM-06 monitors and controls changes to configuration settings, and CM-06(01) verifies the settings with automated mechanisms (KONF.2.5.1). CM-03(07) reviews system changes at a set frequency to find unauthorised ones.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Mobile device management
clauses.rationale: AC-19 sets configuration and connection requirements for organisation-controlled mobile devices and authorises their connection. CM-06(01) manages, applies and verifies device settings centrally with automated mechanisms, which is the job of a mobile device management (MDM) system.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for an MDM to manage mobile devices. BSI's minimum standard for MDM adds features, such as detecting jailbroken or rooted devices, so use it to choose and set up the product.

clauses.title: Sovereign tools
clauses.rationale: SA-09(05) restricts where external services process and store data, which keeps control over jurisdiction and lets tools run in the organisation's own infrastructure. SR-03 applies supply chain controls that limit harm from supplier events, such as a withdrawn service or changed licence. SR-05 uses acquisition strategies that reduce dependence on external suppliers, such as choosing tools that run locally.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for tools the organisation can run independently of vendors, cloud providers and state influence. Make that independence a criterion when you choose and buy tools.

clauses.title: Alternative administrative access
clauses.rationale: AC-02 defines emergency account types, such as break-glass administrator accounts, and the conditions for their use. CP-11 provides alternative communications protocols to keep operating when the primary one fails. SC-47 sets up alternate communications paths for system operations, such as out-of-band management.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a second way to administer central systems, such as console, command-line or API access, for when the usual management interface fails. Set up and document these alternative tools and interfaces.

clauses.title: Secure and authenticated boot process
clauses.rationale: SI-07(09) verifies the integrity of the boot process, and SI-07(10) protects boot firmware. SI-07(06) adds cryptographic mechanisms that detect unauthorised changes to software and firmware.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for hardware trust anchors and a multi-stage boot that checks each step cryptographically, such as Secure Boot on UEFI or ARM systems. Choose hardware and firmware that support this.

clauses.title: Cryptographic hardware storage
clauses.rationale: SC-28(03) provides protected storage for cryptographic keys, such as a hardware-protected key store or Trusted Platform Module (TPM). SC-12 sets the key management requirements for storing keys and controlling access to them.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Storage encryption
clauses.rationale: SC-28(01) encrypts information at rest on system components, including built-in storage. AC-19(05) asks for full-device or container encryption on mobile devices. SC-13 implements the approved type of cryptography for that encryption.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: SIM PIN
clauses.rationale: AC-19 sets configuration requirements for mobile devices, which can include an active SIM PIN. IA-07 authenticates the user to a cryptographic module. A SIM card is such a module, and the SIM PIN is that authentication.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a SIM PIN on every system with a cellular connection, to protect the subscription if the SIM card is lost or stolen. Make the SIM PIN part of the configuration for each such system.

clauses.title: Physical theft protection
clauses.rationale: PE-03(04) uses lockable physical casings to protect system components from unauthorised physical access. AC-19 sets requirements for mobile devices, including their protection outside controlled areas, where the risk of theft arises.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for physical theft protection, such as cable locks that fix a laptop to a desk or other fixed object. Add such locks to your protection measures for mobile devices.

clauses.title: Remote location detection
clauses.rationale: CM-08(08) uses automated mechanisms to track system components by geographic location. PE-20 uses asset location technologies to track and monitor where assets are and how they move.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a way to find a system's location remotely, wherever it is. PE-20 tracks assets within controlled areas, so use CM-08(08) for devices outside them.

clauses.title: Remote wipe or lock
clauses.rationale: MP-06(08) provides the means to purge or wipe information remotely, or under set conditions such as long inactivity (KONF.3.6.1). AC-19 sets configuration requirements for mobile devices, which can include remote locking through device management.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a remote lock as well as a remote wipe. A lock makes the device unusable and leaves its data in place, so add remote lock to your mobile device requirements.

clauses.title: Restricting connected peripherals
clauses.rationale: CM-07(09) prohibits the use or connection of unauthorised hardware. SC-41 disables unneeded connection ports and input and output devices, such as USB and Bluetooth, physically or logically. MP-07 restricts the use of removable media types, such as USB sticks.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Restricting removable media
clauses.rationale: CM-07 restricts unneeded functions such as automatic mounting, and CM-07(02) can block auto-execute features. MP-07 restricts the use of removable media on systems. SC-18(04) prevents automatic execution of mobile code, which includes turning off auto-execute for CDs, DVDs and USB devices.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Connection to a directory service
clauses.rationale: IA-13 uses identity providers and authorisation servers to manage identities and access rights centrally. AC-02(01) manages system accounts with automated mechanisms. IA-02 authenticates users against the directory, with single sign-on under IA-02(10). IA-05 protects authenticators, which is the basis for turning off the forwarding of reusable credentials (KONF.4.1.1).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for systems to stop forwarding reusable credentials, for example through SSH agent forwarding or credential delegation. Turn those features off in each system's configuration.

clauses.title: Connection to DNS servers
clauses.rationale: CM-06 sets the DNS resolvers the organisation authorises as a fixed configuration setting. SC-08(01) encrypts DNS traffic in transit, for example with DNS over TLS or HTTPS (KONF.4.2.1). SC-21 has clients validate DNS responses or use authenticated channels to trusted resolvers.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for each system to use only the DNS resolvers the organisation has authorised. SC-21 focuses on validating responses, so keep a list of approved resolvers and enforce it through CM-06.

clauses.title: Authentication of remote maintenance functions
clauses.rationale: MA-04 asks for strong authentication when nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions start. IA-02 uniquely identifies and authenticates the administrators who use remote maintenance, and IA-02(01) adds multi-factor authentication for privileged accounts. AC-17 authorises each type of remote access before connections are allowed.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Restricting remote maintenance functions
clauses.rationale: AC-17 sets usage restrictions and configuration requirements for each type of remote access, and AC-17(04) limits privileged commands over remote access. CM-07 turns off unneeded remote session features, such as clipboard, drive and device redirection. MA-04 allows nonlocal maintenance tools only as policy and the security plan permit.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Time sources
clauses.rationale: SC-45 synchronises system clocks, which keeps log timestamps consistent across systems. SC-45(01) compares and synchronises the clocks with an authoritative time source the organisation defines, and SC-45(02) adds a secondary source.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for authorised time sources. Authenticate each source to confirm it is the one you authorised, for example with Network Time Security (NTS) or authenticated NTP.

clauses.title: Authentication to the system
clauses.rationale: IA-02 uniquely identifies and authenticates users before they access the system, including before boot (KONF.5.1.2). AC-11 keeps a locked device locked until the user authenticates again. CM-05 restricts who can change firmware settings, for example with a UEFI administrator password (KONF.5.1.1).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for authentication to the firmware and, on mobile devices, before the operating system starts. Scope IA-02 and CM-05 to cover both, for example with a firmware password and pre-boot authentication.

clauses.title: One account signed in at a time
clauses.rationale: AC-10 limits the number of concurrent sessions for each account or account type. A system-wide limit of one session stops several accounts from being signed in at once.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks each system to allow one signed-in account at a time. AC-10's discussion sets aside one user working through several accounts, so configure the system to refuse a second sign-in.

clauses.title: Minimum required access rights for applications
clauses.rationale: AC-06 grants applications and processes only the access rights their tasks need. AC-03(12) has applications declare the access they need and blocks the rest. SC-39 runs each process in its own execution domain, and CM-07(06) runs chosen software in a confined environment (KONF.6.1.2). AC-19(05) uses container-based encryption on mobile devices, which encapsulates the data (KONF.6.1.1). SC-50 separates security domains in software, such as work and personal profiles (KONF.6.1.3).
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for data encapsulation (KONF.6.1.1). SP 800-53 reaches it through container encryption and process isolation, so check that these keep each application's data apart.

clauses.title: Shared directories
clauses.rationale: AC-03 enforces access rights on shared directories, for example with the sticky bit, which lets only a file's owner delete or rename it. AC-06 gives each user and process only the access to shared directories that their tasks need.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Kiosk mode
clauses.rationale: SI-14 runs components non-persistently. They start in a known state and reset at the end of each session, and SI-14(01) refreshes them from trusted sources. That clears changes left behind by malware or earlier users.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Privileged system functions
clauses.rationale: AC-06(10) stops non-privileged users from running privileged functions, and AC-06(01) and (05) restrict security functions and privileged accounts to authorised roles. CM-05 restricts who can change the system configuration and system directories. AC-03(07) enforces role-based access control, and AC-02(07) administers privileged accounts in a role-based scheme (KONF.6.4.1).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Dynamic access control in the system
clauses.rationale: AC-03(13) enforces attribute-based access control that weighs context, such as location or time. AC-16 attaches security attributes, such as data sensitivity, to information and users for access decisions. AC-02(11) enforces usage conditions on accounts, and AC-02(06) manages privileges dynamically.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for access decisions that also weigh the state of the device, such as its health. Add device health to the attributes your access policy evaluates.

clauses.title: Keeping each account's data separate
clauses.rationale: AC-03 enforces authorisations so that each account reaches only its own data. AC-06 limits each account to the data its tasks need. SC-50 treats tenants as separate security domains in software, each with its own access rights configuration (KONF.6.6.1).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Privileged application functions
clauses.rationale: AC-03 enforces the application's authorisations for privileged functions, such as moderation or managing accepted certificates. AC-06(01) and (10) restrict privileged application functions to authorised roles, and AC-06(05) restricts privileged accounts.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Access rights of the web server process
clauses.rationale: AC-03 enforces file permissions that keep the web server process inside the web root and allow writes only to authorised subdirectories. AC-06 gives the process only the rights it needs. CM-07(02) stops it from running programs, such as shell commands, outside the intended interpreters.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Access to code on web servers
clauses.rationale: AC-03 enforces access rules that keep source, configuration and credential files from being served. AC-22 has the organisation review its publicly accessible systems for nonpublic information and remove any it finds.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks web servers to block direct access to source files, such as code and configuration files. Write that rule into your web server's configuration as part of AC-03.

clauses.title: Listing directory contents on web servers
clauses.rationale: CM-07 turns off directory listing as an unneeded web server function, which hides the site's internal structure from attackers. CM-06 sets the web server to the most restrictive configuration that still lets it work.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Restricting uploads to web servers
clauses.rationale: AC-03 allows uploads only from authenticated, authorised users and only into set storage locations. SC-06 uses quotas to limit upload size and storage use. SI-10 checks uploads, and SI-10(05) restricts inputs to approved formats, such as allowed file types.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Moderation of public conference calls
clauses.rationale: SC-15 sets rules for collaborative devices and applications, such as video conferencing. SC-15(04) shows who is currently in an online meeting, which lets a moderator notice unwanted participants.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for moderation of public conference calls, so a moderator controls who speaks and can remove unwanted participants. Turn on the moderation features of your video conferencing application.

clauses.title: Dynamic access control in the application
clauses.rationale: AC-03(13) enforces attribute-based access control in the application, using context such as location or device. AC-16 attaches security attributes, such as data sensitivity, to data and users for access decisions. AC-02(11) enforces usage conditions on accounts, and AC-02(06) manages privileges dynamically.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Browser sandboxing
clauses.rationale: SC-39 keeps a separate execution domain for each process, so each browser process reaches only its own resources. Its discussion names sandboxing. SC-18(05) lets permitted mobile code, such as JavaScript, run only in confined environments.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Virtualised browser environment
clauses.rationale: SC-18(05) lets mobile code run only in confined virtual machine environments. SC-44 provides an isolated, virtualised environment where web content and URL requests run apart from the user's own system.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for the whole browser to run in a virtualised operating system set aside for it, apart from the client. Use a remote-controlled browser system (ReCoBS) or a similar set-up.

clauses.title: Data exchange between virtualised clients
clauses.rationale: AC-04 enforces approved information flows between virtual machines. SC-04 prevents unauthorised transfer of information through shared resources, such as shared memory or clipboards. SC-07 monitors and controls traffic at internal interfaces, such as the virtual networks between machines.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Real-time malware scanner
clauses.rationale: SI-03 configures malicious code protection to scan files in real time as they are downloaded, opened or executed. That gives the automatic check GS++ asks for when someone installs or opens a file.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Regular malware scans
clauses.rationale: SI-03 configures malicious code protection to run periodic scans of the system, at a frequency the organisation defines. Those scans look for potential malicious code in the files already stored on the system.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Host-based intrusion detection
clauses.rationale: SI-04(23) puts host-based monitoring mechanisms on system components, such as servers and workstations. SI-07 checks the integrity of files and critical configuration on the host and detects unauthorised changes to them.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Intrusion detection based on network traffic
clauses.rationale: SI-04(04) monitors inbound and outbound traffic for unusual activity. SI-04(23) runs that monitoring on the host itself, so the system can spot port scans or connections to command-and-control servers.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Alerting on possible malware
clauses.rationale: SI-03 sends an alert to defined personnel or roles when it detects malicious code. SI-04(05) alerts defined personnel or roles when system-generated indicators show signs of compromise.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Automatic updates of malware detection
clauses.rationale: SI-03 updates malicious code protection mechanisms automatically as new releases appear. That keeps signatures and detection rules current against malware that changes to slip past known patterns.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Regular testing of malware protection
clauses.rationale: SI-03(06) tests malware protection with known benign code, such as the EICAR test file, and checks that detection and reporting work. SI-06 verifies at a set frequency that security functions operate correctly and alerts on failed checks.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Dual-engine strategy for malware scanning
clauses.rationale: SC-29 uses a diverse set of technologies for chosen components, such as different scan engines. PL-08(02) takes controls at a given layer from different suppliers, and SP 800-53 gives malware protection as its example. SI-03 lets signature-based and non-signature-based detection run side by side.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Restricting application installation
clauses.rationale: CM-11 sets and enforces policy on software installation by users, and CM-11(02) allows installation only with privileged status. CM-05 restricts the privileges to change the system, including installing software into system locations.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Restricting application execution
clauses.rationale: CM-07(05) keeps a list of authorised software and blocks everything else from running. CM-07(02) prevents program execution that breaks the organisation's rules on software use.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Restricting software libraries
clauses.rationale: CM-07(05) blocks all software by default and permits authorised software by exception, which can extend to libraries such as .dll and .so files. SI-07(12) verifies the integrity of code, including libraries, before it runs.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for control over which software libraries may run. Extend your allow-list to libraries, such as .dll and .so files, as well as programs.

clauses.title: Restricting scripts
clauses.rationale: CM-07(02) and (05) let only authorised scripts run and block the rest. SC-18 defines which mobile code, such as JavaScript or VBScript, is acceptable and controls its use.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for limits on what scripts may do, such as constrained language modes that restrict the system functions a script can call. Turn on features such as PowerShell Constrained Language Mode or Linux secure computing mode (seccomp).

clauses.title: Restricting system calls
clauses.rationale: AC-06 limits each process to the privileges its task needs, including the operating system resources an application may request. CM-07(06) runs software in a confined environment with limited privileges, as seccomp profiles do.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a filter on the system calls each application may make, such as seccomp on Linux. Set up those filters per application as part of confining software.

clauses.title: Code signing in the operating system kernel
clauses.rationale: CM-14 allows a component to install only after its signature from an approved certificate is verified. SI-07(15) authenticates code cryptographically before installation, and SI-07(12) verifies its integrity before it runs.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Local firewall
clauses.rationale: SC-07(12) puts host-based boundary protection, such as a local firewall, on each system. SC-07(05) denies traffic by default and allows it by exception. CM-07 restricts the ports, protocols and services a system uses to those it needs.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Anti-exploit protection
clauses.rationale: SI-16 protects memory from unauthorised code execution (KONF.7.16.1), for example with data execution prevention (DEP) and address space layout randomisation (ASLR). SI-07 protects the integrity of system files, as System Integrity Protection does, and SI-07(17) adds runtime protection against exploits.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for operating system exploit protection beyond memory, such as Defender Exploit Guard and attack surface reduction rules. Turn these features on as part of each system's secure configuration.

clauses.title: Automatic check for security updates
clauses.rationale: SI-02 covers flaw remediation on IT systems. SI-02(02) uses automated mechanisms to check whether the available security updates are installed. SI-02(05) then installs security-relevant updates automatically (KONF.8.1.1).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Automatic updates for applications
clauses.rationale: SI-02 covers flaw remediation for the organisation's systems. SI-02(05) installs security-relevant software updates automatically on the system components the organisation defines, which can include each of its applications.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Storage limit for the user environment
clauses.rationale: SC-06 allocates resources such as storage to users and processes by quota. A quota on the user environment keeps its applications and services within their share of the disk, which leaves room for system services.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Limiting host computing power
clauses.rationale: SC-06 allocates processing resources by priority or quota. A host can use such quotas to cap computing power at the thresholds the organisation sets. One way is to limit the number of cores.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Alternative components for critical functions
clauses.rationale: SI-13 provides substitute components for critical functions, and SI-13(05) adds a way to fail over from active to standby components. CP-08 provides alternate telecommunications services, such as a mobile link when the wired network connection fails.
clauses.gaps: GS++ gives redundant power supplies inside a system as an example. Plan them under SI-13 as substitute components for each critical function.

clauses.title: Baseline configuration for applications
clauses.rationale: CM-02 documents a baseline configuration for the application and keeps it under configuration control. CM-02(03) retains previous versions of the baseline, so you can roll back (KONF.10.1.1). CM-06 establishes and documents the application's security settings.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Cryptographic methods in applications
clauses.rationale: SC-13 determines the cryptographic uses in the application and implements the required type of cryptography for each. SC-12 establishes and manages the keys that this cryptography depends on.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for methods that follow recognised standards, such as BSI TR-02102, in line with its identity and access management requirements. SC-13 leaves the type of cryptography to you, so choose it from those standards.

clauses.title: Default credentials in applications
clauses.rationale: IA-05 has default authenticators changed before first use. That covers default passwords, and also the keys and certificates that an application accepts for sign-in by default.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Disabling unneeded application functions
clauses.rationale: CM-07 configures the application to provide only essential functions and restricts unneeded modules, features and cloud connections. CM-06 sets the application's settings to the most restrictive mode consistent with operations.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Checking the configuration against the baseline
clauses.rationale: CM-06 monitors the application's settings against the documented ones, and CM-06(01) verifies them with automated mechanisms (KONF.10.5.1). CM-03(07) reviews changes at a set frequency to find unauthorised ones.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Authentication before access to protected data
clauses.rationale: IA-02 authenticates the organisation's own users before they reach protected data. IA-08 authenticates external users, such as guests in portals or external participants in scheduled calls (KONF.11.1.1). IA-09 authenticates services and applications before they exchange data, as mutual TLS does (KONF.11.1.2).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Waiting room for video conferences
clauses.rationale: IA-02 authenticates the organisation's own participants before they join a conference, and IA-08 authenticates external participants. SC-15(04) shows the current participants, so moderators can check who is present.
clauses.gaps: GS++ suggests a waiting room, where a moderator checks each participant before letting them into the conference. Turn on that admission step in your conferencing tool.

clauses.title: Publication of domain information in DNS
clauses.rationale: SC-22 separates internal and external DNS roles. Records needed only inside the organisation then stay on internal servers, and the internet sees just the records of services meant for outside use.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Protection against guessing access links
clauses.rationale: AC-07 limits consecutive failed attempts and then locks or delays further tries. The same pattern blocks the guessing of access links. SC-23(03) generates unique, random identifiers that resist brute-force guessing, and access links built that way resist it too.
clauses.gaps: AC-07 counts failed logon attempts. GS++ asks for the same protection on links that grant access by themselves, such as meeting links. Add rate limiting or a CAPTCHA to requests for them.

clauses.title: Restricting unauthenticated telephony connections
clauses.rationale: AC-14 identifies the actions an unauthenticated endpoint may perform, such as emergency calls from a lift phone, and limits it to those. AC-04 enforces flow policies that restrict the destinations such endpoints can reach.
clauses.gaps: The requirement targets telephony endpoints, such as public phones and fax machines in unsecured areas. Set the numbers and meetings each one may reach, and block the rest, such as premium-rate numbers.

clauses.title: Overview of signed-in connections
clauses.rationale: AC-09 tells users about their previous logons when they sign in. AC-09(04) adds details such as location or device, so users can check that each sign-in is theirs.
clauses.gaps: AC-09 reports at each logon. GS++ suggests an overview of the connections signed in right now, with details such as device name or IP address. Turn that view on in the application.

clauses.title: Restricting application interfaces
clauses.rationale: AC-04 enforces approved flows to other applications and external peers, including zone transfers limited to authorised servers (KONF.11.7.1). CA-03 approves and documents each information exchange with other systems. CM-07 restricts enabled interfaces, extensions and cloud functions to those needed. SC-07 controls traffic at managed interfaces, as session border controllers do for telephony (KONF.11.7.2).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Encryption of sensitive data at rest
clauses.rationale: SC-28(01) encrypts sensitive information at rest, such as credentials. IA-05(01) has passwords stored with an approved salted key derivation function, which GS++ accepts in place of encryption.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Input validation
clauses.rationale: SI-10 checks the validity of inputs, and SI-10(06) prevents injection, as a web application firewall does. IA-05(02) validates certificates along the full path to a trust anchor, including revocation status. SC-18 controls mobile code, such as JavaScript and active content in Office files, and enforces content security policies. SI-07 verifies the integrity of loaded scripts, as Subresource Integrity does. SC-08 protects data in transit, and HSTS enforces that protection. IA-04 keeps identifiers unique, which blocks duplicates in the directory tree. CP-10(02) transaction recovery includes file system journaling.
clauses.gaps: GS++ also asks web applications to send HTTP security response headers (KONF.12.1.10) and browsers to enforce the same-origin policy (KONF.12.1.3). Set both up in your server and browser configuration.

clauses.title: Encryption status of the current connection
clauses.rationale: SC-08 protects the confidentiality and integrity of transmitted information. The browser's encryption indicator shows the user whether that protection is in place on the current connection.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the browser to show the user whether the current connection is encrypted, for example with a padlock symbol. Turn that indicator on in your browser settings.

clauses.title: Cookies in web browsers
clauses.rationale: CM-07 limits the browser to the functions it needs. That includes storing cookies, which you can restrict to permitted sites, such as those on your intranet.
clauses.gaps: GS++ addresses browser cookies by name, since they can hold sign-in tokens and personal data. Set a restrictive cookie policy in the browser configuration you deploy.

clauses.title: Storage of credentials in web browsers
clauses.rationale: IA-05(18) uses password managers to manage passwords and protect them. A dedicated password manager with browser integration, or browser storage protected by a master password, fits that enhancement.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Autofill of data in web browsers
clauses.rationale: CM-07 limits the browser to the functions it needs, which lets you restrict autofill. Pages then see just the data the user types into a form.
clauses.gaps: GS++ addresses browser autofill by name, because a page can read filled-in fields before the user sends the form. Restrict it through your browser policy.

clauses.title: Persistent browser history
clauses.rationale: CM-07 switches off persistent history as an unneeded function. SI-14(02) deletes information once it has served its purpose, such as clearing the history when the browser closes.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Extended attributes on file servers
clauses.rationale: AC-16 associates security attributes with information in storage. Extended attributes store them as metadata on each file, for example access rights and status flags. AC-03 enforces the access rights held there.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks file servers to turn on extended attributes in the file system, for example through Samba on Linux or NTFS on Windows. Set this when you build each server.

clauses.title: Joining conferences with video and audio off by default
clauses.title_de: Teilnahme per Default ohne Bild und Ton
clauses.rationale: SC-15 prohibits remote activation of cameras and microphones in collaborative applications, so only the participant can switch them on. It also shows when these devices are in use.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks conferencing tools to have camera and microphone off when a participant joins. Set that default in the tool, so users switch them on when they choose.

clauses.title: No covert recording in video conferences
clauses.rationale: SC-15 shows participants clearly when collaborative devices and applications are in use. PT-05(01) and SC-42(04) tell people when their personal data is being collected, for example by a recording.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the tool to tell every participant about a recording, including those who join late. Switch off any way to record a conference covertly.

clauses.title: Cookie attributes in web applications
clauses.rationale: SC-08 protects cookies in transit, and the Secure attribute enforces that by keeping them on HTTPS. SC-23 protects session authenticity against hijacking and cross-site request forgery, which the HttpOnly and SameSite attributes support.
clauses.gaps: GS++ names the cookie attributes, such as Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite. Turn them on in the application or web server configuration.

clauses.title: Anonymous or pseudonymous communication
clauses.rationale: SC-30 uses concealment techniques to hide identifying details from the other party, such as the caller's identity or internal extension numbers. SC-30(05) conceals system components, such as the network source of a connection.
clauses.gaps: GS++ suggests sending the other party a pseudonym, or withholding the caller ID. Turn on caller ID suppression, or send a general number in place of the extension.

clauses.title: Connection log for users
clauses.rationale: AU-02 names connections as an event type to log, and AU-12 generates the records. AU-03 sets what each record holds, such as the time, duration, peer and direction of a connection.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the telephony application to show each user a log of their own calls. Turn on a call list each user can see, for example in the phone app.

clauses.title: Fax transmission report
clauses.rationale: AU-12 generates a record of each fax transmission. AU-10 provides evidence that a message was sent, which a fax transmission report gives as legal proof.
clauses.gaps: GS++ suggests details for the report, such as the number of pages sent and the status the call ended with. Set the fax application to include them.

clauses.title: False information in DNS answers
clauses.rationale: SC-20 has authoritative servers add origin authentication and integrity data to their answers. SC-21 has resolvers verify the origin and integrity of the answers they receive, including those from upstream servers.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to switch off answer rewriting, such as redirecting unknown names to advertising pages. Check both your own DNS servers and the upstream servers they use.

clauses.title: Filtering harmful messages
clauses.rationale: SI-03 detects and removes malicious code in messages and attachments at entry points, such as mail gateways. SI-08 detects and acts on unsolicited messages at entry and exit points (KONF.13.1.1). SC-18(04) prevents the automatic execution of active content in messages (KONF.13.1.2).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Authenticity of messages
clauses.rationale: SI-08 checks incoming mail at entry points and acts on spoofed or unauthenticated messages. AU-10(02) validates the binding of the sender's identity to the message. SC-08(01) uses cryptography to detect changes to messages in transit.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks mail systems to verify the sending authorisation and the server signature of incoming mail. Turn on Sender Policy Framework (SPF) and DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) checks at your mail gateway.

clauses.title: Cryptographic signature of the mail server
clauses.rationale: AU-10(01) binds the sending domain's identity to each outgoing message. SC-08(01) lets recipients detect changes to messages in transit. SC-13 implements approved cryptography for the signature.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the mail server to sign outgoing mail, for example with DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM). Turn on DKIM signing for each domain you send from.

clauses.title: Cryptographic signature by users
clauses.rationale: AU-10 provides evidence that a user sent a message, through a digital signature that recipients can verify. SC-17 issues the public key certificates that S/MIME needs, under a certificate policy.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Publication of the sending authorisation in DNS
clauses.rationale: SI-08 provides spam protection at entry and exit points. A published sender policy lets receiving spam filters, the organisation's own among them, reject mail that spoofs its domain.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to publish in DNS the servers allowed to send mail for your domain, for example with a Sender Policy Framework (SPF) record. Make that policy strict, as KONF.13.5.1 asks.

clauses.title: Publication of the server signature in DNS
clauses.rationale: SC-12 manages cryptographic keys, including the distribution of public keys. SC-12(03) distributes asymmetric keys, such as the public key for DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM), which receiving servers look up in DNS.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to publish the public key of your server signature in DNS. Add a DKIM record for each domain and signing key.

clauses.title: TLS reports for email
clauses.rationale: AU-06 reviews and analyses the reports at a set frequency for unusual activity. SI-04 uses them as monitoring information to detect attacks on mail transport, such as downgrade or interception attempts.
clauses.gaps: GS++ suggests reviewing TLS reports (TLS-RPT), which other mail operators send about problems delivering mail to you over TLS. Add them to the records you review under AU-06.

clauses.title: Email authentication reports (DMARC)
clauses.rationale: AU-06 reviews and analyses the reports for unusual activity, at a set frequency or when they arrive. SI-04 uses them as monitoring information to detect misuse of the domain, such as failed authentication checks.
clauses.gaps: GS++ suggests reviewing the DMARC reports that receiving mail servers send about mail from your domain. Add them to the records you review under AU-06, ideally with automated analysis.

clauses.title: Publication of the email authentication policy (DMARC)
clauses.rationale: SI-08 provides spam protection at entry and exit points. A published DMARC policy tells receiving spam filters how to treat mail that fails authentication for the organisation's domain.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to publish your DMARC policy as a record in DNS. Add one for each of your domains.

clauses.title: Authenticating server certificates through DNS
clauses.rationale: SC-17 obtains certificates from approved providers only, and Certificate Authority Authorization (CAA) records name those providers in DNS. SC-21 validates DNSSEC signatures on DNS answers, which DNS-based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) relies on. SC-23(05) allows only defined certificate authorities for protected sessions.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks mail servers to check server certificates through DNS, with DANE or CAA records. Publish these records for your mail domains and turn on DANE checks in your mail servers.

clauses.title: Strict transport security for mail (MTA-STS)
clauses.rationale: SC-08(01) enforces encrypted transmission between mail servers, which blocks a downgrade to plain text. SC-23 protects session authenticity against a false server intercepting the mail.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for Mail Transfer Agent Strict Transport Security (MTA-STS), which tells sending servers to deliver to your domain over TLS only. Publish an MTA-STS policy for each mail domain.

clauses.title: Encryption in transit
clauses.rationale: SC-08(01) encrypts information in transit over networks, for example with TLS. SC-13 implements cryptography to the recognised standard the organisation sets. CM-07 disables unencrypted and vulnerable protocols (KONF.14.1.1).
clauses.gaps: GS++ also suggests end-to-end encryption (KONF.14.1.2). SC-08 leaves you to choose where encryption ends, so decide which communication needs end-to-end protection.

clauses.title: Source port randomisation for DNS
clauses.rationale: SC-21 protects the integrity of resolver answers against spoofing and cache poisoning. SC-30(02) introduces randomness into operations, such as random source ports for DNS queries.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks DNS servers to randomise the source ports of their queries, as RFC 5452 describes. Check that your resolver software has this switched on.

clauses.title: Iterative answers to DNS queries from the internet
clauses.rationale: SC-22 separates the external, authoritative roles of DNS servers from internal, recursive ones. CM-07 disables recursion for clients on the internet, so internet-facing servers answer their queries iteratively.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks internet-facing DNS servers to answer queries iteratively. SP 800-53 reaches that through role separation and disabled recursion, so check the setting on each such server.

clauses.title: Caching frequently used data on mobile devices
clauses.rationale: SC-36 distributes processing and storage across several locations, and a local cache on the mobile device is one of them. The cache keeps frequently used data available when the network fails.
clauses.gaps: GS++ suggests caching frequently used data on the device, for speed and to keep working during network outages. Turn on caching in the applications where that helps.

clauses.title: Timeout for network connections
clauses.rationale: SC-10 terminates network connections at the end of a session or after a period of inactivity. AC-12 terminates user sessions automatically on defined conditions, such as idle time.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Limiting storage space per account or tenant
clauses.rationale: SC-06 allocates storage by quota to each account or tenant. A quota, such as 5 or 10 GB, stops a single account or tenant from using up the storage that all of them share.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Limiting computing power per account or tenant
clauses.rationale: SC-06 allocates processing resources by priority or quota to each account or tenant. A directory service, for example, can cap the time that any one search may take.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Protection against denial of service
clauses.rationale: SC-05 protects against denial-of-service events or limits their effects. SC-05(02) manages capacity and redundancy, for example with load balancers, and SC-05(03) detects attacks as they happen.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Overcommitment of virtualised resources
clauses.rationale: SC-06 allocates resources by priority or quota. Fixed quotas can reserve real capacity for each virtual instance, so the hardware can deliver every resource it has promised.
clauses.gaps: GS++ suggests switching off overcommitment, where the platform hands out more virtual resources than the hardware has. Set your virtualisation platform to reserve real capacity for each instance.

clauses.title: Development: procedures and rules
clauses.rationale: SA-01 sets policy and procedures for system acquisition and development, documents them and gives them to the roles that need them (DEV.1.1.1, DEV.1.1.3). SA-03 defines security roles across the development life cycle and names the people who hold them (DEV.1.1.2). SA-15 has development follow a documented process that addresses security.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Development: regular review
clauses.rationale: SA-01 reviews and updates the development policy and procedures at a set frequency and after defined events, such as a serious security incident. SA-15 reviews the development process, its standards and its tools at a set frequency.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Security by design in the architecture
clauses.rationale: PL-08 develops a security architecture that describes how the system protects information. SA-08 applies security engineering principles to the design and development of the system. SA-17 has the developer produce a security architecture and design that allocates security functions to components. SA-11(02) runs threat modelling during development, the method GS++ suggests.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Documenting the software architecture
clauses.rationale: PL-08 documents the system's security architecture, including its dependencies on external systems and services. SA-17 has the developer produce a design specification that describes the components, their interfaces and how the security functions work together.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for the architecture documents to cover the data model as well. Add it to the architecture and design documents you keep under PL-08 and SA-17.

clauses.title: Running with minimal privileges
clauses.rationale: AC-06 lets the application run with only the access its tasks need. SA-08(14) applies the least privilege principle in design, and SA-17(07) structures the software so access can be controlled with least privilege.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks the application to keep working with reduced functions when a permission is withheld, known as graceful degradation. Build and test for it. A photo viewer, for example, still shows saved images when the user refuses camera access.

clauses.title: Restricting write access to source code
clauses.rationale: AC-06 gives write access only to the developers and maintainers whose tasks need it. CM-05 restricts who can make changes, and CM-05(06) limits the privileges to change software in libraries. SA-10 controls the integrity of changes to configuration items such as source code.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Restricting access to application credentials
clauses.rationale: AC-03 enforces access rules on the vault or store that holds the credentials, and AC-06 limits reading and writing them to those who need it. IA-05(07) keeps unencrypted static credentials out of source code, and IA-05 protects authenticator content.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Resistance to common attack patterns
clauses.rationale: SI-10 validates input, and SI-10(06) prevents injection by checking input for embedded commands (DEV.2.6.1). SI-15 checks output against the expected content (DEV.2.6.2). SI-16 protects memory against exploits such as buffer overflows. SA-15 builds secure coding standards into the development process. SA-11(01) and (08) find common flaws with static and dynamic analysis.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for output encoding (DEV.2.6.2). SI-15 checks output against the expected content, so add encoding that suits each output context to your secure coding standards.

clauses.title: Blocking replay attacks
clauses.rationale: IA-02(08) makes authentication resistant to replay, for example with nonces or challenges. SC-23 protects the authenticity of sessions against false or replayed information inserted into them.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for replay protection on every request the application accepts, such as API calls from other systems. Use one-time identifiers or message authentication codes on those requests as well as at sign-in.

clauses.title: Error-handling routines
clauses.rationale: SC-24 makes the application fail to a known state when defined failures occur. SI-10(03) makes it behave predictably when invalid input arrives. SI-11 generates error messages that give the information needed for corrective action.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to handle each exception close to its source and to add a general routine that catches unexpected errors. Write both into your coding standards and test them.

clauses.title: Disabling output of sensitive data in error messages
clauses.title_de: Deaktivierung der Ausgabe schützenswerter Daten durch Fehlermeldungen
clauses.rationale: SI-11 keeps exploitable information out of error messages and reveals them to defined roles only. IA-06 obscures feedback during authentication, so a failed sign-in keeps secret whether the account exists.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Password hashing
clauses.rationale: IA-05(01) has the application store passwords with an approved salted key derivation function, the hash and salt GS++ asks for. SC-13 implements approved cryptography for the hash itself.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Informing users about security-critical events
clauses.rationale: AC-09 tells users about their previous logon when they next sign in. AC-09(03) reports changes to the security settings of their account, and AC-09(04) adds details such as a new location or device.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to alert users when the event happens, for example by email after a password reset or a sign-in from a new device. AC-09 notifies them at their next logon.

clauses.title: Integrating external software from trusted sources
clauses.rationale: CM-10(01) restricts the use of open-source software. SA-09 holds providers of external services and interfaces to the organisation's security requirements. SR-04 documents where each component comes from, so unknown sources show up. SR-05 uses acquisition methods that keep out risky components, and SR-06 assesses suppliers and the components they provide.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to forbid components and interfaces from unreliable or unknown sources. Decide which sources you trust, and make your provenance and supplier checks block the rest.

clauses.title: Software components (software bill of materials)
clauses.rationale: CM-08 keeps an inventory of software components at the level of detail needed, which is what a software bill of materials holds. SR-04 documents the provenance of each component, including its composition and dependencies.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a software bill of materials before each release, in a format such as BSI TR-03183-2. Produce it from your CM-08 inventory, for example with software composition analysis in your build pipeline.

clauses.title: Integrity of external software
clauses.rationale: SI-07(06) and (15) check external artifacts with cryptography, such as hashes and signatures. SR-04(03) validates that components are genuine and unaltered. SR-10 inspects components to detect tampering, such as injected malicious code. SR-11 detects and prevents counterfeit components.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Security updates for external software
clauses.rationale: RA-05 scans the application and its components for known vulnerabilities, as software composition analysis does. SA-15(07) has the developer run automated vulnerability analysis. SI-02 identifies flaws and installs the security updates for bundled components, which GS++ asks for before each release.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Compiler options for security functions
clauses.rationale: SA-15 documents the development tools with their options and configurations, and reviews them. SI-16 protects memory from unauthorised code execution, which compiler options such as stack canaries and control-flow integrity provide.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to switch on the compiler's security options before each release, and the matching options for interpreted languages. Make them part of the tool settings you document under SA-15.

clauses.title: Deterministic binary code (reproducible builds)
clauses.rationale: SA-10(04) compares newly generated object code with earlier versions, and SA-10(05) keeps the build data tied to the master copies. SA-15 documents the tools, options and configurations used to build the software, which describes the build environment.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks for a documented build that turns the same source into bit-for-bit identical binaries. Describe the build environment exactly and remove variable inputs, such as timestamps.

clauses.title: Documenting default credentials
clauses.rationale: SA-05 has administrator documentation describe secure installation and configuration, including any default credentials. IA-05(05) has developers supply unique authenticators or change the defaults before delivery.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Default settings that follow security by default
clauses.title_de: Voreinstellungen nach dem Prinzip "Security by Default"
clauses.rationale: SA-04(05) has the product delivered with its security configurations set as the default. SA-08(23) applies the secure defaults principle to the configuration the product ships with.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Logging code changes
clauses.rationale: CM-03 documents change decisions and keeps records of each change for a set period. SA-10 documents and controls changes to configuration items such as source code.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks each record to show the time, the content, the author and the reason for the change. Set your version control and change records to capture all four.

clauses.title: Testing source code changes
clauses.rationale: CM-03(02) tests, validates and documents changes before they go live. CM-04 analyses each change for its security impact, and CM-04(01) does so in a separate test environment. SA-11 has the developer run unit, integration, system and regression tests, with static and dynamic analysis under SA-11(01) and (08).
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Committing to a period for security updates
clauses.rationale: SA-22 deals with components whose developer or vendor has stopped supplying patches and updates. A committed update period makes that end of support known in advance.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to commit to security updates for a minimum period, counted from a set date such as first release. Set this commitment for each product yourself.

clauses.title: Informing customers of the update period
clauses.rationale: SA-05 has the developer provide documentation for users and administrators. That documentation can state how long the product receives security updates and how customers obtain them.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to tell customers how long you will supply security updates and how they get them. Put both in the documentation you deliver under SA-05.

clauses.title: Integrity checks for installation and update files
clauses.rationale: SA-10(01) has the developer enable integrity verification of software and updates, such as published hashes, and SA-10(06) makes distributed updates match the master copies. SA-05 user documentation explains how to use security functions, such as checking a file's integrity.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to publish checksums over an authenticated channel, such as a website with an X.509 certificate. Tell users there how to check installation, update and patch files.

clauses.title: Approval for use under change and test procedures
clauses.rationale: CM-03 reviews proposed changes, approves or rejects them and implements only the approved ones. SA-10 has the developer implement only changes the organisation has approved, so each release goes into use with an authorisation.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Secure deployment
clauses.rationale: CM-03 implements approved changes in production under change control, and CM-03(03) automates their deployment. SA-10 has the developer perform configuration management during implementation and operation of the system.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than GS++. Check the controls against BSI's wording.

clauses.title: Certificate monitoring for the application's domains
clauses.rationale: SC-17 obtains certificates under a certificate policy or from approved providers, so a certificate from anywhere else stands out. SI-04 monitors for indicators of attack, which can include new certificates for the organisation's domains in Certificate Transparency logs.
clauses.gaps: GS++ asks you to watch Certificate Transparency logs for new certificates issued for every domain the application uses. Add those logs to the sources your SI-04 monitoring covers.
